Course Introduction

Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc.

Event Insurance
Checklist

Planning, Completing, and Submitting Chapter Events Correctly

13 Modules · Knowledge Checks · Scenarios · Final Exam · Certificate

"Good event planning begins before the checklist is submitted. The checklist documents how the chapter has identified, planned for, controlled, and transferred event-related risks."

Course Premise

Brother, most Event Insurance Checklists that get returned are not returned because the chapter did something wrong at the event. They are returned because the chapter tried to describe an event that had not actually been planned yet. Boxes were checked that nobody could support. Fields were left blank because nobody had gathered the information. A contract was referenced but never collected. A flyer said one thing and the submission said another.

This course fixes that at the source. It walks the entire Event Insurance Checklist field by field — what each field is asking, why the information is required, where to get it, how to answer it, what an acceptable answer looks like, what an unacceptable answer looks like, and what causes a submission to be kicked back. Then it walks a complete chapter event from concept to submission packet.

The point is not to teach you how to fill out a form. The point is to teach you how to plan an event so that the form can be completed truthfully.

1 of 20

Why Event Insurance Checklists Matter

The checklist is not paperwork that follows a plan. It is the instrument that shapes the plan — and the record that proves the chapter thought before it committed.

⏱ 15 min📚 Foundational
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) state the fourteen purposes the Event Insurance Checklist actually serves; (2) explain why the checklist must guide planning rather than describe it afterward; (3) explain the three pillars of risk management and where the checklist sits in each; (4) identify which events require an Event Notification Form at all.

The Mistake Almost Every Chapter Makes Once

A chapter decides to host a social. The date is set. The venue is booked with a deposit. The DJ is confirmed by text message. The flyer goes up on Instagram. Two weeks out, somebody says, "We have to do the insurance checklist."

Now the Event Chair sits down with the form and discovers the chapter cannot answer it. Nobody asked the venue for a fire-code capacity. Nobody got a certificate of insurance from the DJ. The contract was signed by a brother in his own name. The flyer says "open bar" but the chapter planned BYOB. The checklist becomes an exercise in figuring out what to write rather than a record of what was planned.

That is backwards, and reviewers can tell. The submission comes back. The event date is now inside three weeks. The chapter is scrambling, and the members who did the work feel like the process failed them.

The goal is not to figure out how to answer the checklist after an event has already been planned. The checklist should guide planning before commitments are finalized.

Core Principle of This Course

The Fourteen Purposes of the Checklist

Brothers often describe the checklist as "the insurance form." That is one purpose out of many. Understanding the full set explains why reviewers ask for detail that can feel excessive when you are only thinking about approval.

01

Event Planning

Working the checklist forces the chapter to answer questions that must be answered anyway — who, where, how many, how controlled.

02

Loss Prevention

Keeping foreseeable harm from happening in the first place: capacity limits, age verification, glass restrictions, one controlled entrance.

03

Loss Control

Limiting the size of a loss when something does happen: monitors, security, removal procedures, food and non-alcoholic beverages.

04

Risk Transfer

Moving defined responsibility to parties better positioned to carry it — licensed and insured vendors, venues, contracts, additional-insured status.

05

Documentation

Creating a written record of what the chapter planned, when it planned it, and on what basis.

06

Identification of Responsible Parties

Naming who is accountable — the officers who sign, the event chair, the co-sponsor contact, the vendor representative.

07

Verification of Vendors

Confirming that the people the chapter is paying are licensed, insured, and under written contract.

08

Verification of Insurance

Obtaining certificates of insurance rather than accepting verbal assurances.

09

Attendance Control

Establishing who may attend, how they are invited, how they are tracked, and how the chapter stays within capacity.

10

Alcohol Control

Establishing the alcohol model, age verification, quantity, distribution, and monitoring — or establishing that the event is dry.

11

Safety Planning

Security, chaperones, monitors, emergency access, removal procedures, and prevention plans in writing.

12

Organizational Protection

Protecting the chapter, its officers, and the Fraternity — including protection of the Fraternity's name and image.

13

Event Approval

Completing the Fraternity's Event Approval process, which is a stated condition for coverage to apply to a special event.

14

Record Retention

Building the packet the chapter is required to keep — checklists, certificates of insurance, contracts, and agreements.

And One More

Demonstration that the chapter considered foreseeable risks before the event. This is the purpose that matters most if something goes wrong. A completed, detailed, internally consistent checklist submitted before the event is evidence that the chapter thought about what could happen and planned for it. A thin, contradictory, last-minute checklist is evidence of the opposite.

The Three Pillars

The Insurance and Claim Manual states plainly that a successful risk management program is built on three pillars, and that responsibility for success rests with the chapter and its members — not with the insurance carrier and not with International Headquarters.

1

Loss Prevention

Stopping the loss from occurring. Every prevention item on the checklist — capacity, one entrance, guest list, no glass, no drinking-game paraphernalia — is loss prevention.

2

Loss Control

Reducing the severity when something does occur. Monitors who can spot a problem early, security who can respond, a plan for removing someone with illegal drugs, food and water available so people are not drinking on an empty stomach.

3

Risk Transfer (Insurance)

Contractually and financially shifting defined risk to parties equipped to carry it. Hiring a licensed and insured third-party vendor to serve alcohol transfers a very large exposure. Obtaining additional-insured status extends specified protection. Insurance is the third pillar, not the first.

Why the Order Matters

Insurance is the last line, not the plan. Chapters get into trouble when they treat the checklist as a way to obtain coverage instead of a way to plan a safe event. Coverage under the General Liability policy depends on successfully completing the Fraternity's Event Approval process and on venues and vendors carrying adequate insurance verified by certificate. If the standard is not met, the manual states plainly that there may be no coverage for the chapter, its officers, and potentially the Fraternity.

Kappa Source · Insurance & Claim Manual

Which Events Require a Form?

The Event Notification Form is to be completed for all events defined in the Risk Management Policy as:

Kappa Source — Definition of a Covered Event"Any activity or event sponsored or endorsed by the chapter, including those that occur on or off chapter or member premises."

Read that carefully, because brothers routinely misread it in three ways.

"It's not at our facility, so it doesn't count"

The definition expressly includes events that occur off chapter or member premises. A rented ballroom, a park, a restaurant, a community center, or a member's home are all inside the definition when the event is sponsored or endorsed by the chapter.

"It's not an official chapter event, brothers just organized it"

The word is endorsed, not just "sponsored." If the chapter's name, letters, crest, or social media are attached to it; if chapter funds or chapter channels were used; if it is being held out to the public as a chapter function — it is inside the definition regardless of how informally it started.

Note the flip side, which cuts against the chapter: the manual is explicit that a member acting outside his responsibility or outside Fraternity policy — for example a "spontaneous social function planned by an individual member" — is not an insured. Brothers sometimes assume an unapproved event is covered because they are members. It is not.

"There's no alcohol, so there's nothing to report"

The definition is not limited to social events with alcohol. A dry event still involves a venue, a crowd, capacity, possibly vendors, possibly a co-sponsor, and possibly a promoter. A scholarship banquet, a step show, a health fair, a community-service day, a fundraiser — all of them are activities or events sponsored or endorsed by the chapter.

Timing

The Event Notification Form is to be submitted to International Headquarters 21 days prior to the event.

Kappa Source · Insurance & Claim Manual

Twenty-one days is the submission deadline, not the start date for planning. Working backwards from it is the single most useful scheduling habit an event chair can build:

  1. Day 21 — SubmitThe complete packet goes in: checklist, contracts, certificates of insurance, and the final flyer.
  2. Day 28–24 — Internal reviewOfficers who must sign review the packet, check it for contradictions, and confirm every checked box can be supported.
  3. Day 45–30 — Documentation collectionCertificates of insurance requested and received, contracts executed in the chapter name, venue capacity confirmed in writing, security arrangement confirmed.
  4. Day 60–45 — CommitmentsVenue and vendors selected; contracts reviewed before anyone signs or pays a deposit.
  5. Day 90–60 — ConceptEvent concept, alcohol model, attendance model, and budget decided. This is when the checklist should first come out — as a planning document.
Practical Tip

Print a blank checklist at the first planning meeting and assign each section to a named brother. Do not wait until submission week to discover that no one owns "certificate of insurance."

▶ Scenario — Sequencing

A chapter's event committee meets nine weeks out and decides on a scholarship social at a hotel. The Event Chair says: "Let's lock the hotel this week so we get the date, then we'll do the checklist when we get closer."

What is wrong with that sequence, and what should happen instead?

Signing the venue agreement first surrenders the chapter's leverage on everything the checklist will later ask about. Once the contract is signed and the deposit is paid, the chapter can no longer negotiate the insurance provisions, the additional-insured requirement, the security arrangement, or the alcohol terms — it can only discover them.

The correct sequence is to bring the blank checklist to that same meeting and treat it as the venue-selection instrument. Before signing: ask for the fire-code capacity in writing; ask whether the venue will contract in the chapter name of the national Fraternity; ask for the venue's certificate of insurance and confirm the limits; ask whether the venue requires an additional insured and, if so, the exact legal entity name; ask what security the venue provides and whether it is written into the agreement; ask how alcohol is handled and whether the venue's bar is a licensed and insured third-party vendor. Then sign.

Locking the date is not worth losing the ability to answer the form truthfully.

Knowledge Check

Orientation · Question 1

A chapter plans a dry community-service cookout at a public park. The Event Chair says the checklist is unnecessary because there is no alcohol and no rented venue. The best response is:

✓ Correct answer: C. The definition is "any activity or event sponsored or endorsed by the chapter, including those that occur on or off chapter or member premises." It is not limited by alcohol, by venue type, or by whether the location is owned. A dry cookout still involves attendance, capacity, possible vendors, and possible co-sponsors. If you chose A or B, the trap is reading the definition as being about alcohol or ownership; it is about sponsorship and endorsement. If you chose D, permits matter but they are not what triggers the notification requirement.
Orientation · Question 2

Which statement best describes the relationship between the checklist and the chapter's event plan?

✓ Correct answer: B. Every field on the checklist asks about a decision that has to be made anyway — capacity, attendance control, vendors, alcohol, security. Making those decisions in the order the checklist asks about them, before contracts are signed, is what makes the answers truthful and the packet complete. If you chose A, that is the common practice that produces returned submissions. If you chose C, the checklist is an event-planning instrument as much as an insurance one. If you chose D, the checklist has value at planning, approval, and record-retention stages regardless of whether anything goes wrong.
Orientation · Question 3

Which of the following is the strongest reason a reviewer needs operational detail rather than just checked boxes?

✓ Correct answer: D. Checking "Venue is properly licensed" states that the chapter believes it to be true. The reviewer's job — and the chapter's protection — depends on there being a real basis for that statement. Detail is how the chapter demonstrates the basis. A, B, and C describe motives that do not exist.

Sources & Authority

Which documents this course draws on, what weight each one carries, and how to read the labels you will see throughout the modules.

⏱ 10 min📑 Reference
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) identify the three source documents behind this course and the weight each carries; (2) recognize the four source labels used in the modules; (3) explain why a Holmes Murphy template recommendation is not automatically a Kappa Alpha Psi requirement; (4) explain why the truncated field labels are preserved exactly as written.

The Sources

1

Kappa Alpha Psi Insurance and Claim Manual, 2020–2021

Prepared for Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. by Holmes Murphy Fraternal Practice. It contains the Undergraduate Event Notification Form, the Alumni Event Notification Form, the insurance program overview, the vendor and third-party requirements, the BYOB procedures, the promoter provisions, the Prevention Ideas list, and the Additional Insured Request procedure.

This is the most recent official Fraternity manual available to the chapter, and this course treats it as the controlling Kappa Alpha Psi source. Where the online checklist shows a truncated field, this manual usually supplies the complete original wording.

2

The online Event Insurance Checklist

The live submission form. Its field labels are the exact text a brother sees on screen — including labels that are truncated or contain typographical artifacts. Those labels are reproduced in this course exactly as they appear, and are never rewritten.

3

Holmes Murphy Fraternal Practice 2026 Risk Management Policy Template

A template. Holmes Murphy states directly that it offers these policy examples "due to client requests for guidance and to provoke thought and discussion," that it "should not be viewed as a mandate or requirement," and that whether an organization adopts any of it "is made at the sole discretion of your organization."

It is used in this course as supplemental risk-management education only, and every time it is used it is labeled.

Source Authority Hierarchy

RankSourceWeight in this course
1Current adopted Kappa Alpha Psi policy and procedureControlling. If the chapter has newer adopted guidance than the material below, that guidance controls.
2Kappa Alpha Psi Insurance and Claim Manual and the Event Notification Forms it containsControlling Kappa source for this course — the last official Fraternity manual available.
3The online Event Insurance Checklist field labelsAuthoritative for wording. What the form says is what the form says.
4Holmes Murphy 2026 TemplateSupplemental education only. Never presented as a Kappa requirement.
When Sources Differ

This course does not silently merge sources and does not guess. Where the template says something the Kappa source does not, the difference is stated openly and the template item is labeled as supplemental. Where the online form's truncated label could be misread, both the system wording and the fuller Kappa source wording are shown side by side.

The Four Labels

Label 1

Kappa Source

Drawn from the Kappa Alpha Psi Insurance and Claim Manual and the Event Notification Forms. Treat these as Fraternity requirements.

Label 2

Supplemental

Holmes Murphy 2026 Template guidance. Educationally valuable, but not adopted Kappa Alpha Psi policy unless your chapter's current adopted policy says so.

Label 3

Training Guidance

Instructional material written for this course — worked examples, sample formats, acceptable/unacceptable illustrations. Good practice; not quoted policy language.

Label 4

Verify Before Submission

Used where the online form contains a field that no available source explains. The course describes the practical purpose and tells you to confirm the current requirement rather than inventing one.

Template-Only Provisions — Read This Carefully

The following appear in the Holmes Murphy 2026 template and are not presented in this course as Kappa Alpha Psi requirements. Several of them are excellent practice. That is a different claim from "policy requires it," and brothers should not tell a venue, a co-sponsor, or a chapter meeting that Kappa requires something it does not.

3:1 guest-to-member ratio

Supplemental · Holmes Murphy 2026 Template

The template states that attendance at events with alcohol is limited to a guest-to-member ratio not to exceed 3:1, and then says directly: "The 3:1 guest-to-member ratio is an NIC Guideline. Other clients may choose to only enforce building code capacity or adjust the ratio."

What the Kappa source requires instead: attendance by non-members at all events must be by invitation only; the chapter must use a system to track attendees; and attendance must not exceed local fire or building code capacity. There is no member-ratio requirement in the Kappa source.

How to use it: as a planning sanity check. If twelve brothers are hosting 400 guests, the ratio is telling you something real about whether your monitors and guest-list controls are adequate — even though it is not a Kappa rule.

15% alcohol-by-volume restriction

Supplemental · Holmes Murphy 2026 Template

The template contains a provision addressed to "NIC Organizations and for consideration by other clients": alcohol products above 15% ABV prohibited on organizational premises or at any event, except when served by a licensed and insured third-party vendor.

What the Kappa source does instead: the Event Notification Form asks the chapter to state how many drinks each person of legal drinking age may bring, broken out by type — beer, wine coolers, ciders, wine, malt beverages, hard liquor, other. That structure controls quantity by category rather than by ABV threshold.

Substance-free new-member events

Supplemental · Holmes Murphy 2026 Template

The template states that any event or activity related to the new-member joining process must be substance free, with no alcohol or drugs present at new-member activities, meetings, or initiation.

Note: Kappa Alpha Psi's own membership-intake and conduct standards govern intake conduct, and the Insurance and Claim Manual makes coverage contingent on following the Fraternity's Risk Management and Member Intake Policies. Follow the Fraternity's intake policy on this point — the template is being cited here only because the master source list asked that template-only provisions be identified.

Overnight events, advisor attendance, event-partner restrictions, retaliation options

Supplemental · Holmes Murphy 2026 Template

The template's "Additional Policies from Holmes Murphy Clients" section contains sample language on overnight events with non-members, advisors attending undergraduate events where alcohol is present, restrictions on hosting with suspended organizations, and three alternative retaliation clauses. These are drafting options offered to client organizations. They are not Kappa Alpha Psi requirements, and this course does not treat them as such.

Where Template and Kappa Source Agree

Several template provisions restate what the Kappa source already requires: comply with all applicable law and the legal drinking age; no illegal drugs or controlled substances; alcohol either sold per-drink by a licensed and insured third-party vendor or brought individually under BYOB; no common sources of alcohol not served by a licensed and insured third party; no purchasing alcohol with organizational funds or pooled funds; no co-hosting with a group that purchases or provides alcohol or drugs; no drinking games or other rapid-consumption activity; invitation-only attendance with a guest-list system; and no strippers or exotic dancers. Where they agree, the Kappa source is cited.

Why Truncated Field Labels Are Preserved

The online checklist displays labels that are cut off mid-word or mid-sentence, and at least one contains a typographical artifact. Examples: Companies Promoter Describ Id method for legal drinking age prevent plans_L1 Vendor Contract Long Additional Attachments Long

This course reproduces those labels exactly. It does not correct, complete, modernize, or clean them up. There are two reasons.

  1. You have to find them on screen. If this course renamed "Describ Id method for legal drinking age" to something grammatical, a brother searching the live form would not find the field.
  2. Truncation causes real misreadings. "No tables or paraphernalia" reads as though the chapter cannot use tables. "Event does not involve physical activi" reads as though nobody may move. Both are wrong, and the Kappa source supplies the complete wording that resolves them.

Wherever the Kappa source establishes the complete original meaning of a truncated field, this course shows both:

System FieldNo tables or paraphernalia
Source Explanation — Kappa Source"No tables or paraphernalia will be used for drinking games."
Rule for Brothers

Never substitute your own interpretation for the system field. When you brief your committee, read the system wording out loud, then read the source wording. If a field is truncated and no source completes it, say so and ask before you check the box.

What This Course Will Not Do

  • It will not invent insurance limits, deadlines, personnel, or contact information beyond what the sources contain.
  • It will not invent functionality for a registration platform that the sources do not describe.
  • It will not present a Holmes Murphy template recommendation as adopted Kappa Alpha Psi policy.
  • It will not rewrite a truncated system label.
  • It will not tell you that checking a box establishes compliance. A checked box is a representation you must be able to support.
  • It will not tell you to block, lock, or obstruct an emergency exit.
  • It will not give legal advice or guarantee that any particular loss will be covered.
A Note on Figures and Names

The Kappa source is the 2020–2021 edition of the manual. Its structural requirements — 21-day submission, minimum vendor limits, additional insured on a primary basis, the BYOB control procedures, the Prevention Ideas list — are used throughout this course as the Fraternity's requirements. Individual staff names, phone extensions, and stated policy-period dates belong to that edition; confirm the current routing address before you send a packet, and let the chapter's current officers tell you where submissions go today.

Knowledge Check

Sources · Question 1

At a chapter meeting, a brother states: "Kappa requires a 3:1 guest-to-member ratio at any event with alcohol." What is the accurate correction?

✓ Correct answer: B. The template itself identifies the 3:1 ratio as an NIC guideline that client organizations may adjust or decline to enforce. The Kappa source requires invitation-only attendance for non-members, a system to track attendees, and attendance within local fire or building code capacity. Stating a template guideline as a Fraternity requirement misinforms your chapter and can create friction with venues and co-sponsors. It remains a useful planning sanity check — just not a rule.
Sources · Question 2

The online form shows the field Event does not involve physical activi. An event chair concludes the chapter cannot hold a step show because stepping is physical activity. The correct analysis is:

✓ Correct answer: C. The Kappa source Prevention Ideas list reads "Event does not involve physical activity (assault and battery)." The concern is fighting and physical confrontation, not performance or ordinary movement. This is exactly why the course shows the system field and the source wording together — and exactly why you should never act on a truncated label alone. Answer B is the habit that produces contradictory submissions.
Sources · Question 3

Which of these is correctly labeled?

✓ Correct answer: A. That language comes directly from the Kappa Event Notification Form's Attendance section. B is the Holmes Murphy template's ABV provision, offered for consideration. C and D come from the template's "Additional Policies from Holmes Murphy Clients" section — sample language from other client organizations, not Kappa requirements. Mislabeling a source is how a chapter ends up enforcing a rule that does not exist while missing one that does.

Event Location / Details

Where the event happens determines who controls the premises, what contracts exist, whose insurance responds, and how nearly every later section of the checklist must be answered.

⏱ 20 min📍 5 fields
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) classify an event location correctly among the four checklist options; (2) explain how location changes venue responsibility, contracting, insurance, security, capacity, access, alcohol procedure, additional-insured needs, and emergency planning; (3) complete the "Other" description field so a reviewer can evaluate it; (4) recognize the location-related answers that get submissions returned.

Why the First Section Sets Up Everything Else

Brothers tend to treat the location section as a formality — four radio-style boxes and a text field. It is actually the section that determines what the rest of your packet must contain.

Choose "Rented Facility" and you have just committed the chapter to producing a venue contract, a venue certificate of insurance, a capacity figure, and probably an additional-insured discussion. Choose "Member(s) Residence" and you have committed to a completely different set of questions about premises control, access, parking, neighbors, and who is responsible if a guest is hurt on a staircase. The location answer is a promise about what documentation follows.

Kappa Source — Event Notification Form, Location of eventLocation of event. Include name of venue, address of event, contact information. ☐ Chapter Property (Either fraternity or university owned) ☐ Rented Facility (Hotel, Restaurant, etc.) ☐ Member(s) Residence ☐ Other:

Note what the Kappa source asks for beyond the checkbox: name of venue, address, and contact information. On the Alumni form these are broken out into separate lines — venue name, venue address, venue contact name, venue contact phone, venue contact email. Even where the online checklist gives you fewer boxes, that is the information a reviewer needs. Put it in the description field rather than leaving the reviewer to guess.

The Four Location Types, Field by Field

Chapter Property (Either fraternity or
System FieldChapter Property (Either fraternity or
Source Explanation — Kappa Source"Chapter Property (Either fraternity or university owned)"

What it means. The event will occur on property owned or controlled by the chapter or the Fraternity, or — in the complete undergraduate wording — owned by the university. The online label is cut off after "fraternity or"; the missing word is "university."

Why it matters. On chapter or university property, the chapter is much closer to being the party in control of the premises. There is often no third-party venue standing between the chapter and an injured guest. That changes several things at once: there may be no venue contract to rely on, no venue security to point to, no venue staff enforcing capacity, and no venue insurance responding first. Premises-liability exposure sits closer to home. If the space is university-owned, the university's facility-use rules and campus policies also apply — and the Kappa source notes that when a host institution's health-and-safety rules conflict with the Fraternity's, the Fraternity's rule controls for insurance purposes.

How to complete it.

  1. Confirm who actually owns and controls the space — chapter, house corporation, Fraternity entity, or university. Do not assume.
  2. If university-owned, obtain the facility reservation or use agreement and read its requirements. Universities frequently require insurance certificates, additional-insured status, and their own event registration.
  3. Obtain the posted occupancy load for the specific room, not the building.
  4. Identify who will control entry, since there is no venue staff doing it for you.
  5. Identify emergency exits and confirm they will remain clear and usable throughout.
  6. Enter venue name, address, and a contact person in the details field even though you own or control it — a reviewer still needs to know where this is.
Acceptable

"Chapter meeting hall, 1420 Elm Street, Denton TX. Posted occupancy 120 (room placard photographed and attached). Facility contact: Bro. J. Rivers, House Corporation, (940) 555-0142. Single controlled entry at the front door; rear door remains an unobstructed emergency exit and is not used for admission."

Not Acceptable

"Our house." No address, no capacity, no contact, no entry plan. A reviewer cannot evaluate a location that has not been identified.

Example. A chapter holds an interest meeting in a university-owned multipurpose room. The chapter checks Chapter Property, enters the building and room number and the campus scheduling office contact, attaches the room-reservation confirmation showing the 90-person occupancy, and notes that campus policy requires the event to end by 11:00 PM.

Common kickback reasons.

  • Box checked but no venue name or address supplied.
  • Capacity left blank because "it's our own space."
  • University-owned space claimed as chapter property with no facility-use agreement attached.
  • Entry control unaddressed because the chapter assumed no one else would come.

Documentation to have ready. Facility-use or reservation agreement if university-owned; posted occupancy load; any campus event-registration approval; house-corporation approval if applicable.

Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "It's our own property, so there's nothing to document."
Fact: Owning or controlling the premises increases the chapter's direct responsibility. It does not reduce the documentation the checklist asks for — it removes the third party who would otherwise have been carrying some of it.

Rented Facility (Hotel, Restaurant, etc)
System FieldRented Facility (Hotel, Restaurant, etc)

What it means. The chapter is using a hotel ballroom, restaurant, banquet hall, event center, community center, union hall, or similar rented location.

Why it matters. Renting introduces another party into the event, and the Kappa source is direct about what follows: all venues and vendors used to host chapter events must carry adequate insurance, and the chapter must verify it by obtaining a certificate of insurance. This is also where contract terms start to matter — who signs, in whose name, what the venue promises, what the venue disclaims, and what the venue requires from the chapter in return.

Kappa Source · Special Events & Adding Additional Insureds

How to complete it.

  1. Check the box and enter the venue's legal name, full street address, and a named contact with phone and email.
  2. Obtain the fire-code capacity for the specific room you are renting, in writing.
  3. Obtain the venue's certificate of insurance and confirm the coverage is in force on the event date.
  4. Confirm the contract will be executed in the chapter name of the national Fraternity — not in a brother's personal name.
  5. Determine what the venue provides: security, staffing, bar service, setup, cleanup. Get it in the agreement, not in conversation.
  6. Determine whether the venue requires additional-insured status and, if so, capture the exact legal entity name from the contract.
  7. Walk the space and identify entrances, exits, and where a controlled admission point will be.
Acceptable

"Grandview Hotel & Conference Center, Magnolia Ballroom, 2900 Corporate Drive, Lewisville TX 75057. Contact: Dana Whitfield, Catering Sales Manager, (972) 555-0188, dwhitfield@grandviewhotel.example. Fire-code capacity 350 for banquet seating, confirmed in writing by the venue on the signed banquet event order. Certificate of insurance received, coverage in force through the event date."

Not Acceptable

"Hotel downtown." Also not acceptable: naming the hotel but supplying no capacity, no contact, and no certificate of insurance because "it's a big chain, they're obviously covered."

Example. An alumni chapter books a hotel ballroom for a scholarship social. The Keeper of Records checks Rented Facility, enters the full venue block, attaches the signed banquet event order showing capacity, and attaches the hotel's certificate of insurance. Because the hotel's contract requires the chapter to name the hotel entity as an additional insured, that requirement is carried forward into the Additional Insured Request section rather than being handled informally.

Common kickback reasons.

  • Venue named but no certificate of insurance attached.
  • Certificate attached but the policy period does not cover the event date.
  • Capacity field blank or a guess.
  • Contract signed by an individual member rather than executed in the chapter name of the national Fraternity.
  • The chapter states "the venue handles security" without identifying who, how many, or where that commitment appears in writing.

Documentation to have ready. Executed venue contract or banquet event order; venue certificate of insurance; written capacity confirmation; any venue additional-insured requirement; venue security arrangement in writing.

Red Flag

If the venue will not put its capacity, its security commitment, or its insurance in writing, stop. A venue that will not document what it provides is a venue whose promises the chapter cannot support on the checklist — and cannot rely on afterward.

Member(s) Residence
System FieldMember(s) Residence

What it means. The event will occur at a residence belonging to a member.

Why it matters. A private residence is not a commercial venue. There is no professional staff, no posted occupancy load, no trained security, no commercial general liability policy behind the premises, and usually no contract. Homeowner's or renter's insurance is not written to respond to an organizational event, and the member personally may be exposed in ways he has not considered. Access control is harder: houses have multiple doors, yards, driveways, stairs, pools, and neighbors.

The event is still inside the notification requirement — the Kappa definition expressly includes events occurring on member premises.

How to complete it.

  1. Check the box and enter the address and the member's name and contact information as the responsible party.
  2. Establish a realistic maximum occupancy for the space and write it down. A residence has no posted fire-code placard, so the chapter must reason it out: usable interior area, exits, seating, and whether the event spills outdoors.
  3. Identify the single controlled admission point — and confirm every other exit stays available for emergency egress.
  4. Address parking and neighbor impact before the event, not during it.
  5. Identify specific hazards: stairs, balconies, pools, hot tubs, fire pits, unfenced yards.
  6. Make the alcohol model explicit and controlled. A residence is exactly where common-source alcohol shows up if nobody plans against it.
  7. Assign monitors by zone, since there is no venue staff.
Acceptable

"Residence of Bro. A. Coleman, 812 Hickory Lane, Denton TX. Planned maximum occupancy 60 based on usable interior space; guest list capped at 55. Admission at front door only; side and patio doors remain unobstructed emergency exits and are staffed by monitors to prevent entry. Pool gate locked and taped off for the duration; no pool access. Two monitors assigned to the patio zone."

Not Acceptable

"Brother's house, invite only." No address, no responsible party, no occupancy figure, no hazard plan, no admission control. Also not acceptable: "capacity — N/A, it's a house."

Example. A chapter holds a small alumni-undergraduate mixer at a member's home. The chapter enters the address and the member's contact information, sets a planned occupancy of 60, uses a numbered-invitation system capped at 55, locks the pool gate, and assigns four monitors — one at the door, one in the main room, one at the patio, one at the beverage station.

Common kickback reasons.

  • Capacity left blank on the theory that residences have no capacity.
  • No responsible member identified.
  • Alcohol answers that describe an uncontrolled house party rather than a controlled BYOB event.
  • Guest-management system described as "word of mouth."

Documentation to have ready. Written occupancy reasoning; the guest list or invitation system; the monitor assignment plan; the member's acknowledgment that he is the responsible resident.

Practical Tip

Have an honest conversation with the member whose home it is. He is putting his residence, and potentially his own insurance and personal assets, behind the event. If he is not comfortable enforcing a guest list at his own front door, choose another location.

Red Flag

"It's just going to be a few people, it's not really an event." If the chapter is organizing it, promoting it in chapter channels, or holding it out as a chapter function, it is an event. Informality is not an exemption — and the manual is explicit that a spontaneous social function planned by an individual member falls outside the definition of an insured.

Other (event Details)
System FieldOther (event Details)

What it means. None of the three named categories accurately describes the location.

Why it matters. "Other" by itself tells a reviewer nothing. The chapter still has to identify the nature of the location so the event can be evaluated. This is one of the most common causes of a returned submission across the entire form — an "Other" box checked with an empty or one-word description field.

How to complete it. Check the box only when the location genuinely does not fit, then complete the description field fully. Common true "Other" locations include a public park, a city or county community center, a church fellowship hall, a school or district facility, a golf course, a bowling or entertainment center, a fairground, an outdoor lot, a private club, or a virtual or hybrid event.

Practical Tip

Before checking "Other," ask whether the location is really a rented facility. A community center you reserve and pay for, a church hall with a use agreement, or a park requiring a paid permit generally behave like rented facilities: there is an owner, an agreement, a capacity, and often an insurance requirement. Choosing "Rented Facility" and describing it accurately is usually better than choosing "Other."

Other Event (Describe):
System FieldOther Event (Describe):

What it means. The narrative description of the "Other" location or arrangement.

Why it matters. Checking "Other" alone does not give a reviewer enough information to evaluate the location and its associated risks. This field is where the chapter demonstrates that it actually understands the space it has chosen.

How to complete it. Write four things: what the location is, who owns or controls it, what agreement or permit governs the chapter's use, and what the capacity or occupancy limit is. Add access and weather considerations for outdoor locations.

Acceptable

"City of Denton — North Lakes Park, Pavilion 3, 2001 W. Windsor Drive. Reserved through Denton Parks and Recreation under permit #PR-24-1188 (attached); permit states pavilion capacity 150 and requires the reservation holder to provide proof of liability insurance. Restrooms on site. Event is outdoors; rain date is the following Saturday, same permit. City requires all trash removed by 8:00 PM."

Acceptable

"Mount Zion Baptist Church Fellowship Hall, 505 Oak Street. Use agreement signed with the church office (attached); posted occupancy 200; church requires a certificate of insurance naming the church as additional insured and prohibits alcohol on the premises — this is a dry event."

Not Acceptable

"Outside." / "Community center." / "TBD." / "Various." / A blank field with the Other box checked.

Example. A chapter co-hosts a health fair at a community recreation center. It checks Other and writes: "Lewisville Recreation Center, Gymnasium A, 1950 S. Valley Parkway. Reserved through the City of Lewisville; facility use agreement attached. Posted occupancy 400. City requires a certificate of insurance listing the City of Lewisville as additional insured; that request appears in the Additional Insured Request section of this checklist. Event is dry; no alcohol permitted on city property."

Common kickback reasons.

  • Box checked, description blank — the single most frequent "Other" failure on the entire form.
  • Description names a place but not the owner, the agreement, or the capacity.
  • Description contradicts another section — for example an outdoor park described here while the alcohol section describes a controlled indoor distribution center.
  • Permit referenced but not attached.

Documentation to have ready. Park or facility permit; use agreement; posted or stated occupancy; any insurance or additional-insured requirement imposed by the owner; rain plan for outdoor events.

How Location Changes the Rest of the Packet

 Chapter / University PropertyRented FacilityMember ResidencePark / Community Center
Who controls premisesChapter, house corporation, or universityVenue, subject to the contractThe memberThe municipality or owner
ContractFacility-use agreement if university-ownedYes — must be executed in the chapter name of the national FraternityUsually none; chapter should document responsibilities anywayPermit or use agreement
Certificate of insuranceFrom the university if it is a separate entityRequired from the venueNot available from a homeowner's policy for an org eventOften required by the owner from the chapter
SecurityChapter must arrangeMay be venue-provided — get it in writingChapter must arrangeChapter must arrange; some permits require paid officers
CapacityPosted occupancy for the roomFire-code capacity from the venue in writingChapter must reason it out and document itStated on the permit or posted
Access controlChapter monitorsShared with venue staff — define the splitHardest case; multiple doors and outdoor areasOpen public space is the hardest to control
Alcohol procedureBYOB controls apply if alcohol is presentVenue bar may be the licensed and insured third-party vendorBYOB controls apply; common source is the live riskFrequently prohibited outright by the owner
Additional insuredUniversity may require itVenue frequently requires itRarely applicableMunicipality frequently requires it
Emergency planningChapter knows the buildingAsk the venue for its emergency procedureChapter must map exits itselfWeather, distance from medical services, restroom access
The Pattern Worth Memorizing

The more the chapter controls the premises, the more of the risk the chapter carries directly and the more it must document itself. The more a professional venue controls the premises, the more the chapter must verify — contracts, certificates, capacity, and security commitments in writing. Neither direction is "safer." They require different work.

Scenarios

▶ Scenario — Venue Insurance

A chapter rents a hotel ballroom. The Event Chair says: "The hotel is a national chain, so we know they're insured. I'm checking the insurance box and moving on."

What should happen before that box is checked?

The chapter must obtain the certificate of insurance and read it. The Kappa source is explicit: all venues and vendors used to host chapter events must carry adequate insurance, and the chapter must verify this by obtaining a certificate of insurance. Reputation is not verification.

Reading it means checking four things: the named insured matches the entity in the contract; the carrier's A.M. Best rating is not less than A-, VII; the coverage is in force on the event date and does not expire or cancel before it; and the limits meet the required minimums — General Liability each occurrence $1,000,000, general aggregate $2,000,000, products/completed operations $2,000,000, and liquor liability $300,000 each common cause and $300,000 aggregate where alcohol is involved.

A certificate that arrives with an expiration date one week before the event is worse than no certificate, because the chapter now knows and has represented otherwise.

▶ Scenario — Late Venue Change

The checklist was submitted twenty-one days out for a rented restaurant. Eight days before the event, the restaurant loses power and cancels. A brother offers his home instead. The Event Chair says the submission is already approved so nothing needs to change.

Is that correct?

No. The approval attaches to the event that was described. Moving from a rented restaurant to a member residence changes the location category, the premises control, the capacity basis, the security arrangement, the alcohol model, the vendor picture, and probably the guest count. The venue contract and certificate of insurance in the packet now describe a venue that is not hosting the event.

The chapter must notify and resubmit with the corrected information. It must also review the flyer, because the flyer now advertises the wrong address — and a flyer that contradicts the submitted event is itself a returned-submission trigger.

The harder question is whether the chapter can actually execute the residence version safely in eight days: occupancy reasoning, monitor assignments, hazard control, and a guest list sized to a house rather than a restaurant. If it cannot, the right answer is to postpone. Moving an event to a location the chapter has not planned for is how incidents happen.

Knowledge Check

Module 1 · Question 1

A chapter reserves a city park pavilion under a paid permit that states an occupancy of 150 and requires proof of liability insurance. On the checklist, the best handling is:

✓ Correct answer: B. Whether you classify a permitted park pavilion as "Rented Facility" or "Other," the reviewer needs the same four things: what the location is, who controls it, what agreement governs the chapter's use, and what the capacity is. A is the classic "Other" failure — a checked box with a one-word description. C is wrong because paying a reservation fee does not make municipal property chapter property. D is never correct.
Module 1 · Question 2

Which statement about a member's residence is accurate?

✓ Correct answer: C. The Kappa definition expressly includes events occurring on member premises. Because a residence has no posted occupancy load, the chapter has to reason one out from usable space and exits and write it down — and then size the guest list below it. A misreads the definition. B is wrong: personal homeowner's or renter's coverage is not written to respond to an organizational event and is not a venue certificate. D would leave the chapter with no capacity control at the location type where crowding is hardest to manage.
Module 1 · Question 3

The venue contract for a hotel ballroom is presented for signature to the Event Chair, made out in his personal name. What should he do?

✓ Correct answer: A. The Kappa source asks the chapter to confirm that the contract is executed in the chapter name of the national fraternity, and requires contracts to be signed and dated by the person authorized by the organization. A personally signed contract can leave the brother individually on the hook and undermines the third-party section of the checklist. B assumes a hotel will amend an executed agreement, which it may refuse to do. D is worse than C — it exposes a member with no authority at all.

Co-sponsored Event

When another organization is involved in planning or working your event, its people, its decisions, and its insurance become part of your risk picture — whatever the flyer calls the relationship.

⏱ 20 min🤝 6 fields
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) determine whether a relationship is actually co-sponsorship; (2) distinguish co-sponsor, vendor, promoter, venue, and community partner; (3) complete all five co-sponsor identification fields properly; (4) explain when a co-sponsor's certificate of insurance is required; (5) apply the alcohol restriction on co-sponsorship.

The Question the Form Is Actually Asking

Kappa Source — Event Notification Form, Co-Sponsored Events"Will other organizations (sororities/fraternities/organizations) be involved in planning or working the event?"

Read the test: involved in planning or working the event. Not "listed on the flyer." Not "called a co-sponsor in the group chat." Not "paying half." The test is participation in planning or working.

That is broader than most chapters assume, and it is why brothers get this section wrong in both directions — declaring co-sponsorship where there is none, and failing to declare it where there plainly is.

Required Attachment

The Kappa source lists among the documents to submit with a completed Event Notification Form: "Certificate of Insurance for co-sponsored events with organizations." If you have a co-sponsor, plan on producing its certificate of insurance. Discovering this three days before submission, when the other organization's insurance contact does not answer email, is one of the most common causes of a late or returned packet.

Kappa Source · Step 4: Submit Documents

Five Relationships That Get Confused

Before touching the fields, get the classification right. The same organization can occupy different roles at different events — and occasionally two roles at the same event.

Co-Sponsor

Plans or works the event with you

Another organization shares in planning, decision-making, staffing, or hosting. It has a say in what the event is. Example: a sorority chapter that co-plans a scholarship gala, splits the committee work, and staffs the door with you.

Vendor

You pay it to perform a service

A contracted service provider under your direction: caterer, DJ, security company, transportation, equipment, restroom services. It does not co-decide the event. Example: the DJ you hire for that gala.

Promoter

Produces, promotes, or monetizes the event

An event company or promoter engaged for events such as fundraisers, concerts, and step shows. Has its own operational role and often its own revenue interest. Carries its own licensing and insurance requirements under the Kappa source.

Venue / Third Party

Owns or controls the premises

The hotel, restaurant, hall, or facility hosting the event. May also be the licensed and insured third-party vendor serving alcohol. Governed by the Third Party section of the checklist.

Community Partner

Lends support without planning or working

A group that donates a raffle item, shares a social post, or provides a letter of support — and takes no role in planning or working the event. Often not a co-sponsor. But read the myth below before you conclude that.

Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "If another organization is only helping with promotion, they can never be considered a co-sponsor."
Fact: Evaluate the actual relationship and responsibilities rather than relying on what the flyer calls it. An organization that "only promotes" but also sells tickets, controls part of the guest list, staffs the door, brings its own members as workers, shares in proceeds, or has a voice in event decisions is functionally involved in planning or working the event. Conversely, an organization whose logo appears as a courtesy and which does nothing else may not be a co-sponsor at all — but if its logo is on the flyer, expect a reviewer to ask, and be ready to explain.

Red Flag

If you cannot answer the question "what specifically is the other organization doing?" in one concrete sentence, you do not yet know the relationship well enough to classify it. Ask them directly and write the answer down before you complete this section.

The Alcohol Restriction on Co-Sponsorship

Kappa Source — BYOB provisions"A chapter must not co-host or cosponsor, or in any way participate in, an activity or event with another group or entity that purchases or provides alcohol, illegal drugs or controlled substances."

This is a hard limit, and it catches chapters that think of it only as a drug rule. It also reaches the organization that offers to "handle the bar," "bring the drinks," "sponsor the liquor," or "cover the alcohol budget." If a co-sponsoring group purchases or provides the alcohol, the chapter cannot co-host with them on that basis. That is not a paperwork problem to be solved on the form — it is a plan that has to change.

Supplemental Note

Supplemental · Holmes Murphy 2026 Template

The template adds a related provision: an organization must not co-host or co-sponsor an event with a bar, event promoter, or alcohol distributor — though it may rent a bar, restaurant, or other licensed and insured third-party vendor to host an event. That distinction between co-hosting with and renting from is a useful way to think about the relationship, and it is consistent with how the Kappa source treats third-party vendors. It is offered here as supplemental guidance, not as adopted Kappa policy.

The Fields

Co-Sponsored Events
System FieldCo-Sponsored Events
Source Explanation — Kappa Source"Will other organizations (sororities/fraternities/organizations) be involved in planning or working the event? Yes / No"

What it means. The chapter is declaring whether another organization is involved in planning or working the event.

Why it matters. Co-sponsorship brings another organization's members, decisions, judgment, and conduct into your event, and brings its insurance into your risk picture. It also creates a question a reviewer must be able to answer: if something goes wrong, who was responsible for what? Declaring the co-sponsor and identifying an accountable contact is how that question gets answered in advance rather than afterward.

How to complete it.

  1. Ask the other organization, in writing, exactly what it will do at and before this event.
  2. Apply the test: is it involved in planning or working? If yes, check the box.
  3. Request its certificate of insurance as soon as the box is checked — not in submission week.
  4. Confirm the other organization is not purchasing or providing alcohol, illegal drugs, or controlled substances for the event.
  5. Put the division of responsibilities in writing — who staffs the door, who owns the guest list, who pays which vendor, who has authority to stop the event.
Acceptable

Box checked, organization named, contact identified with email and cell, certificate of insurance attached, and a written one-page understanding attached describing which organization is responsible for the door, the guest list, the vendors, and the monitors.

Not Acceptable

Box left unchecked while the flyer says "Presented by [Chapter] and [Other Organization]." Also not acceptable: box checked with the identification fields blank.

Example. A chapter and a sorority chapter jointly plan a scholarship gala. Both organizations sit on the planning committee, both staff the check-in table, and proceeds are split between the two scholarship funds. This is co-sponsorship. The box is checked, the sorority chapter is named, its chapter president is listed as contact with email and cell, and its certificate of insurance is attached.

Common kickback reasons.

  • Co-sponsor visible on the flyer but not declared on the form — the single fastest way to get a packet returned, because the reviewer can see the contradiction without asking anyone.
  • Box checked, certificate of insurance not attached.
  • Certificate attached but the policy period does not cover the event date.
  • Roles undefined, so the reviewer cannot tell who is responsible for attendance control.

Documentation to have ready. The co-sponsor's certificate of insurance; a written statement or agreement describing each organization's responsibilities; the contact's name, title, email, and cell.

Red Flag

"We'll figure out who's doing what closer to the date." Undefined shared responsibility is the most common way a co-sponsored event ends up with nobody at the door. Define it now, in writing.

Name of the organization if co-sponsored:
System FieldName of the organization if co-sponsored:

What it means. The identity of the organization participating with the chapter.

Why it matters. It establishes exactly who the other responsible organization is and permits verification of its insurance and its role. Insurance verification depends entirely on getting the entity right — a certificate issued to a national organization does not necessarily evidence coverage for a local chapter, and vice versa.

How to complete it. Enter the full, correct organizational name including the specific chapter or unit. Match the name on the certificate of insurance. If the certificate names a different entity than the one you are working with, resolve that before submitting rather than letting a reviewer discover it.

Acceptable

"Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Inc. — Denton Alumnae Chapter"
"North Texas Black Chamber of Commerce, Inc."
"University of North Texas Student Government Association"

Not Acceptable

"The Deltas." / "SGA." / "A local nonprofit." / "Same as last year." Nicknames and abbreviations cannot be matched to a certificate of insurance.

Common kickback reasons. Informal name that does not match the certificate; chapter or unit omitted; more than one co-sponsor but only one named.

Practical Tip

If there is more than one co-sponsoring organization and the form gives you one line, name the primary co-sponsor here and list all of them, with their contacts and insurance status, in the Additional Attachments field. Do not silently drop the second one.

Name of the contact if co-sponsored:
System FieldName of the contact if co-sponsored:

What it means. The responsible individual representing the co-sponsor.

Why it matters. Organizations do not answer phones; people do. This field provides an accountable point of contact for coordination, documentation, insurance, and questions — before the event and, if necessary, during it.

How to complete it. Name a person who holds actual authority in that organization — its president, its risk manager, its event chair, its executive director — and who has agreed to serve as the contact. Include the title. A named contact who does not know he has been named is not a contact.

Acceptable

"Chelsea Morrow, Chapter President, Denton Alumnae Chapter — confirmed as event contact on 3/14."

Not Acceptable

"Their president." / "Chelsea." / A member of your own chapter listed as the co-sponsor's contact.

Common kickback reasons. First name only; no title; the same person listed as both chapter contact and co-sponsor contact.

Email to contact if co-sponsored:
System FieldEmail to contact if co-sponsored:

What it means. Written-contact information for the co-sponsor's representative.

Why it matters. Email is how documentation and insurance requests are communicated and, critically, retained. A phone call confirming that the co-sponsor will provide a certificate of insurance leaves no record. An email does.

How to complete it. Enter a working address the contact actually monitors — ideally an organizational address rather than a personal one, since personal addresses change when officers turn over. Verify it by sending the insurance request to it before you submit.

Acceptable

"cmorrow@dentonalumnae.example.org (verified — certificate of insurance request sent 3/14, certificate received 3/21)"

Not Acceptable

An address nobody has tested. A shared inbox nobody monitors. "N/A" when a co-sponsor exists.

Practical Tip

Use the insurance request itself as your email verification. If the certificate comes back, the address works and you have the document you needed. Two problems solved with one message.

Cell Phone to contact if co-sponsored:
System FieldCell Phone to contact if co-sponsored:

What it means. Immediate contact information for the co-sponsor's representative.

Why it matters. This is the field for the night of the event. If the co-sponsor's members are staffing the door and something goes wrong — a dispute at check-in, a capacity problem, an incident — the chapter needs to reach a responsible representative immediately, not on Monday.

How to complete it. Enter a mobile number the contact will have with him on the event date. Confirm it, and confirm that he will be reachable during the event or has designated someone who will be.

Acceptable

"(940) 555-0117 (mobile; contact confirmed she will be on site 6:00 PM–midnight)"

Not Acceptable

An office landline for a Saturday-night event. A number that reaches a general voicemail box.

Common kickback reasons. Field blank; office number supplied for an evening or weekend event.

Additional Attachments Long:
System FieldAdditional Attachments Long:

What it means. A system field for attaching or referencing additional documentation. The word "Long" is a database field-type artifact from the platform, not a Kappa Alpha Psi term — no source defines it. Functionally, treat it as the place to attach or describe supporting documents that do not have a dedicated field elsewhere on the form.

Verify Before Submission · label not defined by any source

Why it matters. Supporting documentation is how the chapter demonstrates that its answers are real. The Kappa source requires applicable contracts and certificates of insurance to accompany the Event Notification Form. This field is where the additional material lands.

How to complete it.

  1. List every document you are attaching, by name, with a one-line description of what it establishes.
  2. Attach the co-sponsor's certificate of insurance here if there is no dedicated slot for it.
  3. Attach the written division of responsibilities between the organizations.
  4. If there is a second or third co-sponsor, document them fully here.
  5. Never write "see attached" without naming what is attached — reviewers process many submissions and should not have to reconstruct your packet.
Acceptable

"Attached: (1) Certificate of Insurance — Denton Alumnae Chapter, carrier and policy period covering event date; (2) Signed co-sponsorship memorandum dated 3/14 assigning door/check-in to Kappa and hospitality/program to the Alumnae Chapter; (3) Email confirmation from co-sponsor president accepting event-contact role."

Not Acceptable

"See attached." / "Docs to follow." / Blank when a co-sponsor has been declared.

Common kickback reasons. Referenced documents not actually attached; a certificate attached whose policy period does not cover the event date; attachments named but not identified as to what they prove.

Practical Tip

Build the attachment list before you start uploading. Write the list first, then attach against it, then read the list one more time against what is actually in the packet. Most missing-attachment kickbacks are simple oversights caught by that one re-read.

Why the Other Organization's Insurance Matters

Brothers sometimes ask why the chapter needs another organization's certificate of insurance when the chapter has its own coverage. Three reasons.

  1. Their people are your event's peopleThe co-sponsor's members are working your event. If one of them makes a decision that injures a guest, the question of whose coverage responds is not academic.
  2. It is a required attachmentThe Kappa source lists a certificate of insurance for co-sponsored events with organizations among the documents to submit with the form. It is not optional and it is not conditional on the chapter's judgment.
  3. It tells you whether they are a real, insured organizationAn organization that cannot produce a certificate of insurance may not be organized, funded, or covered the way it presented itself. That is worth knowing before you put your letters next to theirs on a flyer.

Scenarios

▶ Scenario — The "Just Promotion" Partner

A local business organization asks to be on the flyer for the chapter's community day. The chapter agrees. As planning proceeds, the organization also sends four volunteers to run the registration table, brings its own tent and tables, and posts the event as its own on social media. The Event Chair says: "They're not a co-sponsor, they just helped with promotion."

Is that classification correct?

No. The test is involvement in planning or working the event, and this organization is working the event — four of its people are staffing registration, which is an attendance-control function, and it is supplying equipment. The flyer language is irrelevant to the classification; the actual responsibilities decide it.

The chapter should check the co-sponsored box, name the organization, identify a responsible contact with email and cell, and request its certificate of insurance. It should also define in writing who is responsible for the registration table — because right now the chapter has handed a control function to volunteers it does not manage.

Note the reverse case too: if that organization had done nothing but share a social post, it would likely not be a co-sponsor. The difference is not the logo. It is the four volunteers.

▶ Scenario — The Sponsored Bar

A co-sponsoring organization offers to "take care of the bar" for a joint alumni social — meaning it will buy the liquor and bring it to the venue. The Event Chair sees this as a budget win and asks how to note it on the checklist.

How should this be handled?

This cannot be noted onto the checklist, because there is no way to answer the form truthfully and keep the arrangement. The Kappa source states that a chapter must not co-host or cosponsor, or in any way participate in, an activity or event with another group or entity that purchases or provides alcohol. It also prohibits common sources of alcohol not being served by a licensed and insured third-party vendor, and prohibits alcohol purchased with organizational or pooled funds.

The offer has to be declined, and the plan changed to one of two lawful models: alcohol provided and sold on a per-drink basis by a licensed and insured third-party vendor, or individually brought under a controlled BYOB system with age verification, quantity limits, a distribution center, and monitors.

The event chair should also recognize what he is being told about this partner — an organization that proposes to buy the alcohol may not understand the standards the chapter operates under, and that is worth addressing directly before the two organizations put their names on the same flyer.

Knowledge Check

Module 2 · Question 1

Which fact most strongly indicates that another organization is a co-sponsor rather than a community partner?

✓ Correct answer: C. The Kappa test is involvement in planning or working the event. Sitting on the planning committee is planning; staffing check-in is working — and check-in is an attendance-control function, which raises the stakes further. A, B, and D are support activities that on their own generally do not meet the test, though a logo on the flyer will reasonably prompt a reviewer to ask what the relationship is, so be ready to explain it.
Module 2 · Question 2

A co-sponsoring organization offers to purchase and supply the alcohol for a joint social. The correct response is:

✓ Correct answer: B. This provision is a hard limit in the Kappa source, and the supplied alcohol would also be a prohibited common source. Receipts (C) and age screening (D) do not cure the underlying arrangement. Answer A treats the checklist as a place to disclose a prohibited plan rather than as a tool that should have changed the plan.
Module 2 · Question 3

The chapter has declared a co-sponsor and named a contact, but the co-sponsor's certificate of insurance has not arrived four days before the submission deadline. The best course of action is:

✓ Correct answer: D. A certificate of insurance for co-sponsored events is a required attachment; an incomplete packet is a returned packet, so A just delays the problem. B is a false statement on a form the chapter signs as factual and truthful. C misrepresents whose coverage is being evidenced. D is uncomfortable but correct — and an organization that cannot produce a certificate on request is telling you something important about whether it is prepared to co-sponsor.

Undergraduate Established Event

Capacity, anticipated attendance, and the invitation system. This section is where the chapter proves it knows who is coming and how many — before the doors open.

⏱ 25 min🎫 10 fields
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) obtain and document a fire-code capacity; (2) produce a defensible anticipated-attendance figure; (3) choose and correctly describe an invitation or registration system; (4) build a working guest list; (5) explain the difference between controlled registration and uncontrolled public admission.

The Governing Requirement

Kappa Source — Event Notification Form, Attendance"Attendance by non-members at all events must be by invitation only and the chapter must utilize a system to track attendees. Attendance at all events must not exceed local fire or building code capacity of the chapter or member premises or host venue." "For chapter fundraisers, ticket sales prior to the event is required and events must be within fire code capacity."

Three obligations sit in that language, and every field in this section serves one of them:

  1. Invitation only for non-members. Not "open to the public." Not "bring whoever."
  2. A system to track attendees. Not a memory, not a vibe at the door — a system.
  3. Within fire or building code capacity. A hard ceiling set by law, not by the chapter's optimism.
Why Reviewers Focus Here

Overcrowding and uncontrolled admission are the two failure modes that turn a manageable incident into a serious one. A crowd that exceeds capacity cannot evacuate. A crowd nobody screened cannot be accounted for. This is also the section that gets audited after the fact — the Kappa source states that in the event of a policy violation, your organization may be asked to submit your guest list and other supporting documents as part of the conduct process.

The Two Number Fields

Fire code capacity of venue:
System FieldFire code capacity of venue:

What it means. The legally permitted occupancy of the space the chapter is using.

Why it matters. It is the objective ceiling on the event. Every other attendance decision — how many invitations, how many guests per member, whether to use a waitlist, whether the venue is even appropriate — is derived from this number. It is set by fire and building code, not by what the venue would like to sell you or what the chapter would like to host.

How to complete it.

  1. For a commercial venue: ask the venue in writing for the fire-code capacity of the specific room you are renting, in the configuration you are using. A ballroom's capacity for standing reception, banquet rounds, and theater seating are three different numbers.
  2. Get it in writing. An email from the catering manager, the figure printed on the banquet event order, or a photograph of the posted occupancy placard.
  3. For university space: the reservation system or facilities office states the room's occupancy load.
  4. For a municipal facility or park pavilion: the permit or facility-use agreement generally states it.
  5. For a member residence: there is no posted figure. The chapter must reason one out from usable interior space and exits, write down the reasoning, and set the guest list well below it. Say so on the form rather than inventing a code number.
  6. Enter the number as a number, and note the source of it if the field allows.
Acceptable

"350 — Magnolia Ballroom, banquet configuration; confirmed in writing by venue catering manager 3/12 and stated on signed banquet event order."

Acceptable

"Residence — no posted occupancy. Chapter-established planned maximum of 60 based on usable interior area and two available exits; guest list capped at 55."

Not Acceptable

"Big enough." / "About 300, I think." / "N/A." / A number copied from the venue's marketing page describing what the room "accommodates," which is a sales figure, not a code figure.

Example. An event chair is told by a banquet salesperson that the room "holds about 400." He asks specifically: "What is the fire-code occupancy for this room with a dance floor and forty banquet rounds?" The answer comes back 350, and the salesperson puts it on the banquet event order. That is the number that goes on the checklist.

Common kickback reasons.

  • Field blank — one of the most frequent single omissions on the form.
  • A guess, or a marketing capacity rather than a code capacity.
  • Capacity stated for the building rather than the room.
  • Capacity lower than the anticipated attendance elsewhere on the form.

Documentation to have ready. Written capacity confirmation from the venue, the banquet event order, the reservation confirmation, the permit, or a photo of the posted placard.

Red Flag

A venue that will not state a fire-code capacity in writing. Every legitimate commercial venue knows this number, because the fire marshal requires it to. Refusal or vagueness is a signal about how the venue operates.

Anticipated number of guests:
System FieldAnticipated number of guests:

What it means. How many people the chapter genuinely expects to attend.

Why it matters. Comparing expected attendance against fire-code capacity is how a reviewer determines whether the venue is appropriate and whether the admission controls are adequate. It also drives the monitor count, the security arrangement, the food and beverage plan, and the alcohol distribution design.

How to complete it.

  1. Build the number, do not guess it: expected members + expected new members + guests per member × number of members + expected co-sponsor attendees + expected alumni + expected walk-up requests.
  2. Compare it to last year's actual attendance at a comparable event if you have it. Chapters chronically underestimate.
  3. Account for the people who are present but not guests: vendors, DJ and crew, caterer staff, security, venue staff, photographers. Depending on venue procedure these may count toward occupancy — ask.
  4. If the number approaches capacity, redesign now: cap the guest list, use a hard-stop registration, or choose a larger venue.
  5. Enter the realistic figure. A deliberately low number to make the math look comfortable is a false statement on a form the chapter signs as factual and truthful.
Acceptable

"240 attendees anticipated (35 members, 2 guests each = 70 member guests; 90 pre-registered general attendees; 45 alumni). Plus approximately 25 vendor, venue, and security personnel on site. Total planned occupancy 265 against a fire-code capacity of 350. Registration closes at 300 attendees."

Not Acceptable

"A lot." / "200-500." / A number that exceeds or equals the stated fire-code capacity. / A number that contradicts the flyer, which advertises "the biggest party of the year."

Worked Example — Total Planned Occupancy

Training Guidance

Venue fire-code capacity: 300
Anticipated participants: 240
Staff and vendors on site (DJ and assistant, caterer team, two security officers, photographer, venue banquet staff): 25
Total planned occupancy: 265

The chapter has 35 people of headroom. That headroom is not spare capacity to sell — it is the margin that absorbs the guests who bring an uninvited friend, the alumnus who drives in unannounced, and the vendor who brings a second van of crew. Plan to the total, not to the guest count, and confirm with the venue whether its occupancy figure includes staff.

Common kickback reasons. Field blank; anticipated attendance at or above capacity; attendance inconsistent with the invitation system described (for example, 400 anticipated with a numbered-invitation system that only issued 150 invitations); attendance inconsistent with the flyer.

The Invitation and Tracking Systems

Kappa Source — Event Notification Form"What is your system to invite attendees and track attendance?"

Every option below is trying to establish one thing: a controlled invitation or registration mechanism, so that the chapter knows in advance who is authorized to attend and can account at the door for who actually did. The technology varies. The requirement does not.

Spreadsheet or Sign-Up List
System FieldSpreadsheet or Sign-Up List
Source Explanation — Kappa Source"Create a spreadsheet and allow members to add guests' names. Bring the list to a chapter meeting or post it online. Each member members' name should be on the list next to a blank space for each guest they're allowed to invite [e.g. two guests per member/new member]."

What it means. A controlled list that ties each member to the specific guests he is authorized to invite.

Why it matters. It creates an attendance record, and it creates accountability. The structure the source describes is not just a list of names — it is a list of names organized under the members who vouched for them. That is what makes it a control rather than a roster.

How to complete it.

  1. Decide the guest allowance per member before opening the list — two per member is the example given in the source.
  2. Build the sheet with one row per member and named slots for that member's guests.
  3. Set a close date. A list that is still open at the door is not a control.
  4. Print the final list and use it at check-in. Mark people in as they arrive.
  5. Retain the marked-up list after the event with the rest of the packet.
Sample Guest-List Structure

Training Guidance · sample format

Member NameGuest NameGuest ContactAge Verification RequiredRegistration StatusChecked InNotes
Bro. A. ColemanMarcus Hill(940) 555-0131Yes — 21+Confirmed 3/18☐ 
Bro. A. ColemanDenise Parkdpark@example.comYes — 21+Confirmed 3/18☐ 
Bro. T. WhitfieldJordan Reese(972) 555-0164No — under 21, no alcoholConfirmed 3/19☐Wristband not issued
Bro. T. Whitfield— slot unused —    Not transferable
