Bro. R. NunezAlicia Grantagrant@example.comYes — 21+Waitlist☐Capacity hold

Two design points worth noting in that table. First, an unused guest slot is not transferable to another member — otherwise the allowance becomes a pool and the accountability disappears. Second, the age-verification column is filled in at registration, not at the door; the door confirms identification against a decision already made.

Acceptable

"Chapter-maintained spreadsheet, two guests per member, guest names and contact collected at registration, list closed 48 hours before the event, printed and used for door check-in by two assigned brothers, retained after the event."

Not Acceptable

"Sign-up sheet passed around at chapter." with no close date, no contact information, no guest allowance, and no plan for using it at the door. A list that is never used at the door is documentation of an intention, not a control.

Common kickback reasons. System selected but no description of how it will be used at check-in; no close date; no guest allowance stated.

Documentation to have ready. The list itself, the close date, the names of the brothers assigned to check-in.

Numbered Invitations
System FieldNumbered Invitations
Source Explanation — Kappa Source"Distribute numbered invitations to each member to give to his guests. These invitations should be printed professionally or created in a way so they can't be easily copied. Tickets cannot be sold or bartered. Keep a list with each member/new member's name on it and the numbers of the invitations they were given. During the event, keep a sign-in sheet at the door and write the guest's name next to the invitation number as she/he turns in the invitation."

What it means. Uniquely numbered physical invitations, assigned to specific members, redeemed and reconciled at the door.

Why it matters. Numbering connects each invitation to the member who received it. That is what makes reconciliation possible — at the end of the night the chapter can say exactly which invitations were used, which were not, and which member is associated with each. It is the most auditable of the low-tech systems.

How to complete it — the four-step cycle.

  1. ProducePrint professionally, or produce in a way that cannot be easily copied — a distinctive stock, a stamp, a signature, a serialized element. A photocopiable flyer with a handwritten number is not a controlled invitation.
  2. AssignRecord which numbers went to which member. This is the control ledger; without it the numbers mean nothing.
  3. RedeemAt the door, collect the invitation and write the guest's name next to the invitation number on the sign-in sheet.
  4. ReconcileAfter the event, compare issued numbers against redeemed numbers. Unredeemed numbers are fine. Duplicate numbers, or numbers you never issued, tell you the system was breached and need to be addressed with the chapter.
Hard Rule from the Source

"Tickets cannot be sold or bartered." Numbered invitations are an access control, not a revenue instrument. A brother who sells his invitations has converted an access control into a door sale — which also collides with the prevention item prohibiting ticket sales at the door and, for fundraisers, with the requirement that ticket sales occur prior to the event.

Acceptable

"150 professionally printed serialized invitations, numbers 001–150, assignment ledger maintained by the Keeper of Records; invitations collected at the single entrance and guest names recorded against numbers on the door sign-in sheet; reconciliation completed by the Event Chair within 48 hours."

Not Acceptable

"We're printing invites." Also not acceptable: invitations distributed without an assignment ledger, or a plan to "just collect them at the door" with no sign-in sheet.

Common kickback reasons. No assignment ledger described; no door reconciliation described; invitation count inconsistent with anticipated attendance.

Documentation to have ready. The number-assignment ledger; the door sign-in sheet; the reconciliation after the event.

Closed Facebook Event
System FieldClosed Facebook Event
Source Explanation — Kappa Source"Create a closed [non-recurring] event with a specific start and end time. Do NOT allow friends to extend the guest list. Set the Privacy to 'Invite Only.' A designated officer [e.g. Risk Management Chairman] should be set as the host and administrator for the event. Each member should submit the names of guests to the host for invitation to the event or the host should designate a specific time period during which members will be given access to add guests to the event."

What it means. A private, invitation-only social-platform event used as the invitation control, administered by a designated officer.

Why it matters. The source's requirements are all aimed at one failure mode: guest lists that grow on their own. Non-recurring, specific start and end, invite-only, friends cannot extend the list, one officer administers, and guest additions are either submitted to the host or allowed only during a defined window. Strip any one of those away and it stops being a control.

Platform Caution

Verify Before Submission

Social platforms change their privacy settings, event features, and terminology regularly, and the specific labels described in the source may no longer match what you see on screen. Do not assume a setting still exists or still does what it did. Before selecting this option, confirm that the platform can actually deliver the four controls the source requires: private/invite-only, no guest-initiated additions, a single administrator, and a fixed guest list. If it cannot, choose a different system and describe it.

How to complete it.

  1. Name the designated officer who is host and administrator.
  2. Confirm the event is non-recurring with a specific start and end time.
  3. Confirm privacy is set so only invited people can see and join.
  4. Confirm invitees cannot add guests themselves — or, if the platform permits it, that the setting is turned off.
  5. State how members submit guest names to the host, or the defined window during which they may add guests.
  6. Export or screenshot the final attendee list before the event and use it at the door.
Acceptable

"Private, invite-only, non-recurring event administered solely by the Chapter Risk Manager. Guest additions by members are closed; members submit guest names to the administrator, who issues the invitation. Final list exported 48 hours prior and used at the door alongside photo ID check."

Not Acceptable

"Facebook event." / A public event page. / An event where attendees can invite friends. / A recurring event. / Relying on the online RSVP count as the door list without exporting it.

Common kickback reasons. Option selected with no description; description that does not address who administers it or whether guests can extend the list; a public event page contradicted by the "invitation only" requirement elsewhere on the form.

Practical Tip

Whatever the platform, the door does not run on the platform. Export the list to paper or PDF before the event. Venue Wi-Fi fails, phones die, and apps log you out at exactly the wrong moment.

Eventbrite
System FieldEventbrite

What it means. An online attendance and ticket-management option identified by name in the Kappa source's list of online ticket options.

Why it matters. What the checklist is establishing is not brand preference — it is that a controlled registration mechanism exists: attendees register in advance, the chapter holds a list, and admission can be checked against that list.

Kappa Source · Online Ticket Option Verify current platform features yourself

How to complete it. Select the option, then describe the configuration in the nearest available text field: whether registration is public or private/invitation-limited, whether there is a registration cap set below capacity, when registration closes, whether tickets are transferable, and how the list will be used at the door.

The Trap

Selecting an online ticketing platform does not by itself satisfy "invitation only." A public listing anyone can find and buy into is uncontrolled public admission with a receipt. If you use a platform, configure it as a controlled system — private link or invitation-limited registration, a hard cap, a close date — and say so on the form.

Acceptable

"Registration via Eventbrite using a private, unlisted link distributed only to members for forwarding to invited guests. Registration capped at 300 and closes 48 hours prior. Attendee list exported and printed for door check-in against photo ID."

Not Acceptable

"Eventbrite." / A public listing promoted on open social media with no cap and no close date.

Documentation to have ready. The registration settings, the cap, the close date, and the exported attendee list.

Eventzilla
System FieldEventzilla

What it means. Another online registration and ticketing option identified by name in the Kappa source.

Why it matters. Same purpose as any other registration platform: electronic registration and attendance control, producing a list the chapter can work from at the door.

Kappa Source · Online Ticket Option Verify current platform features yourself

How to complete it. Identical discipline to any platform: private or invitation-limited registration, a cap below fire-code capacity, a close date, an exported list, and a door process. Describe those five things rather than naming the tool and stopping.

Acceptable

"Eventzilla registration, invitation-limited, capped at 180, closing 72 hours prior; exported list used at a single check-in table with photo ID verification."

Not Acceptable

"Eventzilla" with no configuration described.

Practical Tip

Do not describe platform features you have not personally confirmed. If you are unsure whether a platform supports a private registration link or a hard cap, log in and check before you write it on a form the chapter signs as truthful.

Event Smart
System FieldEvent Smart

What it means. Another online ticket and registration option identified by name in the Kappa source.

Why it matters. It serves the same attendance-tracking purpose. The checklist is establishing that registration is controlled and a list exists.

Kappa Source · Online Ticket Option Verify current platform features yourself

How to complete it. Select it and describe: registration visibility, cap, close date, export, and door process. The chapter's obligation is unchanged by which vendor is hosting the form.

Acceptable

"Event Smart registration page, link distributed to members only, cap 250, closes 48 hours prior, list exported to PDF and printed for door check-in."

Not Acceptable

"Online registration." Naming no platform and describing no controls tells a reviewer nothing.

Kappareg
System FieldKappareg

Verify Before Submission · not described in available sources

What it means. The online checklist lists this as an invitation and registration option. The available sources do not describe it, so this course will not state what it does, who administers it, or what features it has.

Why it matters. If your chapter uses it, the underlying requirement is unchanged: a controlled invitation or registration mechanism producing a list the chapter can use at the door.

How to complete it. Select it only if the chapter is actually using it. Then describe the same five things you would describe for any system: who administers it, how attendees are invited or registered, whether registration is capped, when it closes, and how the resulting list is used at admission. Confirm with your chapter leadership or International Headquarters what the current expectations for this system are — do not assume, and do not describe functionality you have not verified.

Acceptable

Selected because the chapter is genuinely using it, with the administrator named, the registration and cap described, the close date stated, and the door process explained.

Not Acceptable

Selected because it has "Kappa" in the name and looks like the safe answer. Selecting a system the chapter is not using is a false statement.

Other Invite System
System FieldOther Invite System

What it means. The chapter is using a controlled invitation or registration system not listed among the named options.

Why it matters. The method may differ, but the underlying requirement is the same: the ability to control and track attendance. A reviewer's question is whether your alternative actually delivers that.

What makes an alternative system credible. Test it against six criteria:

  1. Individual registration. Each attendee is identified by name, not counted as part of a group.
  2. Controlled issuance. Invitations or registrations come from the chapter, not from attendees inviting each other.
  3. A cap. Registration stops at a number set below fire-code capacity.
  4. A close date. The list is fixed before the event; it does not stay open through the door.
  5. An exportable, usable list. The chapter can hold the list in hand at the entrance.
  6. Reconciliation. The chapter can tell afterward who was authorized and who actually attended.
Systems That Fail the Test

Open social-media promotion. A public link anyone can share. "Text a brother to get on the list" with no list. Word of mouth. A group chat. Door-based admission decisions. Each of these fails at least two of the six criteria — usually controlled issuance and a fixed list.

Other Invite System (Describe):
System FieldOther Invite System (Describe):

What it means. The narrative explaining how the alternative system works.

Why it matters. Reviewers need enough information to determine whether the alternative provides meaningful attendance control. "Other" with a thin description is one of the most common causes of a returned submission on the entire form.

How to complete it. Write the six criteria into the description: who issues, how attendees register, what the cap is, when it closes, how the list gets to the door, and who checks it.

Acceptable

"Chapter-managed RSVP portal requiring individual registration. Registration closes 48 hours before the event and the exported attendee list will be used at check-in."

Acceptable

"University event registration system administered by the Student Activities Office. Each attendee registers individually with student ID; registration capped at 200 by the office at the chapter's request; roster provided to the chapter 24 hours prior and checked at a single entrance by two assigned brothers against photo ID."

Not Acceptable

"Social media." / "Word of mouth." / "Invite only." / "Members will handle it." / "Group chat."

Common kickback reasons. One- or two-word description; a description of promotion rather than of registration; a system that has no cap or no close date.

Registration Versus Uncontrolled Public Admission

 Controlled registrationUncontrolled public admission
Who may attendPeople the chapter invited or approved in advanceAnyone who shows up or buys in
Who issues accessThe chapterThe attendee, or the open market
List exists beforehandYes, fixed at a close dateNo, or it grows at the door
Capacity controlCap set below code capacityWhoever fits, until someone says stop
AccountabilityEach guest traceable to a member or a registrationUnknown attendees
After the factChapter can produce the guest list if askedNothing to produce
Fundraisers

The Kappa source is specific: for chapter fundraisers, ticket sales prior to the event is required, and events must be within fire code capacity. Selling at the door defeats pre-event attendance control, which is why "Prohibited ticket sales at the door" appears as a separate prevention item in Module 9.

Scenarios

▶ Scenario — The Capacity Squeeze

Fire-code capacity is 300. Registration closed at 285. On the night of the event, 40 alumni arrive who did not register, saying they drove two hours and assumed they would be welcome. The door team counts 262 already inside.

What should the door team do, and what should the chapter have done differently?

At the door: 262 inside plus 40 arrivals is 302, which exceeds the 300 code capacity before counting vendors and staff who are already inside. The chapter cannot admit all 40. The door team admits up to the remaining headroom only after subtracting staff and vendors from the count, and holds the rest outside. This is uncomfortable and it is also the correct answer — capacity is a legal limit, not a chapter preference, and "they drove a long way" is not a defense if the fire marshal walks in.

Whoever is running the door must have been given authority in advance to say no. If the door team has to find the Polemarch mid-crowd to get permission, the crowd is already inside.

What should have been different: the anticipated-attendance calculation should have included expected alumni walk-ups, since this is a predictable pattern at chapter events. The registration cap should have been set with real headroom — 285 out of 300 leaves almost none once vendors and staff are counted. And the flyer and the chapter's communications should have stated clearly that registration was required and closed on a date certain, so unregistered arrivals were not a surprise to anyone.

▶ Scenario — The Guest List That Grew

A chapter sets up an online event and allows members to add guests directly. Two days out, the list has grown from an expected 120 to 310 because several guests added their own friends. The venue's capacity is 200.

What went wrong, and what has to happen now?

The control failed at exactly the point the Kappa source warns about: friends were allowed to extend the guest list. The source's requirements for a closed event — invite-only privacy, a single designated officer as host and administrator, guests submitted to the host rather than added freely, or member additions permitted only during a defined window — exist specifically to prevent this.

What has to happen now: the chapter must close additions immediately, and it cannot simply admit the first 200 who arrive, because 110 people were told they were on the list. The honest move is to notify the people beyond the authorized list that the event is at capacity and their registration cannot be honored, and to do it before the event rather than at the door. If the chapter cannot reduce the list defensibly, it should consider postponing or moving to a venue whose capacity fits the crowd it has already invited.

The submitted checklist also no longer matches reality — anticipated attendance was submitted at 120 against a capacity of 200. That has to be corrected with a resubmission, not managed quietly.

Knowledge Check

Module 3 · Question 1

A chapter selects an online ticketing platform and lists the event publicly with no registration cap. Attendance control is:

✓ Correct answer: C. The platform is a tool, not the control. The Kappa requirement is that attendance by non-members be by invitation only with a system to track attendees, within fire-code capacity. A public uncapped listing fails the invitation-only requirement and provides no capacity ceiling. Configure the platform as private or invitation-limited, cap it below code capacity, close it before the event, and use the exported list at the door.
Module 3 · Question 2

Under the numbered-invitation system, a brother offers to sell his two unused invitations to raise money for the chapter. This is:

✓ Correct answer: B. "Tickets cannot be sold or bartered" is explicit in the Kappa source. The invitation is an access control tied to the member who received it; selling it converts it into a door sale and breaks the accountability chain the numbering exists to create. Where the chapter's purpose is a fundraiser, the source requires ticket sales prior to the event through a proper mechanism — not resale of access-control invitations.
Module 3 · Question 3

Fire-code capacity is 300, anticipated attendees 240, and on-site vendor and staff personnel 25. Which statement is most accurate?

✓ Correct answer: D. Occupancy is about bodies in the room. 240 + 25 = 265 against 300 leaves 35, which is a workable but not generous margin once unregistered arrivals are considered. C is wrong as a blanket statement — venue procedures vary, which is exactly why you ask. A undercounts by ignoring 25 people who will physically be present.

Alumni Established Event

Two boxes, two fundamentally different alcohol-control models. Choosing between them decides who owns the alcohol, who serves it, who verifies age, and who carries the exposure.

⏱ 20 min🍸 2 fields
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) distinguish BYOB from a licensed and insured third-party vendor model; (2) identify who owns, provides, distributes, and verifies under each; (3) explain why BYOB is a controlled system rather than an absence of rules; (4) choose the appropriate model for a given event.

What This Section Is Asking

Kappa Source — Event Notification Form"Will the event have alcohol? Yes / No If yes, how will alcohol get to the event?"

Notice the question. Not "will there be drinking" — how will alcohol get to the event. That is a supply-chain question, and the answer determines the entire control model that follows.

The Kappa source's alumni form lists four possible answers: Alumni Chapter Provides to those 21+, BYOB, Licensed and Insured Third Party Vendor, and Dry Event. The online checklist section shown here presents the two most consequential ones.

A Real Difference Between Sources — Read This

The Kappa alumni Event Notification Form lists "Alumni Chapter Provides to those 21+" as an option. Separately, the BYOB provisions in the same manual state that common sources of alcohol not being served by a licensed and insured third-party vendor are prohibited, and that alcoholic beverages must not be purchased with chapter funds or funds pooled by members or guests. The Holmes Murphy 2026 template takes the same position — alcohol must either be sold per drink by a licensed and insured third-party vendor or brought individually under BYOB.

This course does not merge those and does not guess which controls. If your chapter is considering a model in which the chapter itself supplies the alcohol, confirm the current requirement with International Headquarters before you commit, and do not assume the checkbox on the form settles the question. The two models taught below — BYOB and licensed and insured third-party vendor — are the two that every source supports.

Kappa Source Supplemental Verify Before Submission

The Two Fields

BYOB (Bring Your Own)
System FieldBYOB (Bring Your Own)
Source Explanation — Kappa Source"BYOB (Bring Your Own Beverage)"

What it means. Attendees of legal drinking age bring their own alcoholic beverages, in limited quantity, which are checked in and distributed back to them under a controlled system operated by the chapter.

Why it matters. BYOB is not the absence of a system — it is a system the chapter has to run. Under BYOB the chapter is the operator: chapter people verify age, chapter people run the distribution center, chapter people track quantity, chapter people decide when someone has had enough. That is a substantial operational responsibility, and it stays with the chapter.

The four rules that define the model.

  1. No common sourceCommon sources of alcohol, including bulk quantities, not being served by a licensed and insured third-party vendor, are prohibited. No kegs, no punch bowls, no jungle juice, no "chapter cooler," no bottles set out for general use.
  2. No chapter or pooled fundsAlcoholic beverages must not be purchased with chapter funds or with funds pooled by members or guests. Collecting a cover charge, passing a hat, or using a payment app to fund a liquor run all violate this.
  3. No co-sponsorship with a group that supplies alcoholA chapter must not co-host, cosponsor, or in any way participate in an event with another group or entity that purchases or provides alcohol, illegal drugs, or controlled substances.
  4. No rapid consumptionMembers and guests must not permit, encourage, coerce, glorify, or participate in any activity involving the rapid consumption of alcohol, such as drinking games.

Kappa Source · Complete for BYOB events

How to complete it. Checking this box commits the chapter to answering the entire Alcohol and BYOB section of the checklist — carding responsibility, age-identification method, quantity limits by beverage type, distribution center location and management, monitor count, monitor identity, and check-in method. Do not check it until you have designed all of that. Module 8 covers each field.

Acceptable

Attendees 21 and over may each bring a stated maximum by beverage type; drinks are checked in at the door against a personalized ticket or punch card; the alcohol is held at a single centralized distribution center staffed by assigned monitors; attendees redeem one drink at a time; nothing is shared out of a common supply.

Not Acceptable

"BYOB — everybody brings whatever they want." No quantity limit, no check-in, no centralized control, coolers on the floor, a keg somebody brought, or a bar the chapter stocked with money collected at the door.

Example. An alumni chapter holds a social at a rented hall. Attendees 21+ may bring up to four beers or four wine coolers, or one bottle of wine. Each attendee's drinks are checked at the entrance, personalized with his name, and delivered to the distribution table by a working member. He receives a punch card. Two monitors staff the table and mark the card as each drink is claimed.

Common kickback reasons. BYOB selected but the alcohol-control fields are incomplete; no quantity stated; no distribution center identified; no monitors assigned; carding responsibility not assigned.

Documentation to have ready. The written BYOB procedure; the monitor assignment plan; the age-verification method; the quantity limits by beverage type; the check-in system design.

Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "BYOB means guests control their own alcohol however they want."
Fact: BYOB still requires compliance with applicable policy and event controls. The attendee owns the beverage; the chapter controls the quantity brought, the verification of age, the storage, the distribution, and the monitoring. Ownership and control are different things — and it is the control the chapter is signing for.

Red Flag

Any sentence that begins "we'll just have a cooler for..." Stop there. A cooler available to the group is a common source, and it is prohibited unless a licensed and insured third-party vendor is serving.

Licensed and Insured Third Party Vendor
System FieldLicensed and Insured Third Party Vendor
Source Explanation — Kappa Source"Licensed and Insured Third Party Vendor (bar, hotel, caterer, restaurant, etc.)"

What it means. Alcohol is provided and sold on a per-drink basis by a properly licensed and insured professional — a bar, hotel, restaurant, or caterer — operating under contract.

Why it matters. This model transfers defined responsibilities to a professional whose business is serving alcohol lawfully, who holds a license that can be suspended if it is done badly, and who carries liquor liability insurance. That is genuine risk transfer — the third pillar — and it removes the chapter from the position of deciding who gets served.

What the vendor must assume, in writing. The Kappa source requires the third-party vendor to assume, in writing executed in the chapter name of Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc., all responsibilities that any purveyor of alcoholic beverages would assume in the normal course of business, including but not limited to:

  • Check identification cards upon entry
  • Identify those who are of legal age to consume alcohol
  • All alcohol sales are cash/credit to individuals
  • Refrain from serving minors
  • Refrain from serving individuals who appear to be intoxicated
  • Maintain absolute control of ALL alcoholic containers present
  • No excess alcohol — opened or unopened — is to be given, sold, or furnished to the chapter

Kappa Source · For Events at a Third-Party Vendor

Read the Last Two Again

"Maintain absolute control of ALL alcoholic containers present" means the vendor controls everything — there is no side supply, no bottles at tables the vendor is not managing, no BYOB running alongside the bar.

"No excess alcohol — opened or unopened — is to be given, sold, or furnished to the chapter" closes the most common end-of-night failure: the vendor offering leftover bottles to the chapter. Accepting them converts a clean third-party model into a chapter-held common source in one moment.

How to complete it.

  1. Confirm the vendor is properly licensed by the appropriate local and state authority — ask for the license.
  2. Obtain the certificate of insurance. The carrier must have an A.M. Best rating of A- or higher, with a minimum of $1,000,000 per occurrence and $2,000,000 policy aggregate. Where alcohol is served, the minimum limits also include liquor liability of $300,000 each common cause and $300,000 aggregate.
  3. Confirm Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter are listed as additional insured on a primary basis.
  4. Get the seven purveyor responsibilities into the written agreement, executed in the chapter name of the national Fraternity.
  5. Confirm all sales are cash or credit to individuals — the chapter does not buy rounds, does not pre-purchase drink tickets that function as a chapter-funded bar, and does not host an "open bar" paid from chapter funds.
  6. Complete the Third Party section of the checklist (Module 6) accordingly.
Acceptable

"Hotel's licensed banquet bar operating a cash bar. TABC license number on file; certificate of insurance received showing $1M occurrence / $2M aggregate and liquor liability $300K/$300K, A.M. Best A rating, in force through the event date; Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter named additional insured on a primary basis; the seven purveyor responsibilities incorporated into the banquet agreement executed in the chapter name."

Not Acceptable

"The venue has a bar." No license verified, no certificate, no additional-insured status, no written assumption of purveyor responsibilities. Also not acceptable: an open bar paid for out of the chapter treasury, or the chapter buying drink tickets in bulk and handing them out.

Example. An alumni chapter's scholarship social is held in a hotel ballroom. The hotel operates a cash bar with its own bartenders under its own license. Guests buy their own drinks by card. The hotel checks identification and refuses service to anyone who appears intoxicated. The chapter's role in alcohol is limited to having contracted properly and to monitoring the room.

Common kickback reasons. Third-party vendor selected but no certificate of insurance attached; certificate missing liquor liability where alcohol is served; additional-insured status not shown; contract not executed in the chapter name; purveyor responsibilities not addressed in writing; a "hosted bar" arrangement that is functionally chapter-funded alcohol.

Documentation to have ready. Vendor license; certificate of insurance with all required limits and additional-insured status; the executed contract containing the purveyor responsibilities.

Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "The hotel is responsible for everything because the event is at a hotel."
Fact: The venue may assume contractual responsibilities, but the chapter still owns its event planning, its documentation, its members' conduct, and its approval process. A licensed vendor serving alcohol does not put a monitor in your room, does not manage your guest list, and does not stop a fight between two of your guests.

Decision Comparison

 BYOBLicensed and Insured Third Party Vendor
Who owns the alcoholThe individual attendee who brought itThe vendor, until sold to an individual
Who provides itIndividual attendees, in limited quantityThe licensed vendor
Who distributes itChapter monitors at a centralized distribution centerThe vendor's trained, licensed staff
Who verifies ageChapter members, campus police, or hired security at the doorThe vendor, by contract, upon entry and at service
Who refuses serviceChapter monitors — a hard thing to ask of membersThe vendor, whose license depends on doing it
Quantity controlStated limits per person by beverage type, tracked by ticket or punch cardPer-drink sale; vendor maintains absolute control of containers
PaymentNone — no chapter or pooled funds may buy alcoholCash or credit, individual to vendor. Not chapter funds.
Chapter operational loadHigh — check-in, storage, distribution, monitors, trackingLower on alcohol; the chapter still runs the door, the guest list, and the monitors
Insurance postureExposure stays largely with the chapterDefined responsibility and liquor liability sit with an insured professional
Documentation neededWritten BYOB procedure, monitor plan, ID method, quantity limits, check-in designLicense, certificate of insurance with liquor liability, additional insured, executed contract with purveyor responsibilities
Typical fitSmaller controlled events in chapter-controlled space where no licensed vendor is availableLarger events, hotels, restaurants, banquet halls, anywhere a licensed bar exists
Practical Tip

When both models are genuinely available, the third-party vendor model is usually the better choice for a chapter, because it moves the two hardest jobs — refusing service to someone who has had too much, and refusing service to someone underage — from a brother to a professional whose license depends on getting them right. Asking a 22-year-old member to cut off a fellow brother at a distribution table is a hard thing to ask, and it is where BYOB events most often break down.

Do Not Run Both at Once

Do not operate a BYOB system alongside a vendor bar. The vendor is contractually required to maintain absolute control of all alcoholic containers present, which is impossible if attendees are also bringing their own. Mixing the models breaks the vendor's contractual position and leaves the chapter with an uncontrolled supply in the room. Pick one.

Scenarios

▶ Scenario — The Leftover Bottles

At the close of a scholarship social, the hotel's banquet manager offers the chapter four unopened bottles of wine from the bar stock, saying "you paid for the package, take them." The Keeper of Exchequer sees no harm.

What should the chapter do?

Decline. The Kappa source requires the third-party vendor to assume in writing that no excess alcohol — opened or unopened — is to be given, sold, or furnished to the chapter. Accepting the bottles violates the term the chapter contracted for and converts a clean vendor-controlled event into a chapter-held supply of alcohol.

There is a second problem embedded in the offer: "you paid for the package." A pre-paid alcohol package purchased with chapter funds is not a per-drink sale to individuals, and alcoholic beverages must not be purchased with chapter funds. If the chapter really did buy a package, the arrangement needs to be corrected before the next event — the model should be a cash bar where individuals pay the vendor directly.

The correct response in the moment is simple and polite: "We can't accept alcohol from the bar — it's in our agreement." Then note it and fix the contract structure next time.

▶ Scenario — The Cover Charge

To offset the cost of a BYOB social, a brother proposes a $10 cover at the door, with the money going toward "supplies." Another brother suggests using a payment app so nobody handles cash, and notes that some of the money will cover ice, cups, and mixers.

Where is the line, and how should the chapter structure this?

The line is what the money buys. The Kappa source prohibits alcoholic beverages being purchased with chapter funds or with funds pooled by members or guests. The Holmes Murphy template names the modern version of pooling explicitly — admission fees, cover fees, and collecting funds through digital apps. Using a payment app does not change the analysis; it just makes the pooling easier to trace.

Ice, cups, and mixers are not alcoholic beverages, so a cover charge that funds only those is not prohibited on that ground. But the chapter has to be able to demonstrate the separation, and in practice a cover charge collected at a BYOB event invites the inference that attendees are paying for access to drinks. There are two further problems: the checklist's prevention items address ticket sales at the door, and for fundraisers the source requires ticket sales prior to the event.

The clean structure is to sell tickets in advance through the registration system, state plainly what the proceeds fund, buy no alcohol with any chapter or pooled money, and keep the accounting where the Keeper of Exchequer can show it. If the chapter cannot draw that line cleanly, do not collect at the door at all.

Knowledge Check

Module 4 · Question 1

Which statement most accurately describes the chapter's role under a properly run BYOB event?

✓ Correct answer: C. Ownership and control are different. BYOB moves ownership to the individual but leaves the chapter operating the entire control system — which is why the checklist asks about quantity, ID method, distribution center, monitors, and check-in method. B describes reimbursed pooling, which is prohibited. A and D understate the chapter's responsibility, and understating it is how BYOB events fail.
Module 4 · Question 2

A chapter contracts a hotel bar as its licensed and insured third-party vendor, and separately tells members they may bring their own bottles to their tables. This arrangement is:

✓ Correct answer: A. Each model is permitted on its own; running them simultaneously is not. The purveyor responsibility to maintain absolute control of all alcoholic containers present cannot be met when attendees have their own supply in the room. It also destroys the vendor's ability to manage service to anyone who appears intoxicated, since it no longer knows what a guest has consumed. Verbal agreement (D) changes none of that.
Module 4 · Question 3

Which of the following is prohibited at a BYOB event?

✓ Correct answer: B. A shared cooler available to the group is a common source of alcohol, and common sources not being served by a licensed and insured third-party vendor are prohibited. A, C, and D are the defining features of a properly run BYOB event, not violations of it.

Vendor Attendance

Anyone the chapter contracts with to make the event happen is a vendor — and every one of them needs a contract, a certificate of insurance, and a real human being the chapter can reach.

⏱ 25 min💼 6 fields
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) identify who counts as a vendor; (2) complete all four vendor contact fields to a standard a reviewer can work with; (3) explain why verbal agreements are weak documentation; (4) verify a certificate of insurance before submitting; (5) assemble a complete Vendor Documentation Packet.

Who Is a Vendor?

Kappa Source — Event Notification Form, Vendors"Have any written contract or agreement been signed for any part of this event? This would include services contracted by any Food Caterer, Event Promotion Company/Promoter, Security Guards, Bus/Transportation Company, University Facility, Hotel, Sports Field, DJ/Live Band, Artist, Restroom and Waste Management, Any Other — Yes / No (all contracts must be included with this form)" "All contracts should be signed and dated by both the person authorized by your respective organization (i.e. chapter president, advisor, etc.) and the vendor."

The Kappa source's definition is broad on purpose, and it ends with "Any Other." The operating test is simple: is the chapter contracting with someone to facilitate the event? The manual states it plainly elsewhere — "basically, any third party that will be contracted with to facilitate the event."

Named in the source

Food Caterer

Also relevant to products/completed operations exposure — food and beverage preparation and consumption.

Named in the source

Security Guards

A security company is a vendor. See Module 9 for the difference between security, chaperones, and monitors.

Named in the source

DJ / Live Band

Equipment, power, rigging, volume, and content are all vendor-related exposures.

Named in the source

Artist

A performer engaged for the event, with a rider, hospitality requirements, and possibly its own crew.

Named in the source

Bus / Transportation Company

Moving attendees is a distinct and significant exposure. Verify licensing and insurance carefully.

Named in the source

Hotel / University Facility / Sports Field

Venues are vendors too, and also trigger the Third Party section in Module 6.

Named in the source

Restroom & Waste Management

Portable restrooms, dumpsters, and cleanup crews for outdoor events.

Named in the source

Event Promotion Company / Promoter

Also triggers the separate Companies Promoter section in Module 7 with its own insurance provisions.

"Any Other"

Everything else contracted

Photographer and videographer, event equipment and staging, tent and inflatable rentals, generators, valet, shuttle, florist, printer, ticketing service, cleaning crew.

Red Flag — The Rented Equipment Trap

The manual gives a specific example worth remembering: a chapter rents a portable generator for an outdoor function, and while it is in the care, custody, and control of the chapter it is damaged, and the lessor holds the chapter responsible. The manual states that no coverage is available under the Fraternity's liability policies for property damage to property rented by or in the care of an Insured, with a narrow exception for a premises rented for seven days or less. Read equipment rental agreements before you sign them — the damage waiver is not a formality.

Why Verbal Agreements Are Weak Documentation

Brothers hire DJs by text message and caterers by phone call all the time, and most of those events go fine. The problem is not that verbal agreements always fail. The problem is what happens on the day they do.

  1. There is nothing to submitThe Kappa source states that all contracts must be included with the form. A text thread is not a contract. If the chapter has nothing to attach, the packet is incomplete.
  2. Nobody agreed to the same thing"He said he'd bring lights" and "I said I'd bring lights if the venue didn't have any" are the same conversation remembered two ways. A written scope prevents the argument.
  3. There is no insurance requirement to enforceA written contract is where the chapter requires the vendor to carry insurance and to name the Fraternity as additional insured. Verbally, there is nothing to point to.
  4. The chapter cannot show who was responsibleIf a guest trips on a DJ's cable, the question "who was responsible for cable management" has a written answer or it does not.
  5. Individual members get exposedAn undocumented deal made by one brother in his own name can leave that brother personally holding it. Contracts should be executed in the chapter name of the national Fraternity by the authorized person.
Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "The DJ is a brother's cousin, we don't need paperwork."
Fact: Familiarity is not documentation. The relationship makes it easier to get a signed one-page agreement and a certificate of insurance, not less necessary. If the cousin has no business insurance at all, that is exactly the fact the chapter needs to know before the event, not after.

The Fields

The online checklist provides one contact block labeled "First Contract Contact." The Kappa source's forms provide numbered blocks for multiple contracts — three on the undergraduate form, five on the alumni form, with instructions to submit additional ones separately. If your event has more than one vendor, complete the first block fully and document the rest in the attachment fields. Do not drop vendors because the form ran out of boxes.

First Contract Contact Name:
System FieldFirst Contract Contact Name:

What it means. The name of the vendor's contractual representative — the individual who signs or is authorized to bind the vendor.

Why it matters. It identifies the person responsible for the agreement. If a question arises about scope, timing, insurance, or performance, the chapter needs to know who can answer it with authority rather than who happened to answer the phone.

How to complete it. Enter the full name and, where the field allows, the business name and the individual's role. The name should match the signature block on the contract. Do not enter the name of a brother who arranged the booking — this field is for the vendor's representative.

Acceptable

"Ramon Delgado, Owner — Delgado Sound & Lighting LLC (signatory on the executed agreement dated 3/06)"

Not Acceptable

"DJ Ramon." / "Bro. Whitfield's guy." / The name of the chapter member who booked the vendor.

Common kickback reasons. First name or stage name only; business name with no individual; a chapter member listed as the vendor contact.

First Contract Contact Phone Number:
System FieldFirst Contract Contact Phone Number:

What it means. The vendor representative's telephone number.

Why it matters. Enables immediate communication about the contract or the event — including on the event day, when a vendor is late, in the wrong place, or bringing something the chapter did not expect.

How to complete it. Enter a working number, formatted completely, that reaches the representative on the event date. Note if it is a mobile. If the business number is a daytime line only, get a mobile number for event day and record both.

Acceptable

"(214) 555-0173 mobile; business line (214) 555-0100"

Not Acceptable

An incomplete number. A number with no area code. A number nobody has ever called. A general company voicemail for a Saturday-night event.

Common kickback reasons. Incomplete contact information is one of the named causes of returned submissions. A phone field with seven digits, or blank, will stop a packet.

First Contract Contact Email Address:
System FieldFirst Contract Contact Email Address:

What it means. The vendor representative's email address.

Why it matters. Email is the documented communication channel for contracts, insurance certificates, and records. It is also how the chapter proves it asked. A certificate of insurance request sent by email and unanswered is a very different record from "we asked him about insurance once."

How to complete it. Enter a verified working address. Verify it the useful way — by sending the certificate of insurance request to it and getting a reply.

Acceptable

"ramon@delgadosound.example (verified; COI requested 3/06, received 3/11)"

Not Acceptable

A social-media handle instead of an email. An address transcribed from a business card and never used. Blank.

First Contract Contact Physical Address:
System FieldFirst Contract Contact Physical Address:

What it means. The vendor's physical business address.

Why it matters. It helps establish the legal and business identity of the contracted party. A vendor with a real business address is a vendor that can be identified, verified, served with notice, and matched against a certificate of insurance and a business license. A vendor with no fixed address is harder to establish as a real business at all.

How to complete it. Enter the full street address of the business as it appears on the contract and the certificate of insurance. If the vendor operates from a residence, enter that address rather than leaving the field blank — and treat the mismatch between "business" and "residence" as information worth noticing.

Acceptable

"Delgado Sound & Lighting LLC, 4410 Industrial Row, Suite B, Carrollton TX 75006 (address matches certificate of insurance and executed agreement)"

Not Acceptable

"Dallas." / "P.O. Box only" with no street address anywhere in the packet. / An address that does not match the certificate of insurance, unexplained.

Red Flag

The name on the contract, the name on the certificate of insurance, and the name of the business you are actually dealing with should be the same legal entity. If "Delgado Sound & Lighting LLC" signs the contract but the certificate names "R. Delgado Entertainment," stop and resolve it. Certificates that evidence coverage for a different entity evidence nothing for your event.

Vendor Contract Link:
System FieldVendor Contract Link:

What it means. The system location or URL where the executed vendor contract can be accessed.

Why it matters. The Kappa source requires all contracts to be included with the form. This field is how a reviewer gets to the document. A link that does not open, requires permission the reviewer does not have, or points to a folder rather than a file is functionally the same as no contract at all.

How to complete it.

  1. Upload or store the fully executed contract — signed and dated by both the authorized person for the chapter and the vendor.
  2. Confirm the link opens for someone outside the chapter. Test it in a private browser window or ask a brother who is not on the file's share list.
  3. Link to the specific document, not a folder of documents.
  4. Name the file so a reviewer knows what it is: "2026-04-18 Delgado Sound — Executed DJ Agreement.pdf" beats "scan_0043.pdf."
Acceptable

A working, permission-open link to the single executed agreement, with the file named for the vendor and the event date.

Not Acceptable

A link that requires access approval. A link to a shared drive folder. A link to an unsigned draft. "Contract on file with the KRS."

Common kickback reasons. Broken or permission-restricted link; unsigned contract; contract signed by only one party; contract signed by an individual rather than executed in the chapter name of the national Fraternity.

Vendor Contract Long:
System FieldVendor Contract Long:

Verify Before Submission · "Long" is a platform field-type artifact, not a Kappa term

What it means. A system-generated long-text field associated with the contract. No source defines the word "Long" in this context; it comes from the database field type. Functionally, it is where extended contract information is retained or described.

Why it matters. The underlying Kappa requirement is unchanged: contracts must be included with the form. Treat this field as the place to summarize what the contract actually says, so a reviewer can understand the arrangement without reading fifteen pages of boilerplate.

How to complete it. Write a short structured summary covering seven points:

  1. Parties — exact legal names, and confirmation the contract is executed in the chapter name of the national Fraternity.
  2. Scope — what the vendor is providing, specifically.
  3. Dates and times — including load-in, service window, and load-out.
  4. Cost and payment terms — deposit, balance, cancellation.
  5. Insurance provisions — what the contract requires the vendor to carry, and whether additional-insured status is required.
  6. Indemnity or hold-harmless language — flag anything the chapter is assuming.
  7. Anything unusual — equipment damage waivers, exclusivity clauses, attendance guarantees, security requirements imposed on the chapter.
Acceptable

"Executed agreement between Delgado Sound & Lighting LLC and Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. — Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter, signed 3/06 by the Polemarch and by R. Delgado. Scope: DJ services, sound reinforcement, and basic lighting for a 250-guest ballroom event; load-in 4:00 PM, performance 8:00 PM–midnight, load-out by 1:00 AM. $1,400 total, $400 deposit paid, balance due on completion. Vendor carries CGL $1M/$2M; certificate received and attached; chapter and Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. named additional insured. Contract contains a mutual indemnity clause and requires the chapter to provide two 20-amp circuits."

Not Acceptable

"Contract attached." / "Standard DJ contract." / Blank when a vendor contract exists. / A paste of the entire contract text with no summary, leaving the reviewer to find the relevant terms.

Practical Tip

Writing this summary is the single best proofreading tool the chapter has. If you cannot summarize the contract in seven bullets, you have not read it carefully enough to sign it. Do this before signing, not before submitting.

Contract Review Support

The Kappa source notes that Holmes Murphy can assist with reviewing contracts, and gives an address for contract review. It also states clearly that such a review is provided to assist with compliance with the contract's insurance requirement provisions, does not infer or guarantee coverage for a loss, and does not constitute legal advice or a legal opinion. Use the resource; do not treat a review as a guarantee. Confirm the current routing address with your chapter leadership before sending anything.

The Vendor Documentation Packet

Build one of these for every vendor, not just the big ones. Keep them together so the whole set can be attached at once.

Vendor Documentation Packet — per vendor

  • Executed contract — signed and dated by both the person authorized by the chapter and the vendor, executed in the chapter name of the national Fraternity.
  • Certificate of insurance — showing the vendor's coverage, with the policy period covering the event date.
  • Limits verified — General Liability each occurrence $1,000,000; general aggregate $2,000,000; products/completed operations $2,000,000; liquor liability $300,000 each common cause and $300,000 aggregate where alcohol is involved.
  • Carrier rating verified — A.M. Best rating not less than A-, VII.
  • Workers compensation and employers liability — required by the Kappa source alongside commercial general liability for venues and vendors.
  • Additional insured status — Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter listed, on a primary basis, where required.
  • Licensing — where the vendor's work requires a license: alcohol service, security, transportation, food handling.
  • Contact block — name, title, phone (mobile for event day), email, physical address.
  • Scope summary — the seven-point summary described above.
  • Event-day logistics — load-in time, contact on site, what the chapter must provide (power, tables, parking, meals).
How to Read a Certificate of Insurance in Ninety Seconds

Training Guidance

1. Named insured — does it match the entity on your contract, exactly?
2. Policy period — does it include your event date, with room to spare? A policy expiring the week of the event is a problem.
3. Limits — each occurrence, general aggregate, products/completed operations, and liquor liability if alcohol is involved.
4. Carrier — is the A.M. Best rating at least A-, VII?
5. Additional insured — is Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter actually shown, and shown as primary where required? A blank "certificate holder" box is not additional-insured status.
6. Description of operations — does it reference your event or a scope that includes it?

Certificate Holder Is Not Additional Insured

This is the mistake that catches the most chapters. Being listed as a certificate holder means you were mailed a copy of the certificate. Being an additional insured means the vendor's policy has been endorsed to extend specified protection to you. They are entirely different, and only one of them helps. Module 10 covers this in detail.

Scenarios

▶ Scenario — The Missing COI

Six days before submission, the caterer replies: "We've been doing events for fifteen years, we don't do certificates for small jobs. You can look us up, we're licensed." The Event Chair is inclined to note that on the form and move on.

What should he do?

He should press once, clearly and specifically, then be prepared to change vendors. The Kappa source requires that all venues and vendors utilized to host chapter events carry adequate insurance, verified by obtaining a certificate of insurance from the venue or vendor. That is a condition tied to coverage applying — not a chapter preference.

The right message to the caterer is concrete rather than confrontational: "Our national organization requires a certificate of insurance from every vendor before we can hold the event. Please have your agent send a certificate showing general liability of $1,000,000 per occurrence and $2,000,000 aggregate, with Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and our chapter named as additional insured on a primary basis, covering April 18." Any genuinely insured business can get that from its agent in a day or two at no cost.

The response is informative either way. A vendor whose agent produces it promptly is a vendor with real coverage. A vendor who cannot or will not produce it may not have the coverage he says he has — and "you can look us up" is not verification. If it cannot be produced, the chapter needs a different caterer, and it needs to know that now rather than three days out.

▶ Scenario — The Handshake DJ

A brother books a DJ he has known for years by text: "$500, 8 to midnight, you got it." No contract, no insurance, no written scope. At the event the DJ runs power cables across a walkway, a guest catches a foot and falls, and the guest's family later contacts the chapter.

What did the missing documentation cost the chapter?

Four things, at least.

Submission integrity. The chapter answered a checklist question about vendor contracts either falsely or incompletely, on a form it signed as factual and truthful.

Risk transfer. With no written agreement there is no insurance requirement, no additional-insured status, and no indemnity provision. Whatever protection a properly contracted, insured vendor would have brought to this incident does not exist.

Allocation of responsibility. Nothing in writing says who was responsible for cable management and walkway safety. That question now gets answered by argument rather than by document.

Individual exposure. The brother made the arrangement personally, by text, in his own name. That is exactly the situation the requirement to execute contracts in the chapter name of the national Fraternity exists to prevent.

None of this required a fifteen-page agreement. A one-page scope with a signature line, an insurance requirement, and a certificate would have covered it — and the chapter would have learned in advance whether the DJ carried any insurance at all.

Knowledge Check

Module 5 · Question 1

A chapter rents a hotel ballroom. The event chair says: "The hotel is a national chain, so we know they are insured." What should happen before the applicable insurance field is checked?

✓ Correct answer: B. The Kappa source requires the chapter to verify insurance by obtaining a certificate from the venue or vendor. Reputation, size, and brand are not verification, and a member's past attendance (C) establishes nothing about coverage on your event date. D reverses the entire purpose of a pre-event checklist — and a certificate obtained after the fact cannot inform a decision the chapter has already made.
Module 5 · Question 2

Which of the following would NOT normally be treated as a vendor requiring a contract and certificate of insurance?

✓ Correct answer: D. A volunteer chapter member or alumnus performing a chapter role is not a contracted third party; he is covered by the chapter's own arrangements and appears elsewhere on the form as a chaperone or monitor. A, B, and C are all expressly within the source's vendor list — restroom and waste management, bus/transportation, and security guards are named. Note that the volunteer still needs a defined assignment; not being a vendor is not the same as having no responsibility.
Module 5 · Question 3

A certificate of insurance arrives naming "R. Delgado Entertainment," but the executed contract is with "Delgado Sound & Lighting LLC." The correct action is:

✓ Correct answer: A. Entity names on the contract and the certificate must match, because coverage follows the named insured, not the person's reputation. Ask the vendor's agent to reissue the certificate in the contracting entity's name, or confirm in writing which entity is actually performing and contract with that one. B pushes a defect downstream and gets the packet returned. D is altering an executed agreement unilaterally, which is worse than the original problem.

Third Party

Four checkboxes, four representations. Each one says the chapter has verified something specific — and each one is a box you should not check until you can point to the document that supports it.

⏱ 25 min📄 4 fields
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) identify the contracting party and why it must be the chapter in the name of the national Fraternity; (2) verify licensing rather than assume it; (3) read a certificate of insurance against the required limits; (4) explain additional insured, primary basis, certificate holder, and named insured; (5) know exactly what evidence supports each of the four boxes.

What the Kappa Source Requires

Kappa Source — For Events at a Third-Party Vendor• The Third-Party Vendor (TPV) must be properly licensed by the appropriate local and state authority. • The TPV must be insured by a carrier with an AM Best Rating of A- or higher and a minimum of $1,000,000 per occurrence, $2,000,000 policy aggregate. • Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter must be listed as an additional insured on a primary basis. • The TPV must assume in writing executed in the chapter name of Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. all responsibilities that any purveyor of alcoholic beverages would assume in the normal course of business.

The four checkboxes on the online form are compressed versions of those bullets. Because they are truncated, each one is shown below with the fuller source wording beside it.

A Checked Box Is a Representation

This is the module where the difference matters most. Checking "Venue is properly licensed" is not an act of compliance. It is a statement that the chapter believes, on a reasonable basis, that the venue holds the required licenses. The Kappa source is explicit that by submitting the form, you agree the information is factual and truthful, and that in the event of a policy violation the organization may be asked to produce supporting documents. Check boxes you can support.

The Four Fields

Contract is executed in the chapter
System FieldContract is executed in the chapter
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Contract is executed in the chapter name of the national fraternity"

What it means. The agreement is a contract between the third party and the chapter as an entity of Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. — not between the third party and an individual brother.

Why it matters. Three reasons, in ascending order of seriousness.

  1. It establishes who the contracting party is. Insurance, indemnity, and additional-insured provisions all run to the named party. If the named party is "Marcus T." rather than the chapter, none of it protects the organization.
  2. It protects the individual member. A brother who signs personally can be personally liable for the venue's cancellation fees, damage charges, and minimums — and personally on the hook if the event goes badly.
  3. It is the foundation for everything else in this section. Additional-insured status "for the Fraternity and the chapter" makes sense only if the Fraternity and the chapter are the contracting parties.

How to complete it.

  1. Read the first paragraph and the signature block of the agreement. Identify exactly who is named.
  2. If it names an individual, ask the venue to reissue naming the chapter as an entity of Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. Venues do this routinely; you just have to ask before signing.
  3. Have the authorized person sign — the Kappa source names the chapter president or advisor as examples of the person authorized by the organization.
  4. Sign in a representative capacity: name, then title, then the chapter and organization. Not just a signature on a line.
  5. Confirm both parties have signed and dated. The source requires both.
  6. Only then check the box.
Acceptable

"This Agreement is between Grandview Hotel & Conference Center and Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. — Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter." Signed: A. Coleman, Polemarch, Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter, Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc., dated; countersigned and dated by the venue.

Not Acceptable

An agreement naming a brother personally. An agreement naming "the Kappas" or "Kappa Denton." A contract signed by the chapter but never countersigned by the venue. An undated signature. A brother signing "on behalf of the chapter" when he holds no authority to bind it.

Example. A hotel's standard banquet event order arrives with the Event Chair's personal name and home address in the client block. He emails the catering manager: "Please reissue with the client as Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. — Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter, and address it to our chapter mailing address. Our Polemarch will sign." The revised BEO comes back the next day.

Common kickback reasons. Contract signed by an individual; only one party signed; no dates; the contracting entity's name does not match the entity named as additional insured elsewhere in the packet.

Documentation to have ready. The fully executed contract with both signatures and dates, and the signature block showing representative capacity.

Do Not Check This Box Until…

…you have the fully executed contract in hand, you have read the party block, and the party is the chapter as an entity of the national Fraternity. Not "the venue said they'd fix it." Not "it's in DocuSign." In hand, signed by both, dated.

Venue is properly licensed
System FieldVenue is properly licensed
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"The Third-Party Vendor (TPV) must be properly licensed by the appropriate local and state authority."

What it means. The third party holds the governmental licenses its operations require — which, depending on the venue, may include a business license, a certificate of occupancy, a food-service permit, and, where alcohol is served, a state alcoholic beverage license.

Why it matters. A license is a state's confirmation that a business has met minimum standards and can be held accountable through a mechanism that matters to it — suspension or revocation. An unlicensed operation serving alcohol is not just a compliance problem for the chapter; it is a business with nothing at stake in refusing service to a minor.

How to complete it — what a reasonable basis looks like.

  1. Ask the venue directly, in writing, for its license number and the issuing authority.
  2. Where alcohol is involved, ask specifically for the alcoholic beverage license — in Texas, the TABC permit — and note the number and expiration.
  3. Verify against the issuing authority's public license lookup where one exists. Most state alcoholic beverage commissions publish one.
  4. Look for the posted license at the venue during your site visit. Licensed premises are generally required to display it.
  5. Write the license requirement into the contract so the venue represents its licensed status contractually.
  6. Save what you found — the email, the screenshot, the license number.
Acceptable

"TABC Mixed Beverage Permit MB-1043827, issued to Grandview Hospitality LLC, expires 09/2027; number provided in writing by the catering manager 3/12 and confirmed against the TABC public lookup 3/12. Permit also observed posted at the banquet bar during the 3/09 site visit. Contract Section 9 contains the venue's representation that it holds all required licenses."

Not Acceptable

"It's a popular venue." / "They've been open for years." / "Everybody has events there." / "They wouldn't be allowed to operate if they weren't licensed." / A member's assurance that he has been there before.

Example. Two chapters book the same event hall. One checks the box because the hall is well known locally. The other asks for the permit number, looks it up, finds the permit is held by a different entity than the one on the contract, and asks about it — discovering that the hall's alcohol service is actually run by a separate catering company that will need its own contract and certificate. The second chapter now has an accurate packet; the first has an unsupported representation.

Common kickback reasons. Box checked with no license information anywhere in the packet; alcohol involved but no alcoholic beverage license identified; license held by an entity other than the contracting party.

Documentation to have ready. License or permit number and issuing authority; verification screenshot or email; the contractual representation of licensed status.

Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "If a vendor is popular, it must be properly licensed."
Fact: Popularity is not proof of licensing. Volume of business tells you a venue is busy. It does not tell you which entity holds which permit, whether the permit is current, or whether it covers the service being provided at your event.

Do Not Check This Box Until…

…you have a license number, an issuing authority, and a verification you can point to. "It is a popular venue" is not a reasonable basis. Neither is "they told us they were licensed" with nothing written down.

Venue is insured with a minimum
System FieldVenue is insured with a minimum
Source Meaning — Kappa SourceForm line: "Venue is insured with a minimum of $1,00,000 of general liability insurance Yes / No" Requirement bullet: "The TPV must be insured by a carrier with an AM Best Rating of A- or higher and a minimum of $1,000,000 per occurrence, $2,000,000 policy aggregate."
Note on the Source Text

The form line as printed in the manual contains a typographical error — "$1,00,000" — while the requirement bullet on the same page reads "$1,000,000 per occurrence, $2,000,000 policy aggregate." This course uses the requirement bullet, which is consistent with the Special Events minimum limits stated elsewhere in the manual. Both are reproduced above so you can see exactly what the source says.

What it means. The venue carries general liability insurance meeting at least the stated minimum limits, written by a carrier of acceptable financial strength, in force on the date of your event.

Why it matters. Insurance is the financial mechanism that responds when the venue's operations cause harm — a wet floor, a defective railing, a kitchen fire, an over-served guest. Without it, a claim arising from the venue's negligence has nowhere to go but toward whoever else is standing nearby, which includes the chapter.

The full minimum limits from the Kappa source's Special Events section.

CoverageMinimum limit
General Liability — Each Occurrence$1,000,000
General Liability — General Aggregate$2,000,000
Products / Completed Operations$2,000,000
Liquor Liability — Each Common Cause$300,000
Liquor Liability — Aggregate$300,000
Carrier financial strengthA.M. Best rating not less than A-, VII
Also requiredWorkers Compensation and Employers Liability
TimingIn force on the event date; not cancelled, discontinued, or expiring on that date

How to complete it.

  1. Request the certificate of insurance in writing, stating the limits you require and the event date.
  2. When it arrives, check the named insured against the contracting entity.
  3. Check the policy period against the event date — and note whether it expires within days of your event.
  4. Check each limit line against the table above.
  5. Check the carrier's A.M. Best rating.
  6. Where alcohol is served, confirm liquor liability appears. A general liability policy without liquor liability does not respond to alcohol-related claims.
  7. Attach the certificate to the packet. Then check the box.
Acceptable

"Certificate received 3/14 from venue's agent. Named insured Grandview Hospitality LLC (matches contract). Policy period 01/01/2026–01/01/2027, in force on the 4/18 event date. GL each occurrence $1M, general aggregate $2M, products/completed ops $2M, liquor liability $300K/$300K. Carrier A.M. Best A, XV. Workers compensation evidenced. Certificate attached."

Not Acceptable

"They're insured." / A certificate whose policy period ends before the event date. / A certificate with $500,000 limits. / A certificate with no liquor liability at an event where the venue's bar is serving. / A certificate for a different legal entity. / A certificate the chapter never actually read.

Common kickback reasons. Box checked, no certificate attached. Certificate attached, policy period does not cover the event date. Limits below the minimums. Liquor liability missing where alcohol is served. Named insured mismatch.

Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "If the venue says it has insurance, I can check the insurance box."
Fact: The chapter should have the required documentation or verification rather than relying only on an informal statement. The Kappa source does not say "confirm they have insurance." It says the chapter must verify by obtaining a certificate of insurance.

Do Not Check This Box Until…

…the certificate is in the packet and you have personally read the named insured, the policy period, the limits, and the carrier rating. A certificate you received but did not read is how expired-policy kickbacks happen.

Fraternity is named as an additional
System FieldFraternity is named as an additional
Source Meaning — Kappa SourceForm line: "Fraternity is named as an additional insured on all certificates from vendors Yes / No" Requirement bullet: "Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter must be listed as an additional insured on a primary basis."

What it means. The vendor's or venue's insurance policy has been endorsed to extend specified protection to Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter, and that protection responds on a primary basis — meaning it responds first, rather than sitting behind the Fraternity's own coverage.

Why it matters. Without additional-insured status, the vendor's policy protects the vendor. With it, defined protection extends to the Fraternity and the chapter for covered matters associated with that vendor and event. "Primary basis" matters because it determines whose insurer is expected to respond first — and that determines whether the Fraternity's program is drawn into a matter arising from someone else's operations.

Three Terms Brothers Confuse
Named Insured
The party who bought the policy — the vendor or venue itself. The policy exists to protect this party.
Additional Insured
A party added to the policy by endorsement, receiving specified protection under someone else's policy for liability arising from that party's operations. This is what the Kappa source requires for the Fraternity and the chapter.
Certificate Holder
The party the certificate was sent to. It is a mailing designation. It confers no coverage whatsoever. This is the single most common misunderstanding on the entire checklist.

How to complete it.

  1. Put the requirement in the contract before signing: the vendor shall name Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and [chapter name] as additional insureds on a primary and non-contributory basis.
  2. State the exact names you need endorsed. Ambiguity here produces a useless endorsement.
  3. When the certificate arrives, look at the Description of Operations box — that is normally where additional-insured status is stated, not in the certificate holder box.
  4. Confirm both the Fraternity and the chapter are named, and confirm "primary" appears.
  5. If the certificate names only the Fraternity, or only the chapter, or shows the Fraternity merely as certificate holder, send it back to the agent.
  6. Attach the certificate showing the endorsement. Then check the box.
Acceptable

Description of Operations reads: "Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter are named as additional insureds on a primary and non-contributory basis with respect to the event held 4/18/2026 at the Magnolia Ballroom."

Not Acceptable

The Fraternity appears only in the "Certificate Holder" box. / Only the chapter is named, not the Fraternity. / Additional-insured status is stated but not on a primary basis. / The vendor emails "yes, you're covered" without a certificate showing it. / The endorsement references a different event or date.

Example. A chapter's caterer sends a certificate with "Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc." typed into the certificate holder box and nothing in the description of operations. The Keeper of Records replies to the agent: "We need Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter shown as additional insureds on a primary and non-contributory basis in the Description of Operations, for the 4/18/2026 event. Certificate holder status alone does not meet our requirement." A corrected certificate arrives in two days.

Common kickback reasons. Certificate holder mistaken for additional insured; only one of the two required entities named; "primary" omitted; box checked with no certificate showing any endorsement.

Do Not Check This Box Until…

…you are looking at a certificate that names both Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and your chapter as additional insureds, on a primary basis. If you are looking at the certificate holder box, you are looking at the wrong box.

Different Direction, Do Not Confuse Them

This section is about the vendor's policy naming the Fraternity. Module 10 — Additional Insured Request — is the opposite direction: a venue asking to be added to the Fraternity's national policy. Same vocabulary, opposite flow. Chapters mix them up constantly.

Scenario

▶ Scenario — The Certificate That Says the Wrong Thing

Nine days before the event, the venue's certificate arrives. The Event Chair scans it, sees "Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc." on the page, and checks all four Third Party boxes. The Chapter Risk Manager asks to see it. On review: the Fraternity's name appears only in the certificate holder box; the chapter is not named anywhere; the policy period ends eleven days after the event; liquor liability is not listed, though the venue's bar will be serving; and the named insured is "Grandview Hospitality Group LLC" while the contract is with "Grandview Hotel & Conference Center."

How many defects are there, and what does the chapter do with nine days left?

Four defects, one non-issue.

Defect 1 — certificate holder is not additional insured. The Fraternity's name in the holder box confers nothing. The chapter needs both the Fraternity and the chapter named as additional insureds on a primary basis in the Description of Operations.

Defect 2 — the chapter is not named. The requirement is both entities, not one.

Defect 3 — no liquor liability. The venue's bar is serving. The minimum limits include liquor liability $300,000 each common cause and $300,000 aggregate. A certificate without it does not evidence coverage for the exposure this event actually creates.

Defect 4 — entity mismatch. The named insured and the contracting party are different names. Either the certificate is for the wrong entity, or the contract is with the wrong entity. One of the two has to be corrected, and the chapter needs to know which.

Non-issue: the policy period ending eleven days after the event is fine — the requirement is that coverage be in force on the event date. It is worth noticing, because a renewal that close means the chapter should not accept this certificate for any event after that date.

What to do: one email to the venue's agent, copying the catering manager, listing all four corrections specifically and asking for a corrected certificate.
