Nine days is enough time; agents reissue certificates in one to three business days. Uncheck the boxes in the meantime. Do not submit the packet with four representations the documents do not support — that is a returned submission and, worse, a set of statements the chapter cannot stand behind.

Knowledge Check

Module 6 · Question 1

A certificate of insurance lists Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. in the "Certificate Holder" box and nothing in the Description of Operations. Is the additional-insured requirement met?

✓ Correct answer: C. Certificate holder means the certificate was sent to you. It confers no coverage. The Kappa requirement is that Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter be listed as additional insured on a primary basis, which normally appears in the Description of Operations. D is wrong because a correction after the event is worthless — the endorsement has to be in place while the exposure exists.
Module 6 · Question 2

Which of these constitutes a reasonable basis for checking "Venue is properly licensed"?

✓ Correct answer: A. A license number, an issuing authority, and a verification you can point to constitute a basis. B, C, and D are reputation, familiarity, and marketing copy respectively — none of which tells you which entity holds which permit or whether it is current. Marketing language (D) is particularly weak, because a website is written by the venue and updated whenever it feels like it.
Module 6 · Question 3

The venue's banquet agreement is made out to the Event Chair personally. He plans to sign it because he is acting for the chapter anyway. The most complete objection is:

✓ Correct answer: D. All three objections are real and they reinforce each other. The personal exposure is the one brothers feel; the requirement is the one the form asks about; and the additional-insured mismatch is the one that quietly undermines the rest of the packet, because the protections the chapter is arranging run to parties the contract does not name.

Companies Promoter

A promoter is not a DJ with a bigger budget. When someone else is producing, promoting, or monetizing your event, a distinct set of licensing and insurance provisions applies — and the relationship has to be disclosed.

⏱ 20 min🎤 3 fields
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) recognize when a promoter relationship exists; (2) distinguish a promoter from a venue, a DJ, and a ticketing service; (3) state the promoter insurance provisions from the Kappa source; (4) complete the three promoter fields with supporting documentation.

What the Kappa Source Says

Kappa Source — If using an Event Company/Promoter"If an Event Promotion Company/Promoter is used for events (e.g. fundraisers, concerts, step shows) they must be licensed and insured with the following general liability provisions: • $1,000,000 per occurrence for Bodily Injury and Property Damage • $1,000,000 per occurrence for Personal and Advertising Injury • $1,000,000 per occurrence for Products/Completed Operations • $2,000,000 annual aggregate including Products/Completed Operations • Includes contractual liability • Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter must be listed as an additional insured on a primary basis"

Note that a certificate of insurance for all Promotion Company/Promoter arrangements is also on the Kappa source's list of documents to submit with the completed Event Notification Form.

Note too what is on this list that is not on the general vendor list: personal and advertising injury. That is not an accident. A promoter's core activity is advertising — flyers, graphics, social campaigns, radio spots, name and likeness use. Personal and advertising injury coverage responds to things like defamation, invasion of privacy, and infringement of copyrighted advertising material. If a promoter uses an unlicensed image, misuses someone's likeness, or produces a flyer that defames someone, that is the exposure this coverage addresses.

What Is an Event Company / Promoter?

A promoter is an outside party that produces, promotes, or monetizes the event, usually with its own operational role and often with a financial stake in the outcome. The Kappa source names the settings where promoters typically appear: fundraisers, concerts, and step shows.

Classification depends on actual responsibilities, not the business's name. A company called "Elite Event Promotions" that only prints your flyers is a printer. A person with no business name at all who sells the tickets, books the artist, hires the security, and takes half the door is a promoter.

Five Questions That Reveal a Promoter Relationship

If the answer to two or more of these is yes, you are probably dealing with a promoter and should treat the relationship accordingly:

  1. Does the outside party have a revenue interest in the event — a share of the door, of ticket sales, or of the bar?
  2. Is the outside party producing the event — booking talent, arranging staging or production, engaging its own subcontractors?
  3. Is the outside party promoting the event under its own brand, or driving the marketing?
  4. Does the outside party control ticketing or admission?
  5. Does the outside party bring its own staff to work the event?

Promoter vs. Everything Else

PartyWhat it doesPromoter?What the checklist requires
Concert promoterBooks the artist, produces the show, sells tickets, takes a share of revenue, brings production staffYesCompanies Promoter section: licensed, insured with the six provisions, Kappa named additional insured on a primary basis. Also a vendor with a contract.
Step-show promoterProduces the show, handles ticketing, coordinates teams, splits proceeds with the chapterYesSame as above. Named expressly in the Kappa source.
Outside event-production companyRuns staging, lighting, sound, and show operations for the chapter under its own directionUsually yesEvaluate the five questions. Production control plus its own staff generally puts it in this section.
Ticketing company onlyHosts the registration or ticket page and processes payment. No production role, no promotion, no staff on site, no revenue share beyond a processing feeUsually noTreat as a vendor and as part of the attendance-control system in Module 3. If it also promotes or takes a revenue share, re-evaluate.
DJ onlyPlays music for a flat fee under the chapter's directionNoVendor: contract, certificate of insurance, contact block. Module 5.
VenueOwns or controls the premisesNoThird Party section, Module 6. A venue that also promotes the event is both.
Graphic designerDesigns the flyer to the chapter's directionNoVendor if contracted. The flyer itself is reviewed in Module 11.
Red Flag — The Undisclosed Promoter

The most common promoter failure is not a bad promoter. It is an undisclosed one — a chapter that answers "no" to the promoter question because the arrangement felt like a favor, a partnership, or "a brother who knows the scene." Undisclosed promoter relationships are a named cause of returned submissions, and they are usually discovered the same way: the flyer says "presented by" someone the checklist never mentioned.

Supplemental Note

Supplemental · Holmes Murphy 2026 Template

The template states that an organization must not co-host or cosponsor an event with a bar, event promoter, or alcohol distributor, while permitting the organization to rent a bar, restaurant, or other licensed and insured third-party vendor to host an event. The Kappa source does not phrase it that way — it permits an Event Company/Promoter to be used, subject to the licensing and insurance provisions above. The distinction the template is drawing is still worth understanding: there is a difference between engaging a promoter under a contract on your terms and partnering with one who effectively owns the event while your letters are on the flyer. The second arrangement is where chapters lose control.

The Three Fields

Company/Promoter is properly licensed
System FieldCompany/Promoter is properly licensed
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Event Company/Promoter is properly licensed Yes / No" — under the requirement that promoters used for events such as fundraisers, concerts, and step shows "must be licensed and insured."

What it means. The promoter operates as a properly licensed business.

Why it matters. Licensing is the baseline test of whether you are dealing with a business or with an individual operating informally. A licensed entity has a legal identity, a registered agent, a tax status, and something to lose. An unlicensed promoter can disappear the week after the event, and there is no entity left to hold to the contract.

How to complete it.

  1. Ask for the legal entity name and business registration or license number.
  2. Verify the entity exists with the state — most Secretary of State offices publish a free business-entity search.
  3. Ask what additional licensing the promoter's activity requires in your jurisdiction. Some cities license event promoters, ticket sellers, or public amusement operations directly.
  4. If the promoter is handling alcohol in any capacity, confirm alcoholic beverage licensing — and re-read Module 4, because a promoter purchasing or providing alcohol raises the prohibition discussed there.
  5. Confirm the entity name matches the contract and the certificate of insurance.
Acceptable

"Skyline Event Group LLC, Texas SOS filing number 0803991244, active status confirmed 3/10; entity name matches the executed production agreement and the certificate of insurance."

Not Acceptable

"He's been promoting parties in this city for ten years." / A promoter operating under a name with no registered entity behind it. / An entity name on the contract that does not appear in any state registry. / "He said he's licensed."

Common kickback reasons. Box checked with no entity or license identified; promoter operating personally with no business entity; entity name mismatch between contract and certificate.

Do Not Check This Box Until…

…you have a legal entity name you have verified with a public registry, and that name matches your contract.

Promoter is insured with the provisions
System FieldPromoter is insured with the provisions
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Promoter is insured with the provisions outlined in the Kappa Alpha Psi® Undergraduate Risk Management Policy Yes / No"

What it means. The promoter carries general liability insurance meeting the specific provisions the Kappa source sets for promoters.

Why it matters. A promoter creates independent operational exposure that the venue's policy and the chapter's arrangements do not reach. It is booking talent, running production, driving crowds, and advertising under its own brand. Each of those is a source of claims, and the promoter's own coverage is what should respond first.

ProvisionMinimumWhy it is on the list
Bodily Injury & Property Damage$1,000,000 per occurrenceCrowd injuries, staging and equipment failures, property damage at the venue
Personal & Advertising Injury$1,000,000 per occurrenceThe promoter's advertising activity — defamation, privacy, misuse of images or likeness in promotion
Products / Completed Operations$1,000,000 per occurrenceClaims arising after the work is done, and any food or beverage element
Annual Aggregate$2,000,000 including products/completed operationsTotal available across the policy year
Contractual LiabilityIncludedSo the indemnity the promoter gives the chapter in the contract is actually backed by insurance
Additional InsuredKappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter, on a primary basisExtends specified protection to the Fraternity and chapter and puts the promoter's coverage first

How to complete it. Request the certificate specifying these provisions by name. Read it line by line against the table. Pay particular attention to personal and advertising injury and to contractual liability, because those are the two most often missing from a small promoter's policy.

Acceptable

"Certificate received 3/09. BI/PD $1M per occurrence; personal & advertising injury $1M; products/completed operations $1M; general aggregate $2M including products/completed operations; contractual liability included per policy form; Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter named additional insureds on a primary and non-contributory basis. Policy in force through 12/2026."

Not Acceptable

A certificate showing only bodily injury and property damage. / A certificate with no personal and advertising injury for a party whose entire function is advertising. / An event-specific policy purchased for a different date. / "He's covered under the venue's policy" — the venue's policy insures the venue.

Common kickback reasons. Missing personal and advertising injury; missing contractual liability; aggregate below $2,000,000; certificate not attached; coverage not in force on the event date.

Practical Tip

Send the promoter the exact six provisions in writing when you first discuss the event, not after you have agreed to terms. A promoter who cannot meet them needs to tell you that in week one, not in week nine. And a promoter who reacts badly to being asked for standard insurance provisions has told you something useful about how he operates.

Event Company/Promoter has added Kappa
System FieldEvent Company/Promoter has added Kappa
Source Meaning — Kappa SourceForm line: "Event Company/Promoter has added Kappa Alpha Psi® as an additional insured Yes / No" Requirement bullet: "Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter must be listed as an additional insured on a primary basis."

What it means. The promoter's policy has actually been endorsed to add Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter as additional insureds, on a primary basis.

Why it matters. The word in the field is "has added." Past tense, completed action. Not "will add," not "agreed to add," not "his agent is working on it." This box asks whether it is done.

How to complete it.

  1. Put the requirement into the contract before signing, naming both entities and the primary basis.
  2. Require the certificate as a condition of the deposit or the first payment. Payment is the only leverage the chapter reliably has.
  3. When the certificate arrives, look at the Description of Operations for the additional-insured language — not the certificate holder box.
  4. Confirm both the Fraternity and the chapter appear, and that "primary" appears.
  5. Confirm the endorsement references your event and date.
  6. Attach it. Then check the box.
Acceptable

Certificate in hand whose Description of Operations names Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter as additional insureds on a primary and non-contributory basis for the specific event and date, attached to the packet.

Not Acceptable

"He said his agent is sending it." / Chapter named but Fraternity not. / Fraternity named but chapter not. / Additional insured stated without "primary." / Certificate holder box used instead of the endorsement. / Box checked on the strength of a text message.

Example. A chapter engages a step-show promoter. The contract requires the certificate before the deposit is released. Two weeks later the promoter sends a certificate naming only the chapter. The Keeper of Records replies: "We need both Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter shown as additional insureds on a primary and non-contributory basis for the 4/18 event. The deposit will be released once we have the corrected certificate." The corrected certificate arrives in three days.

Common kickback reasons. Box checked before the endorsement exists; only one entity named; primary basis omitted; endorsement referencing the wrong event or date.

Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "An additional-insured request means the entity has already been added."
Fact: A request and an approved endorsement are not the same thing. This field asks whether the promoter has added Kappa — which you can only answer from a document, not from an intention.

Do Not Check This Box Until…

…you are holding the certificate showing the endorsement. If the certificate is not in the packet, the honest answer to this field is no.

Scenarios

▶ Scenario — "He's Just Helping Us Fill the Room"

A brother's associate offers to help with the chapter's spring concert. He books the headline artist through his own contacts, designs and pays for the flyers, runs the ticket link through his own account, brings four of his own people to work the door and merchandise table, and takes 40% of ticket revenue. The Event Chair describes him on the checklist as "a volunteer helping with promotion" and answers "no" to the Event Company/Promoter question.

How should this relationship actually be classified, and what does the chapter now owe the packet?

This is a promoter relationship, and it is not close. Run the five questions: revenue interest (40% of ticket revenue), production (books the artist), promotion (designs and pays for marketing), ticketing control (runs the ticket link through his own account), own staff on site (four people working door and merchandise). All five are yes.

The label "volunteer" is contradicted by every operational fact, and answering "no" to the promoter question is a false statement on a form the chapter signs as factual and truthful. It is also the kind of discrepancy a reviewer finds easily, because the flyer he designed will carry his brand.

What the chapter now owes: a written contract with a verified legal entity; confirmation of licensing; a certificate of insurance meeting all six promoter provisions including personal and advertising injury and contractual liability; Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter named additional insureds on a primary basis; and the corrected answers on the checklist.

The harder question: he is running ticketing through his own account, which means the chapter does not control admission, does not hold the attendee list, and cannot enforce a cap or a close date — all of which Module 3 requires. And if he has no business entity and no insurance, this arrangement cannot be documented at all, which means it cannot proceed in this form. Better to restructure now than to discover it at 8 PM on show night when 900 people are outside a 600-capacity room.

▶ Scenario — The Ticketing Platform

A chapter uses an online ticketing platform for its scholarship gala. The platform hosts the registration page, processes payments, and charges a per-ticket fee. It does no marketing, sends no staff, and has no say in the event. A committee member asks whether the platform needs to be entered in the Companies Promoter section.

Does it?

No. Run the five questions and only one is arguably yes — it controls the ticketing mechanism — and even that is a hosting function rather than control over admission, since the chapter sets the cap, the close date, and the door process. There is no revenue interest beyond a processing fee, no production role, no promotion, and no staff on site.

The platform belongs in two other places instead: the attendance and invitation system in Module 3, where the chapter describes how registration is configured, capped, closed, exported, and used at the door; and, if the chapter has a contract with it, in the vendor section.

The lesson is that classification follows function. Do not put a party in the promoter section because it touches tickets, and do not leave a party out of it because it never called itself a promoter.

Knowledge Check

Module 7 · Question 1

Which coverage appears in the Kappa source's promoter provisions but not in the general vendor minimums, and why is it there?

✓ Correct answer: B. The promoter provisions expressly include $1,000,000 per occurrence for Personal and Advertising Injury. A promoter produces flyers, graphics, social campaigns, and uses names and likenesses — activities that can generate defamation, privacy, and advertising-infringement claims. Workers compensation (A) is required of venues and vendors generally under the Special Events requirements; liquor liability (C) attaches where alcohol is served rather than to promoters as a class.
Module 7 · Question 2

The checklist field reads "Event Company/Promoter has added Kappa." The promoter has verbally agreed to add the Fraternity and says his agent is processing it. The correct answer is:

✓ Correct answer: A. "Has added" is past tense. Until a certificate shows the endorsement naming both Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter on a primary basis, the honest answer is no — and the chapter should be chasing the certificate rather than the checkbox. D is understandable but produces an incomplete field, which is itself a returned-submission cause; answer accurately and note that the certificate is pending.
Module 7 · Question 3

Which arrangement is most likely to be a promoter relationship requiring the Companies Promoter section?

✓ Correct answer: C — production, promotion, ticketing control, and a revenue interest, which is four of the five diagnostic questions. A and B are vendors performing defined services under the chapter's direction. D is a service provider, addressed in the attendance-system section. Classification follows function, not the party's name or self-description.

Alcohol and BYOB

The longest section of the checklist, and the one where a thin answer does the most damage. Every field here describes a control that has to exist as an actual operation on the night of the event.

⏱ 45 min🍺 18 fields⚠ Highest risk
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) state the governing alcohol rules; (2) assign carding responsibility and choose an age-identification method; (3) set and document drink quantities; (4) design and describe a service distribution center; (5) staff and brief event monitors; (6) operate a ticket or punch card check-in system; (7) walk a controlled BYOB event from arrival to departure.

Part One — The Governing Rules

Before any checkbox, know the rules the checkboxes are implementing. These come from the Kappa source, and several are restated in the Holmes Murphy 2026 template.

1

Legal drinking age

No person under the legal drinking age may possess, consume, provide, sell, or be provided alcoholic beverages. Members and guests must comply with all federal, state, provincial, and local laws.

2

Illegal drugs and controlled substances

No person may possess, use, provide, distribute, sell, or manufacture illegal drugs or other controlled substances on premises or at any activity or event sponsored or endorsed by the chapter. The Prevention Ideas list includes removing any person who has illegal drugs or a controlled substance.

3

Two lawful models only

Alcohol either (a) provided and sold on a per-drink basis by a licensed and insured third-party vendor, or (b) brought by individual members and guests through a BYOB system. There is no third option in which the chapter or a partner organization supplies the alcohol.

4

No common source

Common sources of alcohol, including bulk quantities, not being served by a licensed and insured third-party vendor, are prohibited — that is, amounts greater than what a reasonable person should consume over the duration of an event. No kegs, no punch, no open bottles set out for the room.

5

No chapter funds, no pooled funds

Alcoholic beverages must not be purchased with chapter funds or with funds pooled by members or guests. The template names the modern versions explicitly: admission fees, cover fees, and collecting funds through digital apps.

6

No co-sponsorship with a supplier

A chapter must not co-host or cosponsor, or in any way participate in, an event with another group or entity that purchases or provides alcohol, illegal drugs, or controlled substances.

7

Promoter requirements

An Event Company/Promoter must be licensed and insured to the promoter provisions in Module 7, with Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter named additional insured on a primary basis.

8

No drinking games or rapid consumption

Members and guests must not permit, encourage, coerce, glorify, or participate in any activities involving the rapid consumption of alcohol, such as drinking games. This is the rule behind the "No tables or paraphernalia" prevention item in Module 9.

9

Intoxicated persons

A licensed and insured third-party vendor must refrain from serving individuals who appear to be intoxicated. Under BYOB, that judgment falls to the chapter's monitors — which is why monitor selection and briefing matter so much.

10

Vendor control of alcohol

A third-party vendor must maintain absolute control of ALL alcoholic containers present, and no excess alcohol — opened or unopened — may be given, sold, or furnished to the chapter.

11

Invitation-only attendance with a guest list

Where alcohol is present, attendance by non-members is by invitation with a system to track attendees, within fire code capacity. Alcohol control and attendance control are the same problem viewed from two angles.

Supplemental Note

Supplemental · Holmes Murphy 2026 Template

The template adds two provisions this course does not treat as Kappa requirements: alcohol above 15% ABV prohibited except when served by a licensed and insured third-party vendor, and a guest-to-member ratio not exceeding 3:1 at events with alcohol (which the template itself identifies as an NIC guideline that clients may adjust). Both are useful planning references. Neither should be stated to your chapter as a Kappa rule.

Part Two — The Fields

Governing policies

Are there BYOB policies
System FieldAre there BYOB policies
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Are there any university or Fraternity/Sorority policies that deal with BYOB events? Yes / No"

What it means. Whether additional governing policies — from a university, a Greek life office, an interfraternity or National Pan-Hellenic Council, or a host institution — apply to a BYOB event at this location.

Why it matters. The chapter must identify every requirement that governs the event before conducting it, not after. Campuses commonly impose their own rules: registration deadlines, mandatory monitor training, prohibitions on alcohol at certain facilities, limits on event hours, or outright bans on BYOB. The Kappa source also notes that where a host institution's health-and-safety rules conflict with the Named Insured's, the Fraternity's rule controls for insurance purposes — which means you may have to satisfy both, and the stricter requirement usually governs in practice.

How to complete it.

  1. For undergraduate chapters: contact the Fraternity and Sorority Life office and ask for the current social-event and BYOB policy in writing.
  2. Check the council policy — NPHC, IFC, or the campus governing council — which may impose additional registration or monitor requirements.
  3. For alumni chapters at a university venue: the facility-use agreement usually incorporates campus alcohol policy by reference. Read it.
  4. Check the venue's own alcohol policy. Many prohibit outside alcohol entirely, which ends the BYOB question.
  5. Answer yes and identify the policies, or answer no because you checked — not because you did not look.
Acceptable

"Yes — UNT Fraternity & Sorority Life Social Event Policy requires event registration 14 days in advance, a minimum of four sober monitors, and a guest list submitted to the office; NPHC council policy additionally requires an advisor present. Both requirements are reflected in this plan and the registration confirmation is attached."

Not Acceptable

"No" entered without checking. / "Not sure." / "N/A" at an event held on a campus with a published social policy.

Common kickback reasons. Answered no at a campus venue where policies obviously exist; answered yes with no policies identified; campus registration referenced but not attached.

Documentation to have ready. The campus or council social-event policy; the campus event-registration confirmation; the venue's alcohol policy.

Carding — who checks identification

Kappa Source — Event Notification Form"Members and guests should be 'carded' at the door to verify their age. This is the responsibility of the: Chapter members / New members [NOT recommended unless chapter members are also participating] / The campus police are providing someone to check IDs / The chapter has hired a security company"
Carding Is Not the Same as Marking

Two distinct acts happen at the door, and brothers collapse them constantly.

Carding is examining a government-issued photo identification, confirming it belongs to the person holding it, and determining that the person is of legal drinking age.

Marking is applying the wristband or hand stamp that tells everyone else in the room that the carding already happened.

Age verification occurs before the attendee is marked. A monitor at the distribution center who sees a wristband is relying on someone else's carding — which is exactly why the wristband must be event-specific and the carding must be done by someone competent to do it.

Carded by chapter members
System FieldCarded by chapter members

What it means. Established chapter members check identification at the door.

Why it matters. Age must be verified before anyone is identified as permitted to consume. Assigning it to chapter members places the responsibility with people who have standing in the organization and who can be held accountable for how they do it.

How to complete it.

  1. Name the specific brothers assigned, and put them on the monitor plan by name and shift.
  2. Assign brothers who will remain sober for the entire event. This is not negotiable and should be stated openly when the assignment is made.
  3. Brief them on what to accept: unexpired government-issued photo identification — driver's license, state ID, passport, military ID.
  4. Brief them on what to do with a questionable ID: decline the wristband, do not confiscate, do not argue, escalate to the officer in charge.
  5. Give them a backup: a second brother at the door so nobody is alone with a difficult guest.
  6. Rotate the assignment so the same two brothers are not at the door for five hours.
Acceptable

"Bro. R. Nunez and Bro. C. Battle at the entrance 7:00–10:00 PM; Bro. D. Hayes and Bro. M. Sloan 10:00 PM–close. All four sober for the duration. Unexpired government-issued photo ID required; dated event wristband applied only after ID verification; questionable IDs escalated to the Chapter Risk Manager, who has authority to refuse."

Not Acceptable

"Members will card." / "Whoever's at the door." / Assigning brothers who intend to drink. / One brother alone at the entrance for the entire night.

Red Flag

A carding assignment with no named brothers is not an assignment. If the plan says "chapter members" and nobody can name them the day before, nobody will be at the door.

Carded by New Members
System FieldCarded by New Members
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"New members [NOT recommended unless chapter members are also participating]"

What it means. New members assist with identification verification at the door.

Why it matters. The Kappa source flags this option and expressly does not recommend it unless chapter members are also participating. The reason is practical: carding requires the person doing it to refuse people, including people with social standing over him. A new member asked to turn away a member's guest is in a position he cannot reasonably be expected to hold.

There is a second consideration. Requiring new members to work while others socialize can shade into differential treatment during the intake period, and chapters should be alert to that. Where new members participate, they should do so alongside established members, in the same roles, on the same terms.

How to complete it. Select this only in combination with "Carded by chapter members," and describe the pairing explicitly.

Acceptable

"Door staffed by two established members (Bro. Nunez, Bro. Battle) with two new members assisting under their direction. Established members make all admission and age determinations; new members handle the guest-list check-in sheet. All four sober."

Not Acceptable

New members carding alone. / New members given authority to refuse admission with no member present. / Selecting this box because no member volunteered.

Practical Tip

If the only people willing to work the door are new members, the chapter has a commitment problem rather than a staffing problem. Fix it at chapter, not at the door.

Carded by people defined the camp police
System FieldCarded by people defined the camp police
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"The campus police are providing someone to check IDs"

What it means. The truncated system label corresponds to campus police providing personnel to check identification. Read "camp police" as "campus police."

Why it matters. It places age verification with trained personnel rather than relying exclusively on event participants. Officers card people professionally, are not socially entangled with your guests, and carry authority that ends arguments before they start.

How to complete it.

  1. Arrange it formally through the campus police department, in writing, well in advance — not by asking an officer at the event.
  2. Confirm how many officers, their hours, and their specific role. "Providing someone to check IDs" is a defined function, not general presence.
  3. Confirm cost and who pays; many departments bill for event coverage.
  4. Get the arrangement in writing and attach it.
  5. Confirm whether this arrangement also satisfies the Security fields in Module 9 — often it does, and it should be described consistently in both places.
Acceptable

"UNT Police Department providing two officers 7:00 PM–12:30 AM under event coverage request #2026-0418, confirmed in writing 3/11; one officer stationed at the entrance for ID verification, one roving. Invoice and confirmation attached."

Not Acceptable

"Campus police will be around." / "We'll ask an officer that night." / Checking this box because a patrol car sometimes passes the venue.

Common kickback reasons. Box checked with no written confirmation; officer presence assumed rather than arranged; inconsistency between this field and the Security fields.

The chapter has hired a security compa
System FieldThe chapter has hired a security compa
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"The chapter has hired a security company"

What it means. A hired security company performs identification verification and related entry-control functions.

Why it matters. It provides designated professional personnel responsible for entry and age control, with training, licensing, and insurance behind them. It also removes the hardest interpersonal moments — refusing a guest, removing someone — from members' shoulders.

How to complete it. A security company is a vendor. That means the full Module 5 packet applies:

  1. Written contract executed in the chapter name of the national Fraternity, with the scope stated: ID verification at entry, number of guards, hours, and what they are and are not responsible for.
  2. Certificate of insurance meeting the minimum limits, with Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter named additional insured on a primary basis.
  3. State licensing verified — private security is a licensed occupation in most states.
  4. An on-site supervisor identified with a mobile number.
  5. A briefing before doors open: who has authority to make decisions for the chapter, what the guest-list procedure is, what the escalation path is, and where the emergency exits are.
Acceptable

"Sentinel Protective Services LLC, four licensed guards 6:30 PM–1:00 AM; contract executed in the chapter name 3/05; scope includes ID verification at the single entrance, bag check, and removal assistance at the direction of the officer in charge; state security license verified; certificate of insurance attached naming Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter as additional insureds on a primary basis; on-site supervisor L. Grant (214) 555-0190."

Not Acceptable

"We hired security." / A verbal arrangement with an off-duty acquaintance. / A security company with no contract and no certificate. / Guards hired but never briefed on the guest list.

Red Flag

Security personnel who arrive without a briefing will make up their own procedure, and it will not be yours. Fifteen minutes before doors is the highest-value fifteen minutes of the entire event.

Age identification method

Wristbands that have been dated
System FieldWristbands that have been dated
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Wristbands that have been dated and marked for that event"

What it means. Attendees verified as being of legal drinking age receive a wristband that is dated and marked specifically for this event.

Why it matters. It gives monitors an immediate visual method for identifying persons already verified as 21 or over, without re-carding at the distribution center. The dated and event-specific requirement is the whole point: a generic wristband can be bought online, brought from another event, or reused next weekend. A wristband marked for tonight cannot.

How to complete it.

  1. Use tamper-evident wristbands — the kind that tears if removed.
  2. Date and mark them for this event: the date, the event name, or a distinctive mark applied on site.
  3. Control the supply. One brother holds the wristbands; they are not left on a table.
  4. Apply them at the door, only after ID verification, and apply them yourself rather than handing them over.
  5. Count what you issue against your guest list — it is a useful cross-check on the door.
  6. Collect or destroy leftovers after the event so they cannot be reused.
Acceptable

"Tamper-evident wristbands pre-printed with the event name and date; applied at the entrance by the carding team immediately following ID verification; supply controlled by the Chapter Risk Manager; unissued bands collected at close."

Not Acceptable

Plain colored wristbands with no date or event marking. / A roll of wristbands sitting on the check-in table. / Handing bands to guests to apply themselves. / Reusing last semester's leftover bands.

Red Flag

Wristbands appearing on people the door team does not remember carding. If that happens, the marking system has failed and the chapter should switch to re-verification at the distribution center for the rest of the night.

Specific hand stamp that is unique to
System FieldSpecific hand stamp that is unique to
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Specific hand stamp that is unique to the event"

What it means. An event-specific hand stamp identifies attendees verified as being of legal drinking age.

Why it matters. Same function as the wristband — a visible signal to monitors that carding already happened. The controlling word is unique. A generic star or smiley stamp available at any craft store can be duplicated by anyone who sees it. Uniqueness is what makes the mark mean something.

How to complete it.

  1. Use a stamp that is not generic — a custom design, an unusual shape, or a distinctive ink color chosen for this event and not announced in advance.
  2. Keep the stamp with the carding team at all times. Do not leave it on the table.
  3. Apply it yourself after ID verification.
  4. Brief the distribution-center monitors on exactly what tonight's mark looks like, so they can spot a hand-drawn imitation.
  5. Consider the practical limits: stamps smudge, sweat off, and wash off, which is why wristbands are generally the more reliable choice for a long event.
Acceptable

"Custom event stamp in a single ink color selected the day of the event; held by the carding team; applied after ID verification; distribution-center monitors briefed on the mark at the 6:45 PM staff meeting."

Not Acceptable

A common star or heart stamp from a craft store. / A stamp left unattended. / A marker line drawn on the hand, which anyone can reproduce.

Other Id method for legal drinking age
System FieldOther Id method for legal drinking age

What it means. The chapter is using a different system to distinguish attendees verified as being of legal drinking age.

Why it matters. Alternative systems are permitted, but they must be identified so a reviewer can judge whether they actually work.

What makes an alternative reliable. Test it against five criteria:

  1. Applied only after ID verification — the mark follows the check, never replaces it.
  2. Event-specific — it cannot be brought in from elsewhere or reused later.
  3. Not easily duplicated — a guest who sees it cannot recreate it.
  4. Durable for the length of the event — it survives dancing, sweating, and hand washing.
  5. Visible at a glance — a monitor at the distribution center can read it in a moment, in the actual lighting of the room.
Practical Tip

A common alternative is a two-color credential system: everyone receives a wristband at check-in, with one color for legal-age attendees and another for under-21 attendees. Everyone is marked, so nobody is singled out by having no band, and monitors can read the room instantly. If you use it, describe both colors and what each means.

Describ Id method for legal drinking age:
System FieldDescrib Id method for legal drinking age:

What it means. The narrative describing the alternative age-identification method. The label is truncated and missing a letter; it reads "Describ" on the live form and is reproduced here exactly.

Why it matters. Reviewers need enough detail to determine whether the method provides adequate control. An "Other" selection with a thin description is a standard cause of returned submissions.

How to complete it. Write the five criteria into the answer: what the mark is, when it is applied, why it cannot be duplicated or reused, how long it lasts, and who reads it.

Acceptable

"Two-color tamper-evident wristband system. All checked-in attendees receive a band: crimson for verified 21+, white for under 21. Bands are pre-printed with the event name and date and applied at the entrance by the carding team immediately after examination of unexpired government-issued photo ID. Distribution-center monitors serve crimson bands only. Unissued bands are controlled by the Chapter Risk Manager and collected at close."

Not Acceptable

"Wristbands." / "We'll know who's 21." / "Members will vouch for their guests." / Blank with the Other box checked.

Never Acceptable

"Members vouch for their guests" is not an age-identification method. Vouching is not verification, it is not documented, and it puts a brother's word in place of a government-issued ID on a question with legal consequences.

Quantity and distribution

How many drinks will you allow:
System FieldHow many drinks will you allow:
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"How many drinks will you allow each person of legal drinking age to bring to the social event? Beer: # ____ Wine Coolers: # ____ Ciders: # ____ Wine: # ____ Malt Beverages: # ____ Hard Liquor # ____ Other: # ____"

What it means. The maximum quantity, by beverage type, that each attendee of legal drinking age may bring to the event.

Why it matters. The field exists to establish a defined control rather than unlimited quantities. It is also the operational expression of the common-source rule: the prohibition targets amounts greater than what a reasonable person should consume over the duration of an event. Setting a number is how the chapter draws that line before anyone arrives, rather than arguing about it at the check-in table.

This Course Does Not Set a Number

The Kappa source provides the structure — a stated quantity per beverage type — but does not fix a universal figure, and this course will not invent one. The number is a chapter decision constrained by the current controlling policy, by any university or council policy that applies, and by the common-source rule. Confirm the current requirement, then set a number your monitors can actually enforce.

How to complete it.

  1. Set a limit for each beverage type on the source's list, or state clearly that a type is not permitted.
  2. Make the limits internally consistent — a limit that permits both four beers and a bottle of liquor is not a limit.
  3. Consider the event's length. A four-hour event and a two-hour reception do not warrant the same figure.
  4. Publish the limit in advance, on the invitation and at the door, so nobody arrives with more than he can check in.
  5. Decide in advance what happens to excess: it is not accepted, it does not go into chapter possession, and it goes back to the attendee's vehicle or is turned away with him. Never take custody of it.
  6. Enforce it at check-in, where the ticket or punch card is issued.
Acceptable

A stated per-type quantity, published on the invitation, enforced at check-in, with a written rule that excess is not accepted and never taken into chapter custody. Example format: "Beer: [n] · Wine coolers: [n] · Ciders: [n] · Wine: [n] · Malt beverages: [n] · Hard liquor: not permitted · Other: not permitted."

Not Acceptable

"Reasonable amount." / "Whatever they bring." / "No limit for members." / Field blank at a BYOB event. / A limit stated on the form but never communicated to attendees or enforced at the table.

Common kickback reasons. Field blank while BYOB is selected; a non-numeric answer; a quantity so high it reads as a common source; different limits for members and guests with no basis.

Red Flag

Any answer that begins "we don't want to be strict about it." The quantity field is the control. If the chapter is unwilling to set and hold a number, it is not ready to run a BYOB event.

Where will the service distribution cent:
System FieldWhere will the service distribution cent:
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"How will you manage the service distribution center (bar)? ______ Where will the service distribution center be located? ______ Common organizational recommendations suggest establishing one centralized location for checking in and distributing alcohol."

What it means. The physical location of the controlled point where alcohol is checked in, stored, and distributed back to attendees.

Why it matters. One centralized location for checking in and distributing alcohol is what makes control and monitoring possible. Everything the chapter is trying to do — verify age, track quantity, watch consumption, notice someone who has had too much, prevent a common source from forming — depends on alcohol existing in exactly one place under supervision. The moment there are two places, or coolers under tables, control is gone.

Designing the distribution center — six elements.

  1. CentralizedOne location. Not a bar plus a cooler by the DJ. Not a second table "for the alumni."
  2. Check-inAttendees hand over their beverages on arrival. The beverages are personalized to them — name written on the ticket or punch card — and delivered to the center by a working member.
  3. Storage and controlBehind the table, out of reach of attendees. Nobody serves himself. Nothing is stored where a guest can access it.
  4. DistributionOne drink at a time, redeemed against a ticket or a punch card, to the person whose name is on it.
  5. MonitorsAssigned brothers who remain sober, staff the table for defined shifts, and have authority to decline service.
  6. Visibility and access controlPositioned where monitors can see the room and the room can see the table. Not in a back hallway, not in a room monitors cannot observe.
Acceptable

"Single service distribution center at the northeast corner of the Magnolia Ballroom, adjacent to the check-in table and visible from the main entrance. Two six-foot tables with all beverages stored behind them in coolers accessible only to assigned monitors. Attendees check beverages at arrival; drinks are personalized and delivered to the center by a working member; redemption is one drink at a time against a personalized punch card. No alcohol is permitted anywhere else in the room."

Not Acceptable

"By the DJ." / "In the kitchen." / "Coolers around the room." / "People keep their own drinks." / Blank at a BYOB event. / Two distribution points "so the line moves faster."

Common kickback reasons. Field blank; a location described that is not centralized; a design in which attendees retain custody of their own supply; no description of how the center is managed.

Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "It's their own alcohol, so they can hold onto it."
Fact: If attendees keep custody, there is no quantity tracking, no consumption oversight, and no ability to stop serving someone who has had enough. The check-in and centralized distribution model exists precisely because ownership by the individual does not produce control by anyone.

How many event monitors:
System FieldHow many event monitors:
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"How many event monitors will be assigned to work the service distribution center? ____"

What it means. The number of monitors assigned specifically to the service distribution center. Note the scope — this field is about the distribution center, not the total number of monitors at the event. Module 9 covers event monitors generally.

Why it matters. It establishes whether personnel have actually been assigned to manage the operation, rather than leaving alcohol distribution unattended. An unattended distribution center is a common source with a table under it.

How to complete it.

  1. Enter a real number, and be able to name the people behind it.
  2. Staff for shifts across the whole event, not for a headcount at one moment. Two monitors for a five-hour event means four or six people rotating.
  3. Scale to the crowd and to the length of the check-in line. One monitor cannot both run check-in and distribute.
  4. Every monitor at the center stays sober for the duration of the event.
  5. Never allow the center to be unstaffed — including during the moment when shifts change. Overlap the shifts.
Acceptable

"Two monitors staffing the distribution center at all times, in three overlapping shifts of two: 7:00–9:00, 8:45–11:00, 10:45–close. Six brothers total, all sober for the duration, named on the attached monitor plan."

Not Acceptable

"2" with no names and no shifts. / "As needed." / "Members will help out." / A number that leaves the center unstaffed during shift changes.

Red Flag

A monitor plan that has the same two brothers on the table from 7 PM to 1 AM. They will be tired, they will drift, and by midnight — the point in the evening when judgment matters most — the table will be effectively unsupervised.

Who monitors the distribution center

Chapter members monitors
System FieldChapter members monitors
Source Meaning — Kappa SourceUnder "Which best describes the event monitors?": "Chapter members" and "New members (If you utilize new members, it is recommended it is in conjunction with established members.)"

What it means. Established chapter members serve as the distribution-center monitors.

Why it matters. It identifies who has responsibility for managing the service distribution center. Members carry standing in the organization, which matters when the job requires telling a brother he is done for the night.

Note that where new members participate as monitors, the Kappa source recommends they do so in conjunction with established members — the same principle as carding.

How to complete it. Name the brothers, assign shifts, confirm sobriety, and brief them. The briefing should cover: what the wristband or stamp looks like tonight; the quantity limit; how the ticket or punch card system works; that they serve one drink at a time to the named person; that they do not serve anyone who appears intoxicated; and who to escalate to.

Acceptable

"Six established members named on the monitor plan, rotating in pairs across three shifts, all sober for the duration, briefed at 6:45 PM by the Chapter Risk Manager, who serves as officer in charge and has authority to stop service."

Not Acceptable

"Chapter members" with no names. / Monitors who intend to drink during their shift. / Monitors who were told their assignment as they walked in the door.

The Hardest Part of the Job

Refusing service to a brother is the moment BYOB events fail. Prepare the monitors for it explicitly: give them a script ("I can't serve you right now — let me get you some water"), give them backup (the officer in charge handles escalation, not the monitor), and make clear at chapter beforehand that a monitor's decision is the chapter's decision. A monitor who knows the room will back him will actually make the call.

University is providing someone to monit
System FieldUniversity is providing someone to monit
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"The university is providing someone to distribute alcohol"

What it means. University personnel assist with alcohol distribution and monitoring at the service distribution center.

Why it matters. It identifies an institutional party responsible for this control. Some campuses require this for any registered event where alcohol is present, and campus staff bring training and independence that members do not have.

How to complete it. Arrange it in writing through the office that provides it, confirm how many people and their hours, confirm what they will and will not do, and attach the confirmation. Do not check this box based on an expectation that "the university usually sends someone."

Acceptable

"Two Student Union event staff assigned to the distribution center 7:00 PM–midnight per facility use agreement section 6; confirmation email from the Union scheduling office attached. Chapter monitors work alongside them and retain responsibility for guest-list and wristband verification."

Not Acceptable

"The university handles the bar." / Box checked with no written arrangement. / Assuming campus staff will enforce chapter-specific rules they were never told about.

Practical Tip

University staff enforce university rules. If your chapter's quantity limit is stricter than campus policy, tell them — in the pre-event briefing, in writing, with the limit on a card at the table. Nobody enforces a rule they have not been given.

The chapter has hired a vendor to monito
System FieldThe chapter has hired a vendor to monito
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"The chapter has hired a vendor to distribute alcohol"

What it means. A contracted vendor manages the distribution center — typically a bartending or event-staffing service.

Why it matters. It identifies the outside party responsible for the service operation and moves the hardest judgment calls to trained staff. It also brings a vendor into the packet with all the documentation that entails.

How to complete it. Treat it as a vendor engagement in full: contract executed in the chapter name, certificate of insurance meeting the minimum limits with additional-insured status on a primary basis, licensing verified, on-site supervisor identified, and a pre-event briefing.

An Important Distinction

Hiring a vendor to distribute attendees' own BYOB beverages is not the same as engaging a licensed and insured third-party vendor to sell alcohol per drink. The first is still a BYOB event with paid staff running the table. The second is the vendor model in Module 4, with its own contract requirements and the seven purveyor responsibilities. Be clear which one you are doing, because the rest of the checklist depends on it, and describe it consistently throughout the packet.

Acceptable

"Crown Event Staffing LLC providing three staff to operate the BYOB check-in and distribution center 6:30 PM–1:00 AM. Contract executed in the chapter name 3/07; certificate of insurance attached with $1M/$2M limits and Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter named additional insured on a primary basis; state license verified; on-site supervisor identified. This remains a BYOB event; the vendor does not sell or provide alcohol."

Not Acceptable

"We hired bartenders." / A vendor engaged with no contract or certificate. / A description that leaves a reviewer unable to tell whether the event is BYOB or vendor-sold.

Check-in and redemption

Ticket System
System FieldTicket System
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Each member/guest is given one ticket per drink she/he checks in at the party. The tickets are personalized with the type of drink the guest brings [e.g. Smirnoff Ice, etc.]. The name of the attendee is written on the tickets. The member/guest's drinks are delivered to the service distribution center by a member who is working the social event. The member/guest redeems tickets [one at a time] for his/her drinks at the bar."

What it means. A one-ticket-per-drink system: each beverage checked in produces a personalized ticket, and the attendee redeems tickets one at a time.

Why it matters. It connects the person, the beverage, and the quantity, and it prevents uncontrolled access to the checked-in supply. It also produces a physical record of how much a given attendee has consumed — which is what allows a monitor to notice a pattern rather than guess.

The operational process, step by step.

  1. ArrivalThe attendee is carded, marked, and checked against the guest list at the entrance.
  2. Beverage check-inHe hands over his beverages. A working member counts them against the published limit.
  3. Ticket issuanceOne ticket per drink. Each ticket is written with the attendee's name and the type of drink he brought.
  4. DeliveryA member who is working the event carries the beverages to the distribution center. The attendee does not carry them there himself.
  5. RedemptionThe attendee comes to the center and redeems one ticket at a time for one drink. Monitors match the name and the drink type.
  6. CloseUnredeemed tickets are void at the end of the event. Unclaimed alcohol is not distributed to the chapter or to anyone else — and it never becomes chapter property.
Acceptable

"Personalized ticket per drink checked in, name and beverage type written on each ticket by the check-in team; beverages delivered to the distribution center by working members; one-at-a-time redemption; tickets void at close."

Not Acceptable

Generic tickets with no name. / Handing an attendee all his tickets and letting him collect several drinks at once. / Attendees carrying their own supply to the table. / Tickets that can be traded between attendees.

Red Flag

Tickets being passed between attendees. If tickets are transferable, the system tracks nothing — a legal-age attendee can hand tickets to an under-21 guest, which is the exact failure the whole system exists to prevent. Print or write the name on every ticket, and have monitors check it.

Punch Card System
System FieldPunch Card System
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Each member/guest is given one punch card that has marks for each drink s/he checks in at the party. The punch card is personalized with the type of drink the guest brings [e.g. Smirnoff Ice, etc.]. The name of the member/guest is written on the punch card. The member/guest's drinks are delivered to the service distribution center by a member who is working the social event. The member/guest's ticket is punched or marked at the bar each time s/he claims one of the drinks s/he brought."

What it means. A single personalized card per attendee, with a mark for each beverage checked in, punched as each drink is claimed.

Why it matters. It provides another auditable way to control how many of an attendee's beverages have been distributed — with one practical advantage over tickets: the card stays with the attendee and shows his running total at a glance. A monitor who sees five of six punched at 10 PM has useful information immediately, without counting anything.

The operational process.

  1. Arrival and check-inCarded, marked, guest list checked, beverages counted against the limit.
  2. Card issuanceOne card per attendee, with his name written on it and marks corresponding to the number and type of beverages checked in.
  3. DeliveryA working member takes the beverages to the distribution center.
  4. RedemptionEach time the attendee claims a drink, a monitor punches or marks the card. One drink per visit.
  5. ObservationThe card is a monitoring tool, not just an accounting one. A card filling up quickly is the earliest signal a monitor gets.
  6. CloseCards are collected or voided; unclaimed beverages are not redistributed.
Acceptable

"One personalized punch card per attendee, name and beverage types recorded at check-in, punched by a monitor at each redemption, one drink per visit; monitors instructed to note pace and escalate to the officer in charge if a card is being consumed rapidly."

Not Acceptable

Unnamed cards. / Cards punched in advance. / Attendees punching their own cards. / Multiple drinks per punch.

Practical Tip

Punch cards generally run faster than tickets at a busy event, because there is one item to manage per person rather than a handful of loose tickets that get dropped, wet, and traded. If your event is large, favor punch cards.

Other Check-in
System FieldOther Check-in
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Other [Describe}: ______" — under "How will members and guests check in and collect their alcohol?"

What it means. Another controlled method is used to check in beverages and distribute them.

Why it matters. An alternative is permitted, but the chapter must still identify how distribution will be controlled. The reviewer is asking whether the alternative achieves the same five things.

What an acceptable alternative must accomplish.

  1. Individual attribution — every beverage is tied to a named attendee.
  2. Quantity limit enforced at check-in — excess is not accepted.
  3. Custody by monitors — the supply is held at the centralized distribution center, not by attendees.
  4. One-at-a-time redemption — no bulk collection.
  5. A running record — monitors can tell how much a given attendee has claimed.
  6. Non-transferable — credentials cannot move between attendees.
Acceptable

"Check-in log maintained at the distribution center: each attendee's name, wristband color, beverage type, and quantity are recorded on a numbered line; the attendee's line is initialed by a monitor at each redemption, one drink per visit. Log retained after the event."

Not Acceptable

"Honor system." / "Members will keep track." / "Everyone gets a cup." / Blank with the Other box checked.

Part Three — A Controlled BYOB Event, Arrival to Departure

The fields above describe parts. Here is how they operate as one system across an evening. This is training guidance illustrating the source's requirements in practice, not quoted policy language.

Training Guidance · worked operational example
  1. 6:30 PM — SetupDistribution center built in one location, visible from the entrance, tables positioned so all storage is behind the monitors. Wristband supply, punch cards, markers, and the printed guest list issued to the door team by the Chapter Risk Manager. Emergency exits walked and confirmed clear and unobstructed. Water and non-alcoholic beverages set out at a separate self-serve station. Food service confirmed for 7:30.
  2. 6:45 PM — Staff briefingAll monitors, door staff, and hired security briefed together for fifteen minutes. Covered: tonight's wristband colors and what each means; the quantity limit; the punch card procedure; the one-drink-at-a-time rule; the instruction not to serve anyone who appears intoxicated; the escalation path; the officer in charge; the location of exits; the phone number for venue security. Everyone confirms they are sober for the duration.
  3. 7:00 PM — Doors open, single controlled entranceEach arrival is checked against the printed guest list, carded with unexpired government-issued photo ID, and wristbanded — crimson for verified 21+, white for under 21. Nobody is admitted who is not on the list. The rear doors remain unobstructed emergency exits, staffed by a monitor to prevent entry but never locked or blocked.
  4. 7:00 PM — Beverage check-inLegal-age attendees hand over their beverages at the check-in table beside the entrance. A working member counts them against the published limit; excess is not accepted and goes back with the attendee. A punch card is written with the attendee's name and the beverage types and count. A working member carries the beverages to the distribution center; the attendee does not.
  5. 7:30 PM — Event underwayTwo monitors at the distribution center at all times. Redemption is one drink per visit, matched to the name on the card and the crimson wristband. Zone monitors circulate: entrance, main floor, distribution area, exterior. Nothing alcoholic exists anywhere in the room except behind the distribution table and in the hand of the person who just redeemed a drink.
  6. 8:45 PM — First shift changeOverlapping handoff so the center is never unstaffed. The outgoing pair briefs the incoming pair on anything they noticed — a card filling quickly, a guest who has been argumentative, a group that keeps drifting toward the exterior door.
  7. 9:30 PM — A judgment callA monitor notices an attendee whose speech has changed and whose card shows rapid consumption. He does not argue and does not lecture. He says: "I'm going to hold off for a bit — let me get you some water." He signals the officer in charge, who takes over the conversation. The attendee's card is noted. Nobody is embarrassed in front of the room.
  8. 10:00 PM — Capacity checkThe door team confirms the running count against the fire-code capacity, including staff and vendors on site. Headroom is confirmed before any late arrivals are admitted.
  9. 11:30 PM — Wind-downDistribution stops on the schedule set in advance. Food and non-alcoholic beverages remain available. Music continues. Monitors shift attention toward departures and the parking area.
  10. 12:00 AM — CloseUnredeemed punches are void. Unclaimed alcohol is not distributed, not taken by the chapter, and not carried off by monitors — the chapter never takes ownership of it. Departures are observed; anyone who should not be driving is helped to a ride by a designated brother.
  11. 12:30 AM — WrapGuest list, door sign-in sheet, punch cards, and monitor plan collected and retained with the event packet. The Event Chair and Chapter Risk Manager note anything that went wrong while it is fresh — not to assign blame, but because next semester's plan is written from tonight's observations.
What Made That Work

Not one heroic decision — eleven ordinary ones made in advance. Named people, defined shifts, one entrance, one distribution point, a published limit, a briefing, and an officer whose job was to take the hard conversation off a monitor's shoulders. Every one of those is something the checklist asked about.

Scenarios

▶ Scenario — The Second Cooler

Two hours into a BYOB event, a monitor notices a cooler behind the DJ booth. A brother says some of the alumni "didn't want to wait in the check-in line" so he put their drinks back there and told them to help themselves.

What has happened, and what should the officer in charge do right now?

A second, uncontrolled source of alcohol has been created inside the event. Whether or not it started as individually owned beverages, a cooler people help themselves from is functionally a common source: nobody is tracking who takes what, no age verification is happening at that point, no quantity limit is enforced, and no monitor can see it.

Immediately: the cooler is removed from the floor and its contents are brought under the distribution center's control, or the beverages are returned to their owners to be taken out of the event. The chapter does not take ownership of them. The officer in charge tells the DJ area monitor and the door team what happened so they watch for a repeat.

Then: the brother who set it up is corrected privately, not publicly, and the correction is specific — not "don't do that" but "a self-serve cooler is a common source, and common sources are prohibited; anyone who doesn't want to wait can check in at the table and I'll open a second check-in line."

The root cause is worth fixing: the line was too long, which is a staffing problem the monitor plan should have anticipated. Control failures usually start as convenience workarounds. If the process is painful, people will route around it, so make the process fast enough that nobody wants to.

▶ Scenario — The Guest Without ID

A member's guest arrives without identification. He is visibly an adult, the member vouches that he is 24, and he is on the approved guest list. The door team asks the Event Chair what to do.

What is the correct handling?

He does not receive a legal-age wristband. Being on the guest list establishes that he was invited; it does not establish his age. A member's word is not age verification, appearance is not age verification, and the entire control system depends on the mark meaning that a document was examined.

The workable answer is not to turn him away from the event — it is to admit him under the under-21 credential. He receives the white wristband, he attends, he eats, he socializes, and he does not check in or receive alcohol. If he retrieves his ID from his car or has a valid digital ID the chapter accepts, he can be re-carded and re-banded.

Two notes for the door team. First, do not make the decision an argument in front of a line — step him aside, explain it once, and move the line. Second, publish the ID requirement on the invitation so nobody is surprised at the door. Most of these confrontations are prevented three weeks earlier by one line of text on the invite.

Knowledge Check

Module 8 · Question 1

A monitor at the distribution center sees an attendee wearing tonight's crimson wristband. What has the wristband established?

✓ Correct answer: C. The wristband records that carding happened — and nothing else. Quantity is tracked separately by the ticket or punch card (which is why B and D are wrong), and guest-list status is checked at the door (A). Keeping these functions distinct is what makes the system auditable: if the mark meant several things at once, no monitor could tell which check had actually been performed.
Module 8 · Question 2

Which distribution-center design is consistent with the Kappa source?

✓ Correct answer: B. One centralized location for checking in and distributing is what the source describes, and it is the design that makes monitoring possible. A splits supervision and doubles the failure points — solve line length with more monitors at one point, not a second point. C and D both hand custody back to attendees, which eliminates quantity tracking and consumption oversight entirely.
Module 8 · Question 3

The field "How many drinks will you allow:" is completed as "a reasonable amount." Why is this inadequate?

✓ Correct answer: A. The source structures this field as a per-type quantity precisely so that a number exists before the event — publishable on the invitation and enforceable at the table. "Reasonable" gives the brother counting bottles at check-in nothing to hold, and it guarantees an argument. B confuses the underlying common-source standard with the operational control the field is asking for.
Module 8 · Question 4

At the close of a BYOB event, a quantity of checked-in alcohol is unclaimed. What should happen to it?

✓ Correct answer: D. A and B both convert individually owned beverages into a chapter-held stock, which is the common-source problem arriving after midnight instead of at 7 PM — and B rewards the very brothers whose sobriety the event depended on with alcohol. C hands the problem to a third party without addressing it. Handle unclaimed alcohol as part of your written close-out procedure, decided before the event rather than in the parking lot.

Good Event Planning Guidelines

Twenty-five prevention items and three free-text plans. The Kappa source calls these Prevention Ideas: the steps a chapter takes to create a safe environment before anything goes wrong.

⏱ 50 min🛡 28 fields📝 Includes event image
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) distinguish security, chaperones, and event monitors and staff each correctly; (2) build an event-monitor assignment plan; (3) apply each prevention item accurately, including the truncated ones; (4) review event materials against organizational-image standards; (5) write prevention plans that describe operations rather than intentions.

Kappa Source — Prevention Ideas"Good event planning is done when chapters consider ways to create safe environments through prevention. Listed below are important steps a chapter can take to create safe events. Please check the areas that the chapter will implement during the event."

Read the last sentence again: check the areas that the chapter will implement. Not the areas that sound good. Not the areas that other chapters check. The ones you will actually implement, with named people and a written plan behind them.

Three Roles That Are Not Interchangeable

The single most common error in this section is treating security, chaperones, and event monitors as three words for the same thing. They are three different functions with different authority, different training, and different jobs. A chapter that checks boxes in all three categories and staffs only one has misrepresented its plan.

Role 1

Security

Trained personnel with authority to intervene. Public police, private police, contracted guards, or venue security. They control entry, respond to incidents, remove people, and handle situations members should not handle. They are the only category with professional training in physical intervention.

Role 2

Chaperones

Responsible adults providing oversight and presence. Alumni, university staff, parents, or approved volunteers. They are not security. Their value is judgment, standing, and the willingness to intervene early — a word with a brother before a situation becomes an incident.

Role 3

Event Monitors

Assigned chapter people with specific zones and duties. Members, officers, or other designated students working the door, the distribution center, the floor, and the exterior. They observe, they report, they escalate. They are the chapter's eyes, and they are the role most often checked and least often staffed.

The Test

For every box you check in these three categories, you must be able to answer three questions: Who, specifically? For which hours? Doing what, exactly? If you cannot answer all three, do not check the box — write the plan first.

Security

Kappa Source — Prevention Ideas"Security (check all that apply): Public Police / Private Police / Provided by venue / Paid / Volunteer"

Note the structure: the first three describe who provides security; the last two describe how it is arranged. A single arrangement often touches two boxes — contracted guards are both "Private Police" and "Paid."

Security Public Police
System FieldSecurity Public Police

What it means. Public law-enforcement personnel — municipal police, sheriff's deputies, or campus police — provide security at the event.

Why it matters. Public officers bring trained response to safety, crowd-control, and legal issues, plus the authority to act decisively. Their presence also changes attendee behavior before anything happens.

How to complete it. Arrange formally through the department, in writing, well in advance. Confirm the number of officers, hours, cost, and role. Attach the confirmation. Brief them before doors on the guest-list procedure, who the officer in charge is for the chapter, and where the exits are.

Acceptable

"Two Denton PD officers under extra-duty request #ED-2026-0418, 7:00 PM–1:00 AM, invoice and confirmation attached; one posted at the single entrance, one roving; briefed at 6:45 PM."

Not Acceptable

"Police will be nearby." / "We'll call them if we need them." / Checking the box because the venue is near a police station.

Common kickback reasons. Box checked with no written arrangement, no hours, and no officer count.

Security Private Police
System FieldSecurity Private Police

What it means. Private licensed security personnel are used — a contracted security company or licensed off-duty officers working through a proper arrangement.

Why it matters. It establishes dedicated professional security accountable to a contract. Unlike volunteers, private security is trained, licensed, insured, and can be held to a defined scope.

How to complete it. This is a vendor engagement — the full Module 5 packet applies: contract executed in the chapter name, certificate of insurance with additional-insured status on a primary basis, state security licensing verified, on-site supervisor identified, and a pre-event briefing. Describe the scope: how many guards, which hours, and what they do.

Acceptable

"Sentinel Protective Services LLC, four licensed guards 6:30 PM–1:00 AM; contract executed in the chapter name; certificate of insurance attached with Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the chapter named additional insured on a primary basis; scope covers entry control, bag check, and removal at the direction of the officer in charge."

Not Acceptable

"A brother's friend who does security." / Guards hired with no contract or certificate. / An unlicensed individual paid cash at the door.

Red Flag

An individual offering security services with no company, no license, and no insurance is not private security. He is a person the chapter has asked to physically intervene with guests — which is the arrangement most likely to turn a small problem into a claim.

Security Provided by venue
System FieldSecurity Provided by venue

What it means. The facility supplies security personnel as part of the venue arrangement.

Why it matters. It clarifies that security responsibility has been addressed through the venue — but only if the commitment is real and documented. This is the security box chapters check most often and support least often.

How to complete it.

  1. Get the commitment into the venue contract or banquet event order: how many officers, which hours, and what they are responsible for.
  2. Confirm whether venue security is dedicated to your event or covering the whole building. A hotel with one officer for six floors is not providing security to your ballroom.
  3. Confirm who they report to and whether they will act on the chapter's direction.
  4. Get a name and mobile number for the on-duty supervisor.
  5. Brief them before doors, the same as any other security.
Acceptable

"The signed venue agreement states that two venue security officers will be assigned to the event from 7:00 PM until midnight, and the event chair has confirmed the arrangement."

Not Acceptable

"The hotel normally has security somewhere in the building."

Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "The venue handles security, so we don't need to identify anything."
Fact: "The venue handles it" without identifying who, how many, when, and where it is written is one of the named causes of returned submissions. Saying a third party handles something is not the same as documenting what that third party has committed to.

Security Paid
System FieldSecurity Paid

What it means. Security is specifically paid for and assigned to this event.

Why it matters. Paid security is dedicated security. Payment creates a contractual relationship with a defined scope, defined hours, and accountability — which is precisely what volunteer arrangements lack.

How to complete it. Check this alongside whichever provider box applies, and identify the arrangement, the cost, and what the payment buys. Retain the invoice with the packet.

Acceptable
