"Paid extra-duty coverage, two officers, 6 hours, $540 total, invoice attached; also checked under Public Police."

Not Acceptable

Checking "Paid" when nobody is being paid, because it looks stronger than "Volunteer."

Security Volunteer
System FieldSecurity Volunteer

What it means. Volunteers perform designated security functions.

Why it matters. It demonstrates that the chapter has at least assigned personnel to security responsibilities, and the source identifies volunteer security as one available prevention measure. But be honest with yourself about what a volunteer can do: a brother in a polo shirt has no training in physical intervention, no license, no authority to detain, and no professional backing.

How to complete it. Name the volunteers, assign hours and posts, and — most importantly — define the limits of the role in writing. Volunteers observe, report, and escalate. They do not remove people physically, break up fights, or confront anyone alone.

Acceptable

"Four alumni volunteers posted at the entrance, exterior door, parking area, and distribution center, 7:00 PM–close, named on the attached plan. Role limited to observation, guest-list verification, and escalation to the two paid officers; volunteers do not conduct removals."

Not Acceptable

"Members will handle security." / Volunteers as the only security at a large event with alcohol. / Volunteers expected to remove intoxicated or aggressive attendees.

Red Flag

Volunteer security as the sole security arrangement at a large event where alcohol is present. If the plan depends on members physically managing a situation, the plan needs professional security instead.

Chaperones

Kappa Source — Prevention Ideas"Chaperone (check all that apply): Alumni / University Staff / Parents / Volunteer"
What a Chaperone Actually Does

A chaperone is not a decoration and not a second security guard. The value of the role is early intervention by someone with standing — noticing that a conversation is escalating, that a brother has had too much, that a group is drifting somewhere they should not be, and stepping in before it becomes an incident.

Merely having a person present is not effective supervision. A chaperone who arrives at 9, sits at a table with old friends, and leaves at 10 has chaperoned nothing. Give chaperones a defined role, defined hours, and a defined authority: what they may stop, who they report to, and that the chapter will back them.

Alumni Chaperone
System FieldAlumni Chaperone

What it means. Alumni serve as event chaperones.

Why it matters. Alumni bring judgment, organizational standing, and distance from the undergraduate social dynamic. A word from an alumnus lands differently than a word from a classmate, and undergraduates are far more likely to comply without argument.

How to complete it. Name them, state their hours, and give them a written role. Ask them to arrive before doors for the staff briefing. Ask them to stay sober. Ask them to circulate rather than sit.

Acceptable

"Bro. K. Ellison and Bro. D. Marks (Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter) chaperoning 6:45 PM–close; both attended the pre-event briefing; role is circulation, early intervention, and support to the officer in charge; both sober for the duration."

Not Acceptable

"Some alumni will be there." / An alumnus listed as chaperone who does not know he has been listed. / A chaperone who is drinking.

Supplemental Note

Supplemental · Holmes Murphy 2026 Template

The template contains sample client language prohibiting advisors from attending or supervising undergraduate events where alcohol is present, while permitting attendance at family-oriented events in a support role. That is one client organization's drafting option, not a Kappa requirement, and the Kappa source expressly lists alumni chaperones as a prevention measure. It is noted here only because the template raises the topic — follow your chapter's current adopted policy on advisor and alumni attendance.

University Staff Chaperone
System FieldUniversity Staff Chaperone

What it means. University personnel serve as chaperones.

Why it matters. It provides institutional oversight, and at many campuses it is a condition of holding a registered social event. Staff chaperones also give the chapter an independent witness that the event was run properly.

How to complete it. Arrange through the appropriate office in writing. Name the staff member, state the hours, and attach the confirmation. Brief them on the chapter's own controls, since they will otherwise enforce only campus policy.

Acceptable

"Fraternity & Sorority Life staff member assigned per campus social-event policy, 7:00 PM–midnight; assignment confirmed by email 3/12, attached; briefed on the chapter's wristband and quantity procedures."

Not Acceptable

"University staff usually attend." / Box checked in the hope that someone will be sent.

Parents Chaperone
System FieldParents Chaperone

What it means. Parents serve in a designated chaperone role.

Why it matters. Adds responsible adult supervision. Parent chaperones are most common and most useful at family-oriented events, community programs, and youth-facing events such as scholarship programs, Guide Right activities, and health fairs.

How to complete it. Name them, state their hours, define the role, and brief them. Where an event involves minors, be particularly clear about supervision ratios, sign-out procedures, and who is authorized to release a young person to an adult.

Acceptable

"Four parent chaperones for the Guide Right Saturday academy, 8:30 AM–2:00 PM, assigned one per activity room, named on the attached plan; sign-in/sign-out sheet maintained at the single entrance and youth released only to the adult listed on the registration."

Not Acceptable

"Parents will be around." / Parent chaperones at an event with alcohol, listed to fill a box, with no defined role.

Volunteer Chaperone
System FieldVolunteer Chaperone

What it means. Approved volunteers provide supervision.

Why it matters. It identifies additional responsible personnel rather than leaving supervision undefined. The word doing the work is approved — a volunteer chaperone should be someone the chapter selected deliberately, not whoever was standing nearby.

How to complete it. Name them, state who approved them, state their hours, and define the role. If the event involves minors, apply whatever screening your chapter and the host institution require.

Acceptable

"Two approved community volunteers from the co-sponsoring organization, approved by the Chapter Risk Manager 3/10, chaperoning 9:00 AM–1:00 PM, assigned to the registration area and the youth activity room."

Not Acceptable

"Volunteers." / Anyone who shows up and offers to help, treated as an approved chaperone.

Event Monitors

Kappa Source — Prevention Ideas"Event Monitors (check all that apply): Members / Officers / Other students"

Monitors are the chapter's own supervision system. Unlike security, they have no authority to intervene physically. Unlike chaperones, they have specific assigned zones and duties. Their job is to see things early and escalate.

Members Monitors Event
System FieldMembers Monitors Event

What it means. Members are specifically assigned as event monitors.

Why it matters. Someone must actively observe conditions and identify developing problems. A room with 250 people and no assigned observers is a room where the first anyone hears of a problem is when it becomes an incident.

How to complete it. Name them, assign zones, assign shifts, confirm sobriety, and brief them. See the assignment plan below.

Acceptable

"Eight members assigned as monitors across four zones in two shifts, named on the attached monitor plan, all sober for the duration, briefed at 6:45 PM."

Not Acceptable

"Members will monitor the event." / Monitors named but given no zone. / Monitors who are also drinking.

Officers Monitors Event
System FieldOfficers Monitors Event

What it means. Chapter officers serve as monitors.

Why it matters. It places individuals with organizational authority in active oversight roles. Officers can make decisions a member cannot: stop service, close the door, end the event. The Kappa source's prevention list also includes an "Officer in charge" item — a single identified officer accountable for decisions on the night.

How to complete it. Name the officers and their assignments, and identify one officer in charge with decision authority. Every monitor should know who that is by name before doors open.

Acceptable

"Chapter Risk Manager serves as officer in charge with authority to stop alcohol service, refuse admission, and end the event; Vice Polemarch monitors the entrance zone; Keeper of Records manages the guest list at check-in. All monitors briefed that the Risk Manager's decision is final on the night."

Not Acceptable

Officers listed as monitors with no officer in charge identified. / An officer in charge who is also drinking. / Two officers with unclear precedence.

Name the Officer in Charge

This is the highest-value fifteen seconds of the pre-event briefing. When a monitor has to refuse someone at 11 PM, he needs to know exactly whose name to say and where that person is standing. Ambiguity at that moment is why control breaks down.

Other Students Monitors Event
System FieldOther Students Monitors Event

What it means. Other designated students assist with monitoring.

Why it matters. It increases coverage of the event environment and establishes assigned responsibilities beyond the chapter's own membership — useful at co-sponsored events where the partner organization's members are working alongside yours.

How to complete it. Name them, name the organization they come from, assign zones, and include them in the briefing. If they come from a co-sponsor, the division of responsibility should also appear in your co-sponsorship documentation from Module 2.

Acceptable

"Four members of the co-sponsoring sorority chapter assigned as monitors to the registration and hospitality zones, named on the joint monitor plan, briefed alongside chapter monitors at 6:45 PM; escalation runs to the chapter's officer in charge."

Not Acceptable

"Other students will help." / Partner-organization volunteers given control functions with no briefing and no escalation path.

Sample Event-Monitor Assignment Plan

Main floorBro. Whitfield7:00–10:00Circulate, observe crowd density and mood, watch for drinking games or common-source alcohol, monitor music and DJ areaOfficer in charge
Main floorBro. Ellis10:00–closeSame; increased attention as the evening progressesOfficer in charge
Exterior / parkingBro. Mackey7:00–closeWatch the rear emergency exit for unauthorized entry (never obstruct it), observe parking area, note anyone who should not driveSecurity supervisor, then officer in charge
Officer in chargeChapter Risk Manager6:30–closeAll final decisions: refuse admission, stop service, remove, end the event; liaison with security supervisor and venuePolemarch
What the Plan Buys You

Look at what that table does. Every zone is covered for every hour. Every monitor knows one job. Nobody is on for six straight hours. The hardest decisions route to one named person. And if a reviewer asks "who is watching the door at 11 PM," there is a name.

Attendance and Access Prevention Items

Guest list at the door
System FieldGuest list at the door

What it means. Admission personnel compare arriving attendees against an authorized guest list.

Why it matters. It prevents unrestricted entry and produces a record of who was expected. It is also the point where the invitation system from Module 3 becomes an actual control — a guest list that exists in a spreadsheet but never reaches the door has controlled nothing.

The four operations at the door.

  1. Pre-approved attendance — the list was fixed at a close date before the event.
  2. Check-in — each arrival is found on the list and marked present.
  3. Walk-ins — the chapter decided in advance how these are handled. The default answer is that they are not admitted; if there is an exception process, it runs through the officer in charge and it is recorded.
  4. Reconciliation — after the event, the marked list shows who actually attended, and it is retained with the packet.
Acceptable

"Printed guest list at the single entrance, two brothers assigned to check-in, each arrival marked present; walk-ins not admitted; any exception requires the officer in charge and is noted on the list; marked list retained with the event packet."

Not Acceptable

"We have a list." / A list on one brother's phone that nobody else can see. / A list nobody marks. / A list that grows at the door.

Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "A guest list is just for counting attendance."
Fact: The guest list is an access-control and documentation mechanism. It decides who comes in, it caps the crowd, it ties each guest to a member, and it is the document the organization may be asked to produce if there is a policy violation.

Only one entrance to the event
System FieldOnly one entrance to the event

What it means. Guests enter through one controlled admission point.

Why it matters. It makes ID verification, guest-list checks, capacity counting, and beverage check-in possible. Two entrances means two of everything, or — far more commonly — one controlled entrance and one uncontrolled one.

Critical Clarification — Never Block an Exit

A controlled primary entrance does not mean legally required emergency exits should be blocked, locked, chained, obstructed, or disabled. Ever. Under any circumstances. Every other door must remain fully available for emergency egress at all times.

The way to control a secondary door is to staff it, not to secure it: post a monitor to prevent unauthorized entry while leaving the door completely free to open from the inside. If you find yourself considering a chain, a zip tie, a wedge, a padlock, or a piece of furniture, stop — that is the decision that turns a manageable event into a catastrophe.

How to complete it. Identify the single admission point on the form. Identify each other door and state that it remains an unobstructed emergency exit staffed by a monitor. Walk every exit before doors open and confirm it is clear.

Acceptable

"Single admission point at the ballroom's main north doors. The east service door and the south patio door remain unobstructed emergency exits, each staffed by a monitor to prevent unauthorized entry; neither is locked, blocked, or obstructed at any time. All exits walked and confirmed clear at 6:30 PM."

Not Acceptable

"Side doors will be locked." / "We'll put a table in front of the back door." / Multiple unstaffed entrances. / Any arrangement that impedes egress.

Note on a Related Source Item

The Kappa source's undergraduate prevention list includes "Doors to residential living will be locked/secured during the event." That item is about preventing access into private residential areas of a facility during an event — bedrooms and living quarters — not about restricting egress from the event space. Secure private areas; never impede an exit path.

Attendance won't exceed fire code capaci
System FieldAttendance won't exceed fire code capaci
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Attendance won't exceed fire code capacity"

What it means. Attendance remains at or below the legal occupancy limit throughout the event.

Why it matters. Life safety. Occupancy limits exist because a room can only be evacuated so quickly. This is also a legal requirement enforced by the fire marshal, who does not need the chapter's permission to walk in.

How to complete it — a capacity-control procedure, not just a checkbox.

  1. Know the number (Module 3) and put it in writing at the door.
  2. Count. Assign one person on each shift to maintain a running count.
  3. Count everyone in the room, not just guests. Vendors, DJ crew, caterer staff, security, photographers, and venue staff are all occupants. Confirm with the venue whether its figure includes staff.
  4. Set a stop number below the limit and give the door team authority to stop admitting when it is reached — without needing to find an officer first.
  5. Have a plan for the stop: where people wait, what they are told, and whether one-out-one-in applies.
Worked Example

Training Guidance

Venue capacity: 300
Anticipated participants: 240
Staff and vendors: 25
Total planned occupancy: 265

The chapter sets its door stop at 290, holding a 10-person buffer for miscounts. At 290 counted, admission stops regardless of who is outside. That decision is made at a planning meeting in a quiet room — not by a brother at the door at 11 PM with forty people in front of him.

Acceptable

"Fire-code capacity 300, confirmed in writing by the venue. Running count maintained at the single entrance by the assigned door monitor; count includes vendors and staff. Admission stops at 290. The door monitor has standing authority to stop admission without further approval."

Not Acceptable

Box checked with no counting method. / "We won't get that many." / A stop number equal to capacity with no buffer. / A door team with no authority to say no.

Prohibited ticket sales at the door
System FieldProhibited ticket sales at the door
Source Meaning — Kappa SourcePrevention item: "Prohibited ticket sales at the door" Attendance requirement: "For chapter fundraisers, ticket sales prior to the event is required and events must be within fire code capacity."

What it means. Tickets are not sold at the entrance.

Why it matters. Door sales destroy every attendance control the chapter built. Selling at the door means the crowd is whoever shows up with money, the guest list is meaningless, the cap is unenforceable, and the chapter cannot say afterward who attended. It also creates cash handling at the busiest, least supervised point of the event. For fundraisers, the source affirmatively requires ticket sales prior to the event.

How to complete it. Sell in advance through the registration or invitation system, close sales on a date certain, publish that the event is pre-registration only, and instruct the door team on what to say to someone who arrives with cash: "We're not able to sell at the door — registration closed Thursday."

Acceptable

"All tickets sold in advance through the chapter's registration page; sales closed 48 hours prior; no sales at the door; door team scripted and no cash accepted at the entrance."

Not Acceptable

"Limited tickets available at the door" printed on the flyer while this box is checked — a direct contradiction a reviewer will catch immediately. / Accepting cash "just for alumni." / An exception process that exists in practice but not on the form.

Red Flag

Check the flyer against this box before submitting. "Tickets at the door" on the flyer and this box checked on the form is one of the most common self-inflicted kickbacks in the entire packet.

Environment and Conduct Prevention Items

Smoking prohibited
System FieldSmoking prohibited

Verify Before Submission · not in the source's prevention list

An honest note. This field appears on the online checklist, but the Prevention Ideas list in the Kappa Insurance and Claim Manual does not contain a corresponding item. This course will not invent a policy basis for it or attribute an explanation to the manual that the manual does not contain.

Practical purpose. Prohibiting smoking inside an event space reduces fire and property risk, avoids conflicts with venue rules and local ordinances, and removes a common reason attendees drift outside the controlled area — which matters for capacity counting and guest-list integrity.

How to complete it. Comply with applicable venue rules and legal requirements, and describe what the chapter is actually doing. If the venue prohibits smoking, say so. If there is a designated outdoor area, identify it and confirm a monitor covers it. Verify the current requirement for this field with your chapter leadership before treating it as a Fraternity mandate.

Acceptable

"Venue prohibits smoking indoors under its facility rules and municipal ordinance; designated outdoor smoking area at the north patio, covered by the exterior monitor; attendees who exit re-enter through the single controlled entrance and are re-counted."

Not Acceptable

Box checked with no arrangement, at an event where attendees will predictably step outside to smoke and re-enter through an uncontrolled door.

Person removed if they have Illegal drug
System FieldPerson removed if they have Illegal drug
Source Meaning — Kappa SourcePrevention item: "Person removed if they have illegal drugs or controlled substance" Policy: "No person may possess, use, provide, distribute, sell, and/or manufacture illegal drugs or other controlled substances while on premises or at any activity or event sponsored or endorsed by the chapter."

What it means. Any individual possessing illegal drugs or controlled substances is removed from the event.

Why it matters. The prohibition is absolute, and the manual's coverage provisions are unforgiving on this point: individuals whose illegal or intentional actions result in death, injury, or property damage are not insureds. An event that knowingly tolerates illegal drugs puts the chapter, its officers, and potentially the Fraternity outside the protection they assume they have.

Do Not Improvise a Confrontation

This is the prevention item most likely to get a brother hurt if it is handled badly. Event personnel must not search people, seize substances, physically confront anyone, or attempt an arrest. Those are not chapter functions, and a member who tries one has put himself in physical and legal jeopardy.

The procedure is: observe → report to the officer in charge → the officer in charge directs security or law enforcement → removal is carried out by security or law enforcement.

How to complete it — write the procedure.

  1. Observe and reportA monitor who sees something reports it to the officer in charge. He does not intervene himself and does not announce it to the room.
  2. Officer in charge assessesOne person decides, so the response is consistent and nobody freelances.
  3. Security or law enforcement handles itVenue security, contracted guards, or police conduct the removal. Where the situation warrants it, law enforcement is called.
  4. Emergency procedures if anyone is impairedIf someone appears medically compromised, call 911 first. Care for the person comes before every other consideration.
  5. Document afterwardRecord what happened, when, who was involved, and what was done. The manual's incident reporting guidance is clear: if you question whether to report a potential claim, report it.
Acceptable

"Any monitor observing illegal drugs or controlled substances reports immediately to the officer in charge (Chapter Risk Manager) and does not intervene. The officer in charge directs the contracted security supervisor to conduct the removal; law enforcement is contacted where the situation warrants. If any person appears medically compromised, 911 is called first. The incident is documented on the chapter's incident form the same night."

Not Acceptable

"We'll kick them out." / Members instructed to search bags or confront individuals. / A plan that relies on a brother physically removing someone. / No procedure at all behind a checked box.

Food and non-alcoholic beverages avail
System FieldFood and non-alcoholic beverages avail
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Food and non-alcoholic beverages available"

What it means. Food and non-alcoholic beverage options are available to attendees throughout the event.

Why it matters. This is a genuine loss-prevention measure, not hospitality. Food slows alcohol absorption. Available water and soft drinks give attendees something to do with their hands that is not another drink, and give a monitor something to offer instead of a confrontation — "let me get you some water" is a de-escalation tool. It also means attendees who are not drinking, including everyone under 21, have somewhere to go.

How to complete it. Describe what, where, and for how long. The most common failure is not the absence of food but its timing — food served for one hour at the start of a five-hour event is not available for the period when it matters most.

Acceptable

"Hot buffet 7:30–9:30 PM, with sandwiches, fruit, and snacks replenished at the hospitality station until close. Self-serve water, soft drinks, and coffee available at a separate station away from the distribution center, staffed and stocked from doors until close."

Not Acceptable

"Chips and water." / Food served only during the first hour. / A single water pitcher at the alcohol distribution center. / Box checked with no arrangement described.

Practical Tip

Put the non-alcoholic station somewhere other than the alcohol distribution center, and keep it stocked all night. Attendees who want water should not have to stand in the drink line to get it.

Glass bottles prohibited
System FieldGlass bottles prohibited

What it means. Glass beverage containers are not permitted at the event.

Why it matters. Broken glass on a crowded floor causes lacerations, ruins a dance floor, and is hard to clean mid-event. A glass bottle can also become a weapon in a confrontation. The rule is straightforward and it prevents a category of injury that otherwise happens regularly.

How to complete it. Publish it in advance so attendees are not surprised at check-in, enforce it at the beverage check-in table, and give the check-in team a procedure. The cleanest approach: glass is not accepted at check-in and goes back to the attendee's vehicle. Do not pour beverages out of glass into cups — that creates an unlabeled open container the chapter cannot attribute.

Acceptable

"No glass containers permitted; stated on the invitation and posted at the entrance; glass is not accepted at beverage check-in and is returned to the attendee. Venue serves in plastic. Non-alcoholic station uses cans and plastic only."

Not Acceptable

Box checked while the venue bar serves in glass. / Enforced only for guests. / Glass decanted into cups at the check-in table.

Practical Tip

If the venue's bar serves in glass, the chapter's "glass prohibited" representation is inconsistent with what will actually happen in the room. Either negotiate plastic service into the banquet agreement or describe the arrangement accurately — do not check a box the venue is about to contradict.

Event does not involve physical activi
System FieldEvent does not involve physical activi
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Event does not involve physical activity (assault and battery)"

What it means. This is one of the most misread fields on the entire checklist. The truncated label suggests that ordinary physical movement is prohibited. It is not. The source ties this item to assault and battery — physical confrontation between people.

What This Field Does Not Mean

It does not prohibit stepping, strolling, dancing, a step show, a basketball tournament, a 5K, a field day, a Guide Right sports clinic, or setting up chairs. Reading the truncated label literally would make it impossible for a chapter to hold most of the events it exists to hold.

Why it matters. Assault and battery is a serious exposure. The Holmes Murphy 2026 template states the underlying rule directly: in any activity or event sponsored or endorsed by the organization, no chapter, member, or guest shall engage in assault and battery as defined in the state statutes where the event occurs. The Kappa manual makes the insurance consequence explicit — any insured who participates in, supervises, or directs others to participate in Excluded Acts including Assault and Battery is not an insured, and "participate" reaches observers and those who have knowledge and fail to aid or respond.

How to complete it. Check it when the event does not involve physical confrontation as a feature, and back it with a plan for how a physical altercation would be prevented and handled: security presence, monitors watching for escalation, an officer in charge with authority, and a rule that members do not break up fights themselves.

If your event does involve organized physical activity — athletic competition, a step show, a fitness event — describe it accurately in the prevention-plan fields rather than pretending it does not exist. That is a different risk conversation (waivers, medical support, appropriate surfaces, supervision) and it deserves a real answer. The Kappa source includes a Participant Release and Liability Waiver template for exactly these situations.

Acceptable

"Event is a seated banquet with a dance floor; no combative or confrontational activity. Monitors briefed to report escalating disputes to the officer in charge immediately; contracted security handles any physical situation; members do not intervene physically."

Acceptable

"Event includes an exhibition step show performed by trained teams on a matted surface, with a certified athletic trainer present and participant waivers on file. No combative activity. This is described in prevention plan L2."

Not Acceptable

Checking the box at a full-contact athletic event. / Reading the field as prohibiting all movement and cancelling a step show over it. / Checking it with no plan for how an altercation would actually be handled.

Music will not be disrespectful
System FieldMusic will not be disrespectful
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Music will not be disrespectful or degrading to a group of people or culture."

What it means. The complete source wording is the operative standard: music that is disrespectful or degrading to a group of people or culture.

Why it matters. Music is part of the event environment. A set that degrades a group of people creates a hostile atmosphere, alienates attendees the chapter invited, and can be captured on video and attached to the Fraternity's name within minutes.

What This Standard Is — and Is Not

This is not a rule against mature themes, explicit language, or adult content generally. It is not a directive to sanitize the music at a grown folks' event, and this course is not going to pretend otherwise. Hip-hop, R&B, and the rest of the culture the chapter's events are built on are not the target.

The standard is about material that degrades a group of people or a culture — and about the event environment the chapter is responsible for creating.

Acceptable

Ordinary contemporary and classic sets with mature content, played at an adult event. A DJ briefed that the chapter is a Kappa Alpha Psi event and that material degrading to any group is out. A DJ who reads the room and adjusts.

Not Acceptable

Material whose content degrades a racial, ethnic, religious, or cultural group. Content that demeans women or any population as its point. Material glorifying violence against a group. Chants or call-and-response that target another organization or community.

How to complete it. Put it in the DJ's contract in one line, brief the DJ before doors, and assign a monitor to the DJ area with a direct line to the officer in charge. The practical version of this standard is simple: the DJ works for the chapter, and the chapter can ask for a change at any time.

Practical Tip

Have the conversation with the DJ at booking, not at 11 PM. One sentence in the agreement — "the chapter may direct changes to music content at any time during the event" — makes the on-site request routine rather than confrontational.

No tables or paraphernalia
System FieldNo tables or paraphernalia
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"No tables or paraphernalia will be used for drinking games."
Read That Again — Tables Are Not Prohibited

The truncated label reads as though the chapter cannot use tables. That is not what it means. The complete source wording is "No tables or paraphernalia will be used for drinking games." The subject of the sentence is drinking games. The prohibited thing is the game, and the equipment used to play it.

Why it matters. Drinking-game setups facilitate rapid alcohol consumption, which the BYOB provisions expressly prohibit — members and guests must not permit, encourage, coerce, glorify, or participate in any activity involving the rapid consumption of alcohol. This prevention item is the physical-equipment expression of that rule.

Acceptable

Dining tables. Registration and check-in tables. Awards and program tables. Vendor tables. Food and buffet tables. The beverage check-in table. The service distribution center's own tables. Cocktail rounds. A DJ table. A photo-booth table.

Not Acceptable

A beer-pong table or any table set up for pong. A flip-cup setup. Drinking funnels or beer bongs. Ice luges. Shot ski boards. Any equipment whose purpose is rapid consumption — and any improvised version of the same thing using ordinary furniture.

How to complete it. Check the box, and brief the monitors on what to watch for. The realistic failure mode is not someone carrying in a pong table; it is a game that spontaneously forms on an ordinary table late in the evening. A monitor should be able to end it quietly — move the cups, say a word, redirect — without making it a scene.

Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "This field means we can't have tables at our banquet."
Fact: It means no tables or paraphernalia will be used for drinking games. Set your banquet rounds. This is precisely why the course shows the system field and the source wording side by side.

Event does not involve strippers
System FieldEvent does not involve strippers
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Event does not involve strippers, exotic dancers, or similar, whether professional or amateur."

What it means. The event does not involve strippers, exotic dancers, or similar performers — professional or amateur.

Why it matters — and this is not optional guidance. The Kappa source lists the absence of such performers among the required prevention measures on the Event Notification Form. The Holmes Murphy 2026 template states the underlying rule as a flat prohibition: "The employment or use of strippers, exotic dancers or similar, whether professional or amateur, at any fraternity activity or event as defined in this policy is prohibited."

Treat this as prohibited conduct, not as a preference. Confirm the current adopted policy language if you need to quote it to someone, but do not present this to your chapter as a judgment call.

"Whether Professional or Amateur"

Those four words close the loophole chapters reach for. It is not limited to hired performers from an agency. An attendee who performs, a guest who is encouraged to perform, a "surprise" arranged by a member, a birthday stunt — all of it is inside the same rule. So is a performance that is not billed as such but is functionally the same thing.

How to complete it. Check it when true. Then make sure it stays true: put it in the entertainment contract, brief the DJ and any performer, tell the event committee plainly, and instruct monitors to escalate immediately to the officer in charge if anything of the kind begins. If a brother proposes it, the answer is no, and it is not a negotiation.

Acceptable

"Entertainment is limited to the contracted DJ and a scheduled program. The entertainment agreement states that no exotic or adult performance of any kind is permitted. Monitors are briefed to escalate immediately to the officer in charge."

Not Acceptable

Any arrangement involving such performers, however described — "dancers," "entertainment," "a surprise for the birthday brother." Checking the box while a member has arranged something the committee has not disclosed.

Red Flag

"It's not really a stripper, it's just a dancer we know." The source language covers strippers, exotic dancers, or similar, professional or amateur. If the question is being asked at all, the answer is no.

Event Image and Organizational Representation

System FieldEvent theme/materials are respectful
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Event theme/materials are respectful and not degrading to any person or population"

This is one checkbox with a large footprint. "Materials" reaches promotional graphics, flyers, social-media posts, themes, decorations, photography, signage, merchandise, and anything else that represents the event publicly. When a stranger sees your event, this is what they see.

The requirement itself — that the theme and materials be respectful and not degrading to any person or population — comes from the Kappa source. The worked examples below are training guidance developed for this course to help brothers apply that standard. They are not verbatim policy language and are labeled accordingly.

Kappa Source · the requirement Training Guidance · the examples below

Acceptable

Acceptable

Professional organizational branding

Clean, consistent presentation of the chapter and the Fraternity, with correct names and marks used as authorized.

Acceptable

Approved crest and logo usage

Use of the coat of arms and Fraternity marks where the chapter is authorized to use them, reproduced accurately and not altered.

Acceptable

Formal-event imagery

Photography and design consistent with a banquet, gala, scholarship program, or awards event.

Acceptable

Community-service imagery

Images reflecting service, mentorship, Guide Right, health initiatives, and community partnership.

Acceptable

Leadership imagery

Officers, honorees, speakers, and scholarship recipients presented with dignity.

Acceptable

Social imagery consistent with the approved event

People enjoying themselves in a manner that matches what the chapter actually submitted and had approved.

Acceptable

Tasteful entertainment imagery

DJ, band, step, and performance imagery presented professionally.

Acceptable

Accurate sponsor information

Sponsors and co-sponsors identified correctly, with permission, at the level of involvement that actually exists.

Acceptable

Event information matching the submission

Name, date, time, venue, ticketing, and alcohol arrangements identical to what the checklist describes.

Not Acceptable

Material that:

  • Can reasonably be viewed as obscene.
  • Is sexually explicit or pornographic.
  • Uses excessive sexualized imagery inconsistent with the event being held.
  • Depicts or glorifies illegal drug use.
  • Uses cocaine, pills, needles, marijuana, or other illegal-drug imagery as party promotion.
  • Glorifies intoxication.
  • Makes alcohol the central identity of an event when that is inconsistent with the approved event controls.
  • Depicts drinking games.
  • Shows people appearing dangerously intoxicated.
  • Promotes rapid alcohol consumption.
  • Depicts hazing.
  • Promotes assault or violence.
  • Uses degrading racial or cultural imagery.
  • Demeans a person or population.
  • Misrepresents the organization.
  • Uses unauthorized logos.
  • Falsely represents sponsorship.
  • Conflicts with the character of the organization.
  • Could reasonably lead an outside viewer to believe Kappa Alpha Psi endorses prohibited conduct.
The Practical Test

"Would a reasonable member of the public viewing only this flyer understand the event in a way consistent with how it was submitted and approved?"

Only the flyer. Not the flyer plus your explanation, not the flyer plus the group chat, not the flyer plus knowing the brothers. Just the image, seen by someone who knows nothing else. If that person would form a picture of the event that does not match your checklist, the material needs to change — or the checklist was not accurate.

Why This Matters Beyond the Event

A flyer outlives the event. It is screenshotted, reposted, and searchable years later, and it carries the Fraternity's name to people who will never meet the chapter. The last item on the unacceptable list is the one to hold onto: material that could reasonably lead an outside viewer to believe Kappa Alpha Psi endorses prohibited conduct. That is a reputational exposure the chapter cannot recall once it is posted.

Practical Tip

Put flyer review in the hands of two people who are not the designer, and give them the thirteen-question checklist in Module 11. The person who made the graphic is the worst reviewer of it — not because of judgment, but because he already knows what he meant.

Prevention Plans

System FieldsDescribe any specific prevent plans_L1: Describe any specific prevent plans_L2: Describe any specific prevent plans_L3:
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Please describe any specific prevention plans for the above areas (if applicable)"

The "_L1," "_L2," and "_L3" suffixes are platform field-name artifacts for the three text lines. These fields are where the chapter converts checked boxes into described operations.

A checked box identifies a control. A written plan explains how the chapter will actually implement it, who is responsible, and what procedures will be followed. This is the difference between a submission that reads as considered and one that reads as filled out.

Poor

"Security will be there."

Better

"Two venue security officers will staff the designated entrance from 7:00 PM through event close. All attendees will be verified against the approved guest list before admission."

Poor

"We will monitor alcohol."

Better

"Two assigned event monitors will remain at the centralized BYOB distribution station. Legal-age attendees will be identified using event-specific wristbands after ID verification."

The Five-Part Formula

Every prevention statement should answer five questions. If one is missing, the sentence is an intention rather than a plan.

WHO
Named people or a named role — "the Chapter Risk Manager," "two contracted guards," "Bro. Nunez and Bro. Battle." Not "members" or "someone."
WHAT
The specific action — verify against the guest list, apply wristbands after ID check, punch cards at redemption, count occupancy.
WHERE
The physical location — the single north entrance, the northeast distribution center, the south patio.
WHEN
Actual times — "7:00 PM through close," "6:45 PM briefing," "service stops at 11:30 PM." Not "throughout the event."
HOW
The mechanism — printed list marked at check-in, tamper-evident dated wristbands, personalized punch cards, running count with a stop at 290.

With three lines available, use them for the three areas where your event carries the most risk. A workable division for a social with alcohol:

Example — prevent plans_L1 (attendance and access)

Training Guidance · worked example

"Admission is through the single north entrance only, 7:00 PM to 11:00 PM. Bro. Nunez and Bro. Battle (7:00–9:30) and Bro. Hayes and Bro. Sloan (9:15–close) verify each arrival against the printed guest list, examine unexpired government-issued photo ID, and apply a dated event wristband — crimson for 21+, white for under 21. A running occupancy count including vendors and staff is maintained at the entrance; admission stops at 290 against a fire-code capacity of 300, and the door monitor has standing authority to stop admission without further approval. The east service door and south patio door remain unobstructed emergency exits, each staffed by a monitor to prevent unauthorized entry; neither is locked or blocked at any time. No tickets are sold at the door."

Example — prevent plans_L2 (alcohol control)

Training Guidance · worked example

"This is a BYOB event with a single service distribution center at the northeast corner of the ballroom, visible from the entrance. Legal-age attendees check beverages at arrival with Bro. Grant, who counts them against the published per-type limit and refuses excess; excess is returned to the attendee and never taken into chapter custody. Beverages are carried to the distribution center by a working member and held behind the table. Each attendee receives a personalized punch card with his name and beverage types. Two monitors staff the center at all times in three overlapping shifts (7:00–9:00, 8:45–11:00, 10:45–close), redeeming one drink per visit against the punch card and the crimson wristband, and declining service to anyone who appears intoxicated. Service stops at 11:30 PM. All monitors and door staff are sober for the duration and were briefed at 6:45 PM by the Chapter Risk Manager, who is officer in charge with authority to stop service. No alcohol exists anywhere in the room outside the distribution center."

Example — prevent plans_L3 (safety, response, and environment)

Training Guidance · worked example

"Two contracted licensed guards from Sentinel Protective Services (supervisor L. Grant, mobile on file) work 6:30 PM to 1:00 AM and conduct all removals; members do not intervene physically. A monitor observing illegal drugs or controlled substances reports to the officer in charge and does not confront anyone; the officer in charge directs security, and law enforcement is contacted where warranted. If any person appears medically compromised, 911 is called first. Hot food is served 7:30–9:30 PM with snacks replenished until close, and a staffed water, soft drink, and coffee station operates from doors to close, separate from the distribution center. No glass containers are accepted at check-in. Monitors are briefed to end any drinking game immediately and quietly and to report it to the officer in charge. All exits were walked and confirmed clear at 6:30 PM. Departures are observed from 11:30 PM, and designated brothers arrange rides for anyone who should not drive."

Additional Prevention Items in the Kappa Source

The manual's Prevention Ideas list includes three items that do not appear as separate fields on the online checklist. They are worth adopting and describing in the prevention-plan fields:

  • Officer in charge — one named officer with decision authority on the night.
  • Third-party vendor stops the sale of alcohol one hour before the event ends — a scheduled service stop, which is why the worked examples above end service at 11:30 for a midnight close.
  • Doors to residential living will be locked/secured during the event — securing private residential areas of a facility against access. This is about keeping people out of bedrooms and living quarters; it never means impeding an exit path.

Scenarios

▶ Scenario — The Flyer With the Wrong Message

A brother designs a flyer for the chapter's spring social. The background is a stylized image of stacked liquor bottles and spilled pills; the tagline reads "GET FADED WITH US"; the venue name is smaller than the phrase "OPEN BAR ALL NIGHT"; and the chapter's crest sits in the corner. The submitted checklist describes a controlled BYOB event with per-type quantity limits and a centralized distribution center.

How many problems are there, and what does the chapter do?

Five, and they compound.

1. Illegal-drug imagery. Pills used as party promotion is unacceptable material on its face, and it sits next to the Fraternity's crest.

2. Glorifying intoxication. "Get faded with us" promotes intoxication as the event's purpose.

3. Alcohol as the event's central identity. The design makes drinking the point, which is inconsistent with the controlled event the chapter described.

4. A direct contradiction of the submission. "Open bar all night" describes an arrangement the checklist does not contain — and one that would be prohibited as described, since a chapter-funded open bar is not a per-drink sale by a licensed vendor. A reviewer comparing the flyer to the form sees the conflict instantly, and this alone gets the packet returned.

5. Organizational representation. Apply the practical test: a member of the public seeing only this flyer would conclude that a Kappa Alpha Psi chapter is hosting a drug-and-alcohol party. That is the last item on the unacceptable list.

What the chapter does: the flyer is not used. Not revised at the margins — replaced. The design starts from what the event actually is: a social with a program, at a named venue, on a date, presented by the chapter. If it has already been posted, it comes down, and the chapter should assume a reviewer may have seen it and address it directly in the submission rather than hoping otherwise.

The process fix: flyer review by two people who did not design it, using the Module 11 checklist, before anything is posted. The designer is never the reviewer.

▶ Scenario — The Boxes Nobody Staffed

A chapter's submission checks Public Police, Private Police, Security Provided by venue, Alumni Chaperone, University Staff Chaperone, Members Monitors, and Officers Monitors. On the night, there are two venue security officers, no police, no chaperones, and four brothers who were told at 6:50 PM that they were monitors.

What went wrong, and what is the exposure?

The chapter checked boxes that described an aspiration rather than a plan. Seven categories were represented; one was staffed.

The immediate operational problem: four brothers told at 6:50 that they are monitors have no zones, no shifts, no briefing, and no idea who the officer in charge is. By 10 PM they will be socializing, because nobody gave them a job. The event is effectively running on two venue officers who were never briefed on the guest list.

The documentation problem is worse. The chapter signed a form representing that these controls would be implemented. If an incident occurs and the chapter is asked to produce its monitor plan, its chaperone list, and its police arrangement, there is nothing — and the gap between what was represented and what existed is now part of the record.

What should have happened: check only what will be implemented. Two venue security officers, four named monitors with zones and shifts, and one officer in charge is a legitimate plan for many events, and it would have been honestly described in three sentences. A modest plan that is real is worth more than an impressive plan that is not — and it is what the source actually asks for: "check the areas that the chapter will implement during the event."

Knowledge Check

Module 9 · Question 1

The field "No tables or paraphernalia" means:

✓ Correct answer: B. The source completes the field as "No tables or paraphernalia will be used for drinking games." The prohibited thing is the drinking game and its equipment — beer pong, flip cup, funnels, shot skis. Banquet rounds, check-in tables, awards tables, and buffet tables are all fine. This is the clearest example on the entire form of why a truncated label must never be acted on alone.
Module 9 · Question 2

A chapter checks "Only one entrance to the event." Which implementation is correct?

✓ Correct answer: C. Control entry by staffing, never by obstructing egress. A, B, and D all impede an exit path and are unacceptable under any circumstances — D is not saved by having someone hold a key, because in an emergency there is no time to find him. The related source item about securing doors to residential living is about keeping people out of bedrooms and living quarters, not about restricting exit.
Module 9 · Question 3

Which prevention statement best satisfies the WHO/WHAT/WHERE/WHEN/HOW standard?

✓ Correct answer: A. It names who (two assigned monitors), what (identify legal-age attendees, redeem one drink at a time), where (the centralized distribution station), when (7:00 PM to close, overlapping shifts), and how (dated event-specific wristbands after ID verification, personalized punch cards). B, C, and D are intentions. A reviewer cannot evaluate an intention, and neither can a monitor at 11 PM.
Module 9 · Question 4

A monitor sees an attendee take something from his pocket that appears to be an illegal substance. What should the monitor do?

✓ Correct answer: D. Observe, report, escalate. Members do not search, seize, or physically confront — A, B, and C each put a brother in physical and legal jeopardy and are not chapter functions. And if anyone appears medically compromised, 911 comes before everything else; care for the person is the first priority, not the removal.

Additional Insured Request

A venue asks to be added to the Fraternity's policy. This is the opposite direction from Module 6 — and a request is not an approval.

⏱ 25 min💳 4 fields
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) define additional insured and distinguish it from certificate holder and named insured; (2) explain why a venue requests it; (3) recognize that a request is not an approval; (4) capture the exact legal entity name and address; (5) route the resulting certificate to the right recipient.

The Governing Language

Kappa Source — Additional Insured Request"If there is a request for an additional insured, review of event procedures and approval of your headquarters office is required. Holmes Murphy Fraternal Practice will provide information and request approval on your behalf. In all cases, issuance of additional insured protection is at the full discretion of the underwriter. Submission of a request does not automatically grant the requested additional insured protection."

Three things are established in those four sentences, and every one of them surprises somebody:

  1. Headquarters review and approval is required. The chapter cannot grant additional-insured status.
  2. Holmes Murphy makes the request on the Fraternity's behalf. The chapter does not deal directly with the carrier.
  3. Issuance is at the full discretion of the underwriter, and submitting a request does not automatically grant it.
Never Tell a Venue It Is Covered

The most damaging thing a brother can do in this section is tell a venue "you're added" before an endorsement has actually been issued. The venue then relies on it, the chapter signs a contract representing it, and if the request is not granted the chapter has made a promise it cannot keep. Say what is true: "We have submitted the request through our national headquarters. Issuance is at the underwriter's discretion and we will forward the certificate as soon as it is issued."

Direction Matters — Do Not Confuse the Two Flows

 Module 6 — Third PartyModule 10 — Additional Insured Request
Whose policyThe vendor's or venue's policyThe Fraternity's national policy
Who is being addedKappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and the chapterThe venue, university, municipality, or other requesting entity
Who asksThe chapter asks the vendorThe venue asks the chapter
Who approvesThe vendor's insurerHeadquarters review, then the underwriter's discretion
What you collectThe vendor's certificate showing the endorsementThe exact legal entity name, address, reason, and where to send the certificate
What "done" looks likeA certificate in your packet naming both Kappa entities on a primary basisAn issued certificate delivered to the requesting entity's named contact

The Vocabulary, Once More

Named Insured
The party that owns the policy. On the Fraternity's national program, that is Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc. and its recognized entities. The policy exists for them.
Additional Insured
A party added by endorsement, receiving specified protection under someone else's policy for liability arising in connection with the named insured's operations or the specified event. It is real coverage, granted for a defined purpose and usually a defined scope.
Certificate Holder
The party the certificate was mailed to. A delivery address. No coverage. None.
Certificate of Insurance
A summary document evidencing that coverage exists as described. It is evidence of insurance, not the insurance contract itself.
Primary basis
An arrangement in which one policy is expected to respond first, before other available coverage. The Kappa source requires this when the Fraternity is added to a vendor's policy.
What Additional Insured Is Not

It is not a guarantee that a particular claim will be paid. It is not unlimited protection. It does not make the added party a partner or a member of the Fraternity. It does not make the Fraternity responsible for the venue's own conduct, and it does not make the venue responsible for the chapter's. It extends specified protection, subject to the terms, conditions, and exclusions of the policy — nothing more and nothing less.

Why Venues Request It

It is rarely personal and almost never negotiable at the front desk. Venues, universities, and municipalities require additional-insured status as standard contracting practice, because if a claim arises out of your event on their property, they want the event host's coverage to respond rather than their own. Most of the time the requirement is buried in a standard clause the sales contact has never read closely.

Where you will encounter it: hotel and conference-center banquet agreements; university facility-use agreements; city and county park or recreation-center permits; church and community-hall use agreements; and equipment or tent rental contracts.

Find It Before You Sign

Search the contract for "additional insured," "insurance," and "certificate" before signing. Discovering the requirement after execution means the chapter has already promised something it does not control and cannot guarantee. Discovering it before means the chapter can start the request early, or — if it cannot be met — choose a different venue while it still has a choice.

The Fields

Additional insured's to be added:
System FieldAdditional insured's to be added:
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Name of Entity to be added to the national policy: ______"

What it means. The exact legal entity requesting additional-insured protection.

Why it matters. The insurer must know precisely which legal entity is being asked for. An endorsement naming the wrong entity protects nobody and satisfies no contract. Hotels, universities, and municipalities routinely operate under legal names that differ from their trade names — the "Grandview Hotel" may be owned by "GVH Lewisville Operating LLC," and a contract requiring the latter is not satisfied by an endorsement naming the former.

How to complete it.

  1. Find the additional-insured clause in the contract and copy the entity name from it verbatim. Do not retype it from memory and do not abbreviate.
  2. If the contract names more than one entity — a common pattern is "Owner, Manager, and their affiliates" — capture all of them, and use the extended field for the full list.
  3. Confirm with the venue contact in writing that the name you have is the one they require.
  4. Match it against the venue's own certificate of insurance if you have one; the named insured there is usually the correct legal entity.
  5. Reproduce it exactly, including "Inc.," "LLC," "L.P.," "d/b/a," commas, and ampersands.
Acceptable

Exact legal entity name copied from the contract requiring additional-insured status — for example: "GVH Lewisville Operating, LLC d/b/a Grandview Hotel & Conference Center."

Not Acceptable

"Hotel."

Example. The banquet agreement's insurance clause reads: "Licensee shall name GVH Lewisville Operating, LLC, its owners, managers, and affiliates as additional insureds." The Keeper of Records copies that string exactly into this field and puts the full clause into the extended field below.

Common kickback reasons. Trade name instead of legal name; abbreviated name; only one of several required entities named; the name here not matching the name in the contract attached to the same packet.

Documentation to have ready. The contract page containing the additional-insured clause; written confirmation from the venue of the exact entity name.

Red Flag

A venue contact who says "just put the hotel name, it's fine." He is not the person whose contract clause has to be satisfied, and he will not be the one explaining the mismatch later. Get it in writing from someone who can confirm it.

Additional insured's to be added Long:
System FieldAdditional insured's to be added Long:
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Address of Entity to be added to the national policy: ______"

Verify Before Submission · "Long" is a platform field-type artifact

What it means. The extended field associated with the additional-insured information. The word "Long" is a database field-type label, not a Kappa term. The underlying source form asks for the address of the entity to be added, and this field is the natural place for it along with the full clause and any additional entities.

Why it matters. Complete legal and entity information is needed to process the request. An address disambiguates entities with similar names, and it is what appears on the endorsement.

How to complete it. Include four things:

  1. The full mailing address of the entity to be added, as stated in the contract.
  2. Every additional entity the clause requires, if there is more than one.
  3. The exact contractual language, quoted, so headquarters can see precisely what is being required.
  4. A pointer to where in the contract it appears — section and page.
Acceptable

"GVH Lewisville Operating, LLC d/b/a Grandview Hotel & Conference Center, 2900 Corporate Drive, Lewisville, TX 75057. Contract Section 11(b), page 4, requires: 'Licensee shall name GVH Lewisville Operating, LLC, its owners, managers, and affiliates as additional insureds on a primary and non-contributory basis for the term of this Agreement.' Contract page attached."

Not Acceptable

"Lewisville, TX." / Blank. / "See contract" with no contract attached and no clause quoted.

Common kickback reasons. Address omitted; contract language not quoted; multiple required entities reduced to one.

Reason for adding additional insured:
System FieldReason for adding additional insured:

Verify Before Submission · this specific wording is not explained in the source manual

An honest note. The online form asks for a reason. The 2020–2021 manual's Additional Insured Request block asks for entity name, address, event name, dates, times, and the contact for sending the certificate — it does not contain a "reason" line. This course therefore explains the field's evident practical purpose without representing the explanation as quoted source language.

What it means. Why this entity needs additional-insured status — almost always a contractual or venue requirement.

Why it matters. The source makes clear that review of event procedures and headquarters approval is required, and that Holmes Murphy requests approval on the Fraternity's behalf. A reviewer and an underwriter both benefit from knowing whether the request arises from a contract clause, a permit condition, or something else — and whether the scope being requested is ordinary.

How to complete it. State the source of the requirement, the document and section it appears in, and the scope requested. One or two specific sentences beat a paragraph of generality.

Acceptable

"Required by Section 11(b) of the executed venue agreement as a condition of use of the Magnolia Ballroom for the April 18, 2026 Annual Scholarship Social. The clause requires additional-insured status on a primary and non-contributory basis for the term of the agreement. Contract page attached."

Acceptable

"Required by City of Denton Parks and Recreation permit #PR-26-1188, condition 7, which requires the permit holder to name the City of Denton as an additional insured for the duration of the permitted use."

Not Acceptable

"They asked." / "Venue requirement." / "Standard." / Blank.

Name/email/phone number of where to send:
System FieldName/email/phone number of where to send:
Source Meaning — Kappa Source"Contact Name and Email of where to send certificate: ______"

What it means. The person who should receive the resulting certificate of insurance if one is issued.

Why it matters. A certificate that is issued but never reaches the venue's insurance or contracts desk has not satisfied the contract. The chapter will then get a call two days before the event saying the venue has no certificate on file — which is a preventable emergency.

How to complete it.

  1. Ask the venue who should receive it. Do not assume it is your sales contact — large venues route certificates to a risk, legal, or contracts department.
  2. Capture the person's name, title, email, and direct phone.
  3. Ask whether the certificate must also be uploaded to a vendor portal, and note that.
  4. Ask whether there is a deadline in the contract for delivering it.
  5. Once the certificate is issued, send it, then confirm receipt in writing and keep that confirmation with the packet.
Acceptable

"Priya Raman, Risk & Contracts Administrator, GVH Lewisville Operating LLC, praman@grandviewhotel.example, (972) 555-0142 direct. Certificate must be on file 14 days before the event per Section 11(d). Sales contact Dana Whitfield to be copied."

Not Acceptable

"The hotel." / An email address with no name. / The chapter's own email address. / A sales contact who does not handle certificates.

Common kickback reasons. Incomplete contact information; no email; the chapter's own contact listed as the recipient.

Practical Tip

Ask for the certificate recipient at the same time you ask for the fire-code capacity and the venue's own certificate of insurance. One email, three answers, three weeks earlier than you would otherwise have needed them.

What Else the Source Asks For

The Kappa source's Additional Insured Request block also asks for the name of the event, the date of the event, and the beginning and ending times. Even where the online form does not repeat these fields here, make sure they appear in the submission and match the rest of the packet exactly. An endorsement is typically written for a specific event on a specific date; a mismatch between the event details here and the event details elsewhere in the packet is both a kickback and, if it survives review, a defective endorsement.

Timing the Request

Additional-insured requests take the longest of anything in the packet, because they travel the farthest: chapter → headquarters review → Holmes Murphy → underwriter → issuance → delivery to the venue. Start it the day you find the clause, not the week you submit. And remember what the source says — the request may not be granted. If the venue's contract makes additional-insured status a condition of use, the chapter needs to know early enough to have alternatives.

Scenario

▶ Scenario — The Hotel's Requirement

A hotel contract for the chapter's scholarship social contains this clause: "The Grand Chapter of Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. to be listed as additional insured." The Event Chair reads it, decides it is asking for something about the Fraternity, and moves on. Three days before the event the hotel's contracts desk emails: "We have no certificate on file. Access to the ballroom cannot be released without it."

What did the Event Chair miss, what information should have been collected, and where does it belong?

What he missed. He read the clause as boilerplate about the Fraternity rather than as an obligation the chapter had to act on. It is an obligation: the chapter is contractually required to produce evidence that an entity has been named as additional insured. The clause as drafted is also worth a second look — it names "The Grand Chapter of Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc.," which is a Kappa entity rather than the hotel. That is either an unusual drafting choice or a template the hotel adapted badly, and the chapter needed to clarify which before signing, because the two readings lead to completely different actions.

Clarify first. Ask the hotel's contracts desk in writing: "Section 11(b) names the Grand Chapter of Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. Can you confirm which entity you require to be named as additional insured, and on whose policy?" Nine times out of ten the answer is that the hotel wants its own operating entity named on the event host's coverage — the ordinary direction — and the clause was written carelessly.

Then collect, once clarified. The exact legal entity name from the corrected clause; its full mailing address; the reason, quoting the section and page; and the certificate recipient — name, title, email, and direct phone at the contracts desk, plus any portal upload requirement and the contractual deadline for delivery.

Where it belongs. Entity name in "Additional insured's to be added." Address, the full quoted clause, and any additional entities in "Additional insured's to be added Long." The contractual basis in "Reason for adding additional insured." The contracts-desk contact in "Name/email/phone number of where to send." The event name, date, and times must match the rest of the packet exactly.

And what he must not say now. He cannot tell the hotel it is covered. Headquarters review and approval is required, Holmes Murphy makes the request, and issuance is at the underwriter's full discretion — submitting a request does not automatically grant the protection. With three days left, the honest message is that the request is being submitted, plus a direct conversation with the chapter's leadership about whether the event can proceed if the certificate does not arrive in time.

The lesson. Search every contract for "additional insured" before signing. This clause was visible on day one and became an emergency on day eighty-eight.

Knowledge Check

Module 10 · Question 1

A chapter submits an additional-insured request for a venue. The venue asks whether it is covered. The correct response is:

✓ Correct answer: B. The source states that issuance is at the full discretion of the underwriter and that submitting a request does not automatically grant the protection. A and D assert coverage that may not exist and that the venue will rely on. C is wrong twice over — the chapter does not approve additional insureds; headquarters review and the underwriter do.
Module 10 · Question 2

Which entry for "Additional insured's to be added" is acceptable?

✓ Correct answer: A. An endorsement names a legal entity, and only the exact name satisfies the contract. B is uselessly vague. C fails whenever the operating entity differs from the trade name, which is common in hospitality. D names a person, not an entity — individuals are not what a venue's insurance clause requires.
Module 10 · Question 3

Which statement correctly distinguishes the two additional-insured flows?

✓ Correct answer: C. Same vocabulary, opposite direction. In Module 6 the chapter asks the vendor's insurer to protect Kappa; in Module 10 an outside entity asks Kappa's insurer to protect it, which requires headquarters review and is at the underwriter's discretion. Chapters mix these up constantly, and the mix-up usually surfaces as a certificate that names the wrong party on the wrong policy.

Event Flyer

The flyer is the only part of your event most people will ever see. It is also the fastest way for a reviewer to discover that your submission does not describe the event you are actually holding.

⏱ 25 min🖼 2 fields
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) explain why the flyer is a submission document; (2) review thirteen specific elements of a flyer against the checklist; (3) recognize acceptable, questionable, and unacceptable flyers; (4) build a flyer review process that catches problems before anything is posted.

The Flyer Is Not Decoration

Kappa Source — Step 4: Submit Documents"If applicable, submit the following with a completed Event Notification Form. • All contracts • Any event marketing/flyer • Certificate of Insurance for co-sponsored events with organizations • Certificate of Insurance for all Third-Party Vendors • Certificate of Insurance for all Promotion Company/Promoter"

"Any event marketing/flyer" sits on the required-attachment list alongside contracts and certificates of insurance. It is a submission document, and it does something none of the others do: it documents how the event is represented publicly.

That gives it two functions in the review. First, it is the reviewer's cross-check — the fastest way to compare what the chapter says it is doing against what the chapter is telling the world it is doing. Second, it is the organizational-image record, reviewed against the prevention item "Event theme/materials are respectful and not degrading to any person or population" from Module 9.

Why Reviewers Read the Flyer First

A reviewer processing a stack of submissions can read a flyer in four seconds. If it advertises an open bar and the form describes BYOB, if it names a co-sponsor the form does not declare, if it says "tickets at the door" while the form checks "Prohibited ticket sales at the door," or if it shows a date the form does not — the packet is returned before anyone reads page two. Most flyer kickbacks are not about taste. They are about contradiction.

The Two Fields

Event Flyer File Long:
System FieldEvent Flyer File Long:

Verify Before Submission · "File Long" is a platform field-type artifact

What it means. The system field that stores or references the event flyer or marketing document. No source defines the technical "File Long" label; it comes from the database field type.

Why it matters. The event's public advertising is part of the documentation submitted for review, and this field is where it lives or is described.

How to complete it. Identify the flyer precisely: what it is, which version, when it was or will be distributed, and through which channels. If there is more than one piece of marketing — a print flyer, a square social graphic, a story graphic, an email header — say so, because all of them are event marketing and all of them represent the organization.

Acceptable

"Final flyer, version 3, dated 3/14/2026 — the version being distributed. Formats: 8.5x11 print PDF, 1080x1080 social graphic, and 1080x1920 story graphic, all identical in content. Distribution: chapter social accounts, chapter email list, and printed copies at the March chapter meeting. Earlier drafts were not distributed."

Not Acceptable

"Flyer." / A draft uploaded while a different version is already circulating. / One format submitted while three are in use. / Blank when marketing exists.

Red Flag

Submitting a "clean" version while a different version is what people are actually seeing. Every version that goes out is event marketing. If two versions differ in any material way — time, venue, alcohol references, co-sponsors, imagery — submit both and explain, or stop distributing the one you did not submit.

Upload Flyer Of The Event
System FieldUpload Flyer Of The Event
Source Meaning — Kappa SourceRequired attachment: "Any event marketing/flyer"

What it means. Upload the actual event flyer or other marketing material.

Why it matters. This allows the event being advertised publicly to be compared with the event submitted for review. That comparison is the point — and it is why the version you upload must be the version you are distributing.

How to complete it.

  1. Upload the final version, in a readable format, at a resolution where the fine print can actually be read.
  2. Upload every distributed variant if they differ.
  3. Name the file usefully: "2026-04-18 Scholarship Social — Final Flyer v3.pdf."
  4. Run the thirteen-question review below before uploading.
  5. If the flyer is not yet finalized, say so and state when it will be submitted — do not upload a placeholder and forget it.
Acceptable

A legible, final, distributed flyer, uploaded with a descriptive filename, matching the submitted event in every detail.

Not Acceptable

A phone photograph of a flyer on a wall. / A low-resolution screenshot where the details are unreadable. / A draft. / Nothing uploaded when a flyer exists and is already circulating.

Common kickback reasons. Flyer missing entirely; flyer contradicts the application; flyer contains imagery inconsistent with the event or with organizational standards; unreadable file; a version different from the one being distributed.

Myth vs. Fact

Myth: "If a flyer is already posted, we can upload it later."
Fact: Event promotion should align with the event being submitted and approved. A flyer that is already circulating has already made representations to the public on behalf of the chapter and the Fraternity. Uploading it late does not undo what it said — and if it says something the checklist does not, the chapter now has a public contradiction to explain rather than a private one to fix.

What to Review on a Flyer

Read the flyer against the submitted checklist, element by element. These are the fourteen places where flyers and forms diverge.

ElementWhat to checkCommon failure
Event nameIdentical to the name on the checklist"Annual Scholarship Social" on the form, "Kappa Klassic" on the flyer
Event dateIdentical, including the yearA date changed after the form was submitted
Event timeStart and end match the submissionFlyer says "til" or "late" while the form says 8:00 PM–midnight
LocationVenue name and address match"Location TBA" or "DM for address" — both of which undercut controlled attendance
SponsorThe chapter is identified accuratelyChapter or Fraternity name misstated or abbreviated in a way that misrepresents
Co-sponsorEvery organization shown is declared on the formA logo on the flyer that appears nowhere in the submission
Logo usageMarks used are authorized and reproduced accuratelyAltered crest; unauthorized third-party logos; a sponsor logo used without permission
Alcohol referencesConsistent with the alcohol model on the form"Open bar" / "drinks on us" / "BYOB, bring what you want" against a controlled model
EntertainmentPerformers shown match the vendors declaredA headline artist the form never mentions
TicketingMatches the attendance system and door-sales answer"Tickets at the door" against "Prohibited ticket sales at the door"
ImagesMeet the organizational-image standard in Module 9Drug imagery, glorified intoxication, drinking games, excessive sexualized imagery
Dress / themeConsistent with the event describedA theme that reads as degrading, or one that contradicts a formal event
Public languageTone consistent with an event bearing the Fraternity's nameLanguage that promotes intoxication or demeans a population
Contact informationA real, monitored contact for questions and registrationNo contact at all, or a personal number no one answers

Flyer Pre-Submission Review

Run these thirteen questions before the flyer is posted and again before the packet is submitted. Two people who did not design the flyer should run them.

  1. Does the flyer match the event name submitted?Word for word, not approximately.
  2. Does the date match?Including the year, and including any date change made after the form was drafted.
  3. Does the venue match?Name and address. "TBA" is not a venue.
  4. Are co-sponsors accurately identified?Every organization on the flyer must be declared on the form, and every declared co-sponsor should be represented accurately.
  5. Does the flyer imply alcohol arrangements different from the submitted checklist?Look for "open bar," "drinks included," "hosted bar," "free drinks," "bottomless," and any drink specials. Also look for what is implied by imagery.
  6. Does imagery accurately represent the organization and the approved event?Apply the practical test: would a member of the public seeing only this flyer understand the event the way it was submitted?
  7. Are logos authorized?The Fraternity's marks, the chapter's marks, sponsor marks, venue marks — each used with authorization and reproduced accurately.
  8. Does any image depict illegal drugs?Including stylized or "artistic" depictions — pills, powder, needles, leaves used as party decoration.
  9. Does any image depict drinking games?Pong tables, funnels, shot skis, cups arranged in a triangle.
  10. Does any image reasonably appear obscene?Apply the standard as an outside viewer would, not as the designer intended it.
