  11. Does any image depict hazing, violence, or conduct contrary to policy?Including imagery that reads as line formations, forced activity, or intimidation.
  12. Could the flyer reasonably cause the public to misunderstand the organization's involvement?Does it suggest the Fraternity endorses something it does not? Does it suggest a sponsorship that does not exist?
  13. Is this the final version actually being distributed?Not the clean version. The real one, in every format it is going out in.
The Two-Reviewer Rule

Training Guidance

The person who designed the flyer should never be its only reviewer. He knows what he meant, which makes him the least able to see how it reads to someone who does not. Assign two reviewers who did not touch the design — ideally the Chapter Risk Manager and one officer — and give them these thirteen questions and the submitted checklist side by side.

Three Flyers

Training Guidance · illustrative examples

Acceptable

Acceptable Flyer

What it shows. Chapter crest at the top, used as authorized. Headline: "Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter — Annual Scholarship Social." Beneath it: "Saturday, April 18, 2026 · 8:00 PM – 12:00 AM · Grandview Hotel & Conference Center, Magnolia Ballroom, 2900 Corporate Drive, Lewisville TX." A photograph of last year's scholarship recipients receiving awards. "Semi-formal attire." "Advance registration required — register by April 11 at [link]. No tickets sold at the door." "Proceeds benefit the chapter's scholarship fund." Contact: "Questions: events@dlakappa.example."

Why it works. Every reviewable element matches the submission. The name, date, time, and venue are exact. The imagery reflects the actual purpose of the event and presents the organization with dignity. Registration and the no-door-sales rule are stated, which reinforces the attendance controls rather than undermining them. Alcohol is not mentioned at all — which is fine, because the flyer is not required to describe the bar, only to avoid contradicting it. There is a monitored contact. A stranger reading only this flyer would understand exactly the event the checklist describes.

Questionable

Questionable Flyer

What it shows. Strong design, chapter crest present. Headline "SPRING AFFAIR." Date and time read "Sat April 18 · 9PM – til." Location reads "Lewisville — address released to registered guests." Three organizational logos across the bottom, one of which is a sorority chapter and one a local business. Small text at the bottom: "21+ · Cash bar · Limited tickets available at the door."

What has to be corrected before submission.

  • "9PM – til" does not match a submitted end time. State the actual end time.
  • Event name mismatch. If the form says "Annual Scholarship Social" and the flyer says "Spring Affair," align them or explain the relationship.
  • Withheld address. Releasing the address only to registered guests can be a legitimate attendance control, but the flyer must not read as though the venue is a secret. Name the venue, or state clearly that the event is at a Lewisville hotel with the address provided on registration — and make sure the form's venue block is complete.
  • Three logos. Every organization shown must be declared. If the sorority chapter is planning or working the event, it is a co-sponsor and needs a certificate of insurance. If the business is a sponsor, its involvement should be accurately characterized and its logo used with permission.
  • "Tickets at the door" directly contradicts the prevention item "Prohibited ticket sales at the door" and, for a fundraiser, the requirement that ticket sales occur prior to the event. Remove it.
  • "Cash bar" is fine if the venue's licensed bar is the alcohol model — but the form must say so. If the form says BYOB, this line is a contradiction.

The point. Nothing here is offensive. Every problem is a mismatch, and every one of them is fixable in an afternoon — if someone reads the flyer against the form before it is posted.

Unacceptable

Unacceptable Flyer

What it shows. Background of stacked liquor bottles and scattered pills. Tagline "GET FADED WITH US." "OPEN BAR ALL NIGHT" in the largest type on the page. A photograph of a beer-pong table in the corner. Heavily sexualized stock imagery. The chapter's crest in the bottom corner. Venue and date in small print.

Why it cannot be used.

  • Illegal-drug imagery used as party promotion — unacceptable on its face, and placed next to the Fraternity's crest.
  • Glorified intoxication. "Get faded with us" makes intoxication the event's stated purpose.
  • Alcohol as the event's central identity, in the largest type on the page.
  • Drinking-game imagery, promoting exactly the rapid-consumption activity the source prohibits.
  • Excessive sexualized imagery inconsistent with the event.
  • "Open bar all night" describes an arrangement the checklist almost certainly does not contain — and a chapter-funded open bar would not be a per-drink sale by a licensed vendor.
  • Organizational representation. A member of the public seeing only this flyer would conclude that a Kappa Alpha Psi chapter is hosting a drug-and-alcohol party.

What happens. The flyer is not revised — it is replaced, starting from what the event actually is. If it has already been posted, it comes down, and the chapter addresses it directly in the submission rather than hoping it went unseen. A flyer outlives the event: it is screenshotted, reposted, and searchable for years, and it carries the Fraternity's name to people who will never meet the chapter.

Scenario

▶ Scenario — The Late Change

The packet was submitted twenty-one days out with a flyer showing an 8:00 PM start at the Grandview Hotel. Twelve days out, the hotel moves the chapter to a different ballroom and the start shifts to 8:30. A brother updates the social graphic and posts it. Nobody tells the Event Chair, and the submitted flyer still shows the old room and time.

What is the exposure, and what should happen?

The exposure has three parts. First, the flyer in the packet no longer matches the event being advertised — and the flyer is a submitted document. Second, the checklist itself now describes a room and a start time that are not the event, which means the venue block, and possibly the capacity figure, are wrong. Third, the chapter's own committee is operating on two different sets of facts, which is how monitors end up briefed for a room they are not in.

What should happen. The Event Chair notifies and resubmits with the corrected venue details, capacity for the new room confirmed in writing, corrected times, and the updated flyer attached. If the new ballroom has a different fire-code capacity, the anticipated-attendance math has to be rerun — a smaller room can turn a comfortable 265-against-300 into a problem.

The process fix. One person owns the flyer, and no version goes out without that person's approval and without the checklist being checked against it. A chapter with three people posting graphics has no version control, and version control is what this entire module is about.

Knowledge Check

Module 11 · Question 1

The submitted checklist describes a BYOB event with per-type quantity limits. The flyer says "OPEN BAR ALL NIGHT." What is the primary problem?

✓ Correct answer: C. It is a contradiction a reviewer will catch in seconds, and it is a public statement about how the chapter runs events. A chapter-funded open bar is also not one of the two lawful alcohol models. B is the mistake behind most flyer kickbacks — the flyer is a required submission document, not separate marketing. D does not help: a disclaimer under a headline that says the opposite fools nobody.
Module 11 · Question 2

A sorority chapter's logo appears on the flyer. The checklist's co-sponsor box is unchecked. What should happen?

✓ Correct answer: A. Classification follows the actual relationship, and the flyer is what prompts the question. A logo with no declared relationship is one of the most common flyer-versus-form discrepancies. D would be a false statement and would also commit the chapter to producing a certificate from an organization that does not know it has been declared. B is concealment, and screenshots exist.
Module 11 · Question 3

Which version of the flyer should be uploaded?

✓ Correct answer: D. The comparison the reviewer performs is between the submission and what the public is actually seeing, so uploading anything other than the distributed version defeats the purpose. If the print flyer, the square social graphic, and the story graphic differ in any material way, all of them are event marketing and all of them belong in the packet.

Why Event Insurance Checklists Get Returned

Almost every returned submission comes back for one of about twenty-five reasons. All of them are avoidable, and most of them are caught by one careful read.

⏱ 25 min🔄 Submission quality
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) name the common causes of returned submissions by category; (2) find contradictions in your own packet before a reviewer does; (3) run the Top 10 pre-submission checks; (4) apply the Stop Before You Submit decision test.

The Underlying Pattern

Returned submissions almost never come back because the chapter planned a bad event. They come back for one of three reasons:

Pattern 1

Incomplete

A required field is blank, a required attachment is missing, or an "Other" box is checked with nothing behind it. The reviewer cannot evaluate what is not there.

Pattern 2

Contradictory

Two parts of the packet describe different events. The flyer says one thing and the form says another; the capacity says 200 and the attendance says 310. The reviewer cannot tell which is true.

Pattern 3

Unsupported

A box is checked that no document backs. "Venue is insured" with no certificate. "Security provided by venue" with nothing in the contract. The representation exists; the basis does not.

The Root Cause Behind All Three

Submitting before planning is complete. Every one of these patterns is what it looks like when a chapter tries to describe an event that has not been fully decided. The fix is not better form-filling — it is finishing the plan first.

The Common Causes

Completeness failures

Missing required fields

The most common single cause. Fire-code capacity, anticipated attendance, contact phone numbers, and the description fields behind "Other" selections are the usual blanks.

Catch it by: reading the form top to bottom before submitting and physically checking that no field is empty. If a field genuinely does not apply, say so — "N/A — dry event" tells a reviewer you considered it; a blank tells him nothing.

Fire-code capacity omitted

The chapter never asked the venue, or asked and never wrote it down.

Catch it by: requesting capacity in writing at first contact with the venue, alongside the certificate of insurance request. Never accept a marketing "accommodates up to" figure as a code capacity.

Anticipated attendance omitted

Without it, the reviewer cannot assess whether the venue and the controls are adequate.

Catch it by: building the number from components — members, guests per member, registered attendees, alumni, plus staff and vendors — rather than guessing.

Venue information incomplete

A venue named but with no address, no contact, or no capacity. Or "TBD."

Catch it by: using the alumni form's structure as your standard — venue name, venue address, venue contact name, venue contact phone, venue contact email — even when the online form gives you fewer boxes.

"Other" selected without explanation

This happens on the location section, the invitation system, the age-ID method, and the check-in method. Every one of them has a description field, and every one of them gets left blank.

Catch it by: searching your own submission for every "Other" you selected and confirming each has a description a stranger could evaluate.

Flyer missing

Event marketing is a required attachment when it exists. A chapter promoting an event on social media and submitting no flyer has an incomplete packet.

Catch it by: asking "is anything about this event public yet?" If yes, that material is the flyer.

Required attachments not included

Contracts, event marketing, and certificates of insurance for co-sponsors, third-party vendors, and promoters.

Catch it by: writing the attachment list first, then attaching against it, then re-reading the list against the packet.

Documentation and insurance failures

Vendor listed without a contract

A DJ, caterer, or security company named on the form with no executed agreement attached. All contracts must be included with the form.

Catch it by: treating "we booked him" and "we have a signed contract" as different states, and tracking them separately.

Vendor contract uploaded without insurance documentation

Half a packet. The contract shows the arrangement; the certificate shows the vendor can stand behind it.

Catch it by: pairing them in your tracker — a vendor is not "done" until both documents exist.

Expired certificate of insurance

A certificate that was valid when the vendor sent it last year, or one that expires before the event.

Catch it by: reading the policy period on every certificate, every time, and comparing it to the event date.

Policy period does not cover the event date

The version of the above that catches careful chapters — the certificate is current today and expires eight days before the event.

Catch it by: asking one question of every certificate: "is this in force on the event date?"

Required insured entities missing

The certificate names the chapter but not Kappa Alpha Psi® Fraternity, Inc., or vice versa. Both are required, on a primary basis.

Catch it by: looking for both names in the Description of Operations, and for the word "primary."

Additional insured not shown

Usually because the certificate holder box was mistaken for additional-insured status. Certificate holder is a mailing designation and confers no coverage.

Catch it by: reading the Description of Operations, not the holder box.

Co-sponsor named without a certificate of insurance when required

A certificate of insurance for co-sponsored events with organizations is a required attachment.

Catch it by: requesting it the day the co-sponsorship is agreed, not the week of submission.

Additional insured requested without complete legal entity information

"Hotel" instead of the exact legal entity name, or an entity named with no address.

Catch it by: copying the entity name verbatim from the contract clause and including the address and the quoted clause.

Disclosure and classification failures

Event type unclear

The reviewer cannot tell what kind of event this is — social, fundraiser, banquet, concert, community program — which makes every other answer harder to assess.

Catch it by: stating plainly what the event is in the description fields.

Promoter relationship not disclosed

An outside party producing, promoting, or monetizing the event, described as "a volunteer" or "a friend of the chapter."

Catch it by: running the five diagnostic questions in Module 7 on every outside party involved.

Member assumes an outside vendor "handles everything"

"The hotel takes care of security." "The promoter handles the tickets." "The venue does the IDs." Each of these may be true, and none of them is documentation.

Catch it by: converting every "they handle it" into a written commitment naming who, how many, when, and where it appears in the agreement.

Alcohol and attendance failures

Alcohol present but alcohol-control questions incomplete

The alcohol model is declared, then the carding, ID method, quantity, distribution, and monitor fields are thin or blank.

Catch it by: treating the alcohol model checkbox as a commitment to complete the entire section, not as an answer by itself.

BYOB selected but no distribution or control plan

The single most common alcohol kickback. BYOB is a system the chapter operates, and the form asks how.

Catch it by: completing the quantity, distribution center, monitor count, and check-in method fields before checking the BYOB box.

Guest-list system unclear

"Invite only" or "we have a list" with no description of issuance, cap, close date, or door process.

Catch it by: describing the six characteristics of a credible system from Module 3.

Prevention boxes checked without operational details

Seven security and chaperone categories checked, no names, no hours, no plan.

Catch it by: applying the who / for which hours / doing what test to every box in Module 9.

Consistency and timing failures

Contradictory answers

Capacity 200 and anticipated attendance 310. "Prohibited ticket sales at the door" checked while the flyer advertises door sales. A dry event with a BYOB distribution plan. Numbered invitations for 150 with 400 anticipated.

Catch it by: the cross-check pass described below.

Flyer contradicts the application

Different name, date, time, venue, alcohol arrangement, co-sponsor, or ticketing than the form.

Catch it by: the thirteen-question flyer review in Module 11, run against the submitted form.

Flyer contains imagery inconsistent with the event or organizational standards

Drug imagery, glorified intoxication, drinking games, excessive sexualized imagery, unauthorized logos.

Catch it by: the two-reviewer rule — the designer never reviews his own flyer.

Submission made before planning is complete

The root cause of most of the list above. A packet submitted while decisions are still open produces blanks, contradictions, and unsupported boxes.

Catch it by: the Stop Before You Submit test below.

Submitted too late

The Kappa source requires the Event Notification Form to be submitted 21 days prior to the event. A late packet has no room to absorb a correction — and a returned late packet has none at all.

Catch it by: working backwards from day 21 using the schedule in the Orientation module.

The Cross-Check Pass

Before submitting, read the packet once looking only for contradictions. Do not read for completeness — read for pairs of statements that cannot both be true. These are the ten pairs that fail most often.

Check thisAgainst this
Anticipated attendanceFire-code capacity — including vendors and staff
Event name, date, time, venue on the formEvent name, date, time, venue on the flyer
Alcohol model on the formAny alcohol reference on the flyer
Co-sponsors declared on the formEvery logo and organization on the flyer
"Prohibited ticket sales at the door"Any ticketing statement on the flyer
Invitation system and its capAnticipated attendance
Every checked insurance boxThe certificates actually attached
Every vendor namedThe contracts actually attached
Security, chaperone, and monitor boxesThe named people and hours in your plan
Additional-insured entity nameThe entity name in the contract clause

Top 10 Pre-Submission Checks

  1. Every field is filledNo blanks. Where something truly does not apply, it says so.
  2. Every "Other" has a descriptionA description a stranger could evaluate, not a single word.
  3. Capacity and attendance are consistentAttendance plus vendors and staff is comfortably below the fire-code figure, and the figure came from the venue in writing.
  4. Every checked insurance box has a certificate behind itAnd you have personally read the named insured, policy period, limits, and additional-insured language on each one.
  5. Every vendor has a contractExecuted in the chapter name of the national Fraternity, signed and dated by both parties.
  6. The alcohol section is complete end to endModel, carding, ID method, quantity, distribution center, monitor count, monitor identity, and check-in method.
  7. Security, chaperones, and monitors have names and hoursAnd an officer in charge is identified.
  8. The flyer matches the formAll thirteen review questions, run by two people who did not design it.
  9. Contact information is completeFull names, working emails, mobile numbers for event day, physical addresses where asked.
  10. An officer other than the preparer has read the whole packetFresh eyes catch what the author's eyes skip.

Stop Before You Submit

Decision Test — Answer All Six Honestly

1. Can I support every box I checked with a document or a named person?
If no — uncheck it or get the document. Do not submit a representation you cannot back.

2. Is anything still "to be determined"?
If yes — the plan is not finished. Finish it, then submit.

3. Does the flyer say anything the form does not?
If yes — fix one of them before a reviewer finds both.

4. Would this packet make sense to someone who knows nothing about our chapter?
If no — add the detail that makes it make sense.

5. If an incident happened at this event, would this packet show that we thought it through?
This is the question that matters most. It is also the one that tells you whether the plan is real.

6. Are we submitting at least 21 days before the event?
If no — submit now, disclose the timing, and expect that a correction may not fit in the time remaining.

One More Thing

A returned submission is not a failing grade. It is a reviewer catching something before the event rather than after. The chapters that get frustrated by kickbacks are usually the ones submitting at day 21 with no margin; the chapters that barely notice them are the ones who finished the packet at day 30 and had a week to fix anything that came back.

Scenario

▶ Scenario — Find the Contradictions

A packet contains: fire-code capacity 200; anticipated guests 310; BYOB selected; "How many drinks will you allow" blank; "Where will the service distribution cent" blank; "Prohibited ticket sales at the door" checked; a flyer reading "$15 at the door, 21+, open bar"; a DJ named with no contract; and Security Provided by venue checked with nothing in the venue agreement about security.

How many separate kickback causes are present?

At least eight.

1. Attendance exceeds capacity. 310 against 200 — before counting vendors and staff. This alone stops the packet.

2. Quantity field blank at a BYOB event.

3. Distribution center field blank at a BYOB event — there is no described alcohol control at all.

4. Flyer advertises door sales while the form checks "Prohibited ticket sales at the door." Direct contradiction.

5. Flyer advertises an open bar while the form declares BYOB. Second direct contradiction — and the advertised arrangement would not be permitted as described.

6. Vendor listed with no contract. All contracts must be included with the form.

7. Security box checked with no support. "Provided by venue" with nothing in the agreement is the "venue handles it" failure.

8. The packet describes two different events. Taken together, the form describes a controlled BYOB event and the flyer describes a paid-entry open-bar party. A reviewer cannot approve either, because he cannot tell which one is real.

The diagnosis: this packet was assembled, not planned. Every one of these eight is a symptom of submitting before the decisions were made. The fix is not eight corrections to the form — it is going back to the planning meeting, deciding the alcohol model, the attendance model, and the venue for real, and then filling the form out from decisions instead of guesses.

Knowledge Check

Module 12 · Question 1

Which is the single most useful pre-submission action for catching contradictions?

✓ Correct answer: B. The flyer-versus-form comparison catches the largest share of contradictions, because those two documents describe the same event to two different audiences and drift apart whenever anything changes. D is genuinely good practice — submitting early is why kickbacks stop hurting — but it does not find the contradiction; it just gives you time to fix it once someone else does.
Module 12 · Question 2

A chapter checks "Venue is insured with a minimum" because the venue's sales manager said the hotel carries $2 million in coverage. No certificate has been received. This is an example of:

✓ Correct answer: A. The chapter must verify insurance by obtaining a certificate. A verbal assurance from a sales contact is not verification, and the checked box now states something the packet cannot support. B is close but incomplete — the problem is not just a missing attachment, it is a representation made without a basis.
Module 12 · Question 3

Which question in the Stop Before You Submit test best captures the purpose of the whole checklist?

✓ Correct answer: C. Completeness and timing matter, but they are means. The checklist's deepest purpose is to demonstrate that the chapter identified and planned for foreseeable risks before the event — and that question is the honest test of whether it did.

Complete Event Planning Walkthrough

One event, from a sentence at a chapter meeting to a submitted packet. Every checklist section, in the order a chapter actually encounters it.

⏱ 35 min📝 End-to-end🔍 3 mistakes to find
Learning Objectives

After this module you will be able to: (1) sequence an event from concept to submission; (2) see how each checklist section is answered from a real decision; (3) identify defects in a nearly complete packet.

The Event

Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter — Annual Scholarship Social
Saturday, April 18, 2026 · 8:00 PM – 12:00 AM
Grandview Hotel & Conference Center, Magnolia Ballroom, Lewisville, Texas
Approximately 250 anticipated attendees against a fire-code capacity of 350
Hotel's licensed bar · contracted DJ · outside caterer · venue-provided security · online registration · no co-sponsor at the outset

Training Guidance · illustrative worked example

Step 1 — Initial Event Concept

Day 90. At the January chapter meeting, the Vice Polemarch proposes the chapter's annual scholarship social for mid-April: a semi-formal evening honoring the year's scholarship recipients, funded by advance ticket sales, with roughly 250 attendees.

The Polemarch appoints an Event Chair and a four-brother committee, and does one thing that changes everything downstream: he prints a blank Event Insurance Checklist and hands it to the committee at that first meeting. Sections are assigned by name — venue and contracts to the Event Chair, vendors and certificates to the Keeper of Records, attendance and registration to one committee member, alcohol and monitors to the Chapter Risk Manager, flyer and promotion to another.

The committee sets a submission target of day 30, not day 21, so a returned packet still has room to be corrected.

What This Step Decides

Event type (scholarship social, semi-formal, fundraising). Approximate size. Approximate date. Who owns which section of the checklist. Everything that follows is either a decision made against these, or a discovery that forces one to change.

Step 2 — Venue Selection

Day 82. Three venues are shortlisted. The Event Chair visits each with the blank checklist in hand and asks the same eight questions:

  1. What is the fire-code capacity of this specific room, in the configuration we would use, and can you give it to me in writing?
  2. Will you contract with us as Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. — Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter, rather than with an individual?
  3. Can you provide a certificate of insurance, and does your policy include liquor liability?
  4. Does your contract require us to name anyone as an additional insured? If so, what is the exact legal entity name?
  5. What security do you provide, how many officers, for which hours, and is it in the agreement?
  6. Is your bar licensed, and will your staff check identification and refuse service to anyone who appears intoxicated?
  7. May we bring an outside caterer, and what do you require from them?
  8. Where are the entrances and the emergency exits, and can we run a single controlled admission point?

Grandview answers all eight. The Magnolia Ballroom's fire-code capacity is 350 in the banquet configuration, and the catering manager puts it on the draft banquet event order. The hotel will contract with the chapter as an entity. Its certificate is available. Its contract requires the chapter to name "GVH Lewisville Operating, LLC" as an additional insured. It provides two security officers for events over 150 guests. Its bar is licensed and staffed by its own bartenders. Outside caterers are permitted with a certificate of insurance on file.

One shortlisted venue cannot state a fire-code capacity in writing. It is eliminated on that basis alone.

Step 3 — Contract Review

Day 74. The banquet event order arrives, made out to the Event Chair personally. He emails: "Please reissue with the client as Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. — Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter, at our chapter mailing address. Our Polemarch will sign." The corrected BEO comes back the next day.

Before anyone signs, the Event Chair searches the document for three words: insurance, additional insured, and certificate. He finds Section 11(b): "Licensee shall name GVH Lewisville Operating, LLC, its owners, managers, and affiliates as additional insureds on a primary and non-contributory basis," with a certificate required on file 14 days before the event.

He also notes what the agreement says about security (two officers, 7:00 PM to midnight, written into the BEO), about the bar (cash bar, hotel-licensed, hotel staff), about the outside caterer (permitted with certificate on file), and about damage and cancellation terms.

Day 72. The Polemarch signs in representative capacity. The hotel countersigns and dates. A signed copy goes into the packet folder that day.

The Move That Saved the Event

Finding Section 11(b) on day 74 rather than day 5. The additional-insured request travels the longest road in the packet — chapter to headquarters to Holmes Murphy to underwriter to issuance to delivery — and it may not be granted at all. Sixty-nine days is enough. Five is not.

Step 4 — Vendor Collection

Day 68. The Keeper of Records builds a vendor tracker. Four vendors:

VendorRoleContractCOIAdditional insured
Grandview Hotel (GVH Lewisville Operating, LLC)Venue and licensed barExecuted BEO, day 72Requested day 68Requested day 68
Delgado Sound & Lighting LLCDJ, sound, lightingExecuted day 60Requested day 60Requested day 60
Ruby's Table Catering LLCOutside catererExecuted day 58Requested day 58Requested day 58
Grandview in-house securityTwo officers, 7:00 PM–midnightIn BEO Section 8Covered by venue COICovered by venue endorsement

Each vendor gets the same written request: a certificate showing general liability of $1,000,000 per occurrence and $2,000,000 aggregate, products/completed operations of $2,000,000, liquor liability of $300,000/$300,000 where alcohol is involved, workers compensation and employers liability, a carrier rated not less than A.M. Best A-, VII, coverage in force on April 18, 2026, and Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter named as additional insureds on a primary and non-contributory basis.

The DJ's contract includes one line the chapter added: "The chapter may direct changes to music content at any time during the event."

Step 5 — Certificate of Insurance Collection

Days 60–45. Certificates arrive and are read line by line rather than filed on sight.

The hotel's certificate is clean: named insured matches, policy period covers the date, limits meet the minimums, liquor liability present, carrier A rated, both Kappa entities named additional insured on a primary and non-contributory basis in the Description of Operations.

The DJ's first certificate names Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. in the certificate holder box and shows nothing in the Description of Operations. The Keeper of Records replies to the agent: "Certificate holder status does not meet our requirement. We need Kappa Alpha Psi Fraternity, Inc. and the Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter shown as additional insureds on a primary and non-contributory basis in the Description of Operations, for the 4/18/2026 event." A corrected certificate arrives in two days.

The caterer's certificate shows limits that meet the minimums but a policy period expiring April 1, 2026 — seventeen days before the event. The caterer's agent confirms the policy is renewing and sends the renewal certificate on day 47.

Two Defects, Both Caught

Neither of these would have been caught by filing certificates without reading them. Both would have surfaced as kickbacks — or worse, as gaps discovered after an incident.

Step 6 — Attendance Planning

Day 55. The committee builds the number rather than guessing it:

GroupCount
Chapter members and their guests80
Scholarship recipients and families45
Alumni and community attendees (registered)110
Program participants and speakers15
Anticipated attendees250
Hotel banquet and bar staff12
Caterer staff6
DJ and assistant2
Venue security officers2
Photographer1
Total planned occupancy273
Fire-code capacity350
Headroom77

Registration runs through the chapter's online registration page, configured as an invitation-limited link distributed to members and to the chapter's alumni list. Registration is capped at 300 and closes April 11, one week out. The exported list is printed for the door. Tickets are sold in advance only; the flyer will say so explicitly. Anticipating alumni who drive in unannounced, the committee sets a door stop at 330 and gives the door monitor standing authority to stop admission without further approval.

Step 7 — Alcohol Determination

Day 52. The committee considers both lawful models and chooses the licensed and insured third-party vendor model: the hotel's own licensed bar, operating as a cash bar, with hotel bartenders serving per drink.

The reasoning is recorded in the minutes: it moves the two hardest jobs — refusing service to someone underage and refusing service to someone who has had too much — from members to professionals whose license depends on getting them right. It also eliminates the entire BYOB operational load at a 250-person event.

Four things are confirmed and written into the agreement: the hotel's TABC permit number and expiration; the seven purveyor responsibilities from the Kappa source, incorporated by reference; that all sales are cash or credit to individuals, with no chapter-funded open bar and no pre-purchased drink package; and that no excess alcohol, opened or unopened, will be given, sold, or furnished to the chapter at any point, including at close.

The committee also decides, and puts in writing, that there will be no parallel BYOB — the hotel is contractually required to maintain absolute control of all alcoholic containers present, and a side supply would break that.

Per the source's prevention list, the bar stops service at 11:00 PM, one hour before the midnight close.

Step 8 — Security and Monitor Plan

Day 48. Security is the hotel's two officers, 7:00 PM to midnight, written into BEO Section 8, with the on-duty supervisor's name and mobile obtained on day 45.

Chaperones are not applicable at an alumni chapter event of this kind, and those boxes are left unchecked rather than filled for appearance.

Monitors are named, zoned, and shifted:

ZoneAssignedShiftResponsibility
Entrance / check-inTwo brothers7:30–10:00Registration list, running occupancy count, no door sales
Entrance / check-inTwo brothers9:45–closeSame; capacity confirmation before late admissions
Main floorOne brother8:00–10:15Circulate, observe, watch the bar area and DJ area
Main floorOne brother10:00–closeSame, increased attention late
Exterior / parkingOne brother8:00–closeObserve the patio exit (never obstruct), parking area, departures
Officer in chargeChapter Risk Manager7:00–closeAll final decisions; liaison with hotel security supervisor

All monitors are sober for the duration. A briefing is scheduled for 7:15 PM covering the registration list, the capacity stop, the officer in charge, the emergency exits, and the instruction that members do not physically intervene — hotel security handles removals.

Step 9 — Flyer Review

Day 40. The flyer is drafted: crest at the top, "Denton-Lewisville Alumni Chapter — Annual Scholarship Social," the full date, time, venue name and address, a photograph of last year's scholarship recipients, "Semi-formal attire," "Advance registration required — register by April 11," "No tickets sold at the door," "Proceeds benefit the chapter's scholarship fund," and a monitored contact email.

Day 38. Two reviewers who did not design it — the Chapter Risk Manager and the Keeper of Records — run the thirteen questions against the drafted checklist. Two changes result: the draft said "8PM – til," which is changed to "8:00 PM – 12:00 AM," and a stock image of champagne glasses is removed because it made alcohol more visually prominent than the scholarship purpose. Nothing else changes. The flyer posts on day 36.

Step 10 — Additional-Insured Information

Day 70 (started early) through day 42. Because Section 11(b) was found on day 74, the additional-insured request was assembled immediately:

  • Entity to be added: GVH Lewisville Operating, LLC d/b/a Grandview Hotel & Conference Center — copied verbatim from the clause.
  • Extended field: full mailing address; the additional entities named in the clause ("its owners, managers, and affiliates"); the clause quoted in full; and the contract page and section reference. Contract page attached.
  • Reason: required by Section 11(b) of the executed venue agreement as a condition of use of the Magnolia Ballroom for the April 18, 2026 event, on a primary and non-contributory basis, with certificate required on file 14 days prior.
  • Where to send: Risk & Contracts Administrator, with name, title, direct email, and direct phone — obtained by asking the hotel who actually receives certificates rather than assuming it was the sales contact.
  • Event details: event name, date, and 8:00 PM–12:00 AM times, matching every other part of the packet exactly.

The request is submitted through headquarters. The Event Chair tells the hotel: "The request has been submitted through our national headquarters. Issuance is at the underwriter's discretion and we will forward the certificate as soon as it is issued." He does not tell the hotel it is covered.

Day 33. The Event Chair completes the online checklist from the decisions already made. No field requires a guess, because every question was answered as a planning decision weeks earlier.

Step 12 — Final Review

Day 31. The Polemarch — who did not prepare the packet — reads it end to end and runs the cross-check pass. He compares anticipated attendance against capacity, the flyer against the form on all thirteen questions, every checked insurance box against the certificates attached, every vendor against its contract, and the additional-insured entity name against the contract clause. He finds one thing: the flyer's registration deadline says April 11 and the checklist says April 12. The checklist is corrected.

He then runs the Stop Before You Submit test and answers all six honestly. Nothing is "to be determined."

Why This Packet Works

Not one heroic act. Thirteen ordinary steps taken in the right order, starting with a blank checklist handed out at the first meeting. Every answer on the form came from a decision the chapter had already made, which is exactly what the checklist is designed to capture.

Now Find the Mistakes

Three Defects Introduced

Below is the same event with three specific mistakes introduced. Read the variant, identify all three, then reveal the analysis.

▶ Find the Mistakes

Variant packet, submitted day 22.

Everything above holds, except:

(a) On day 30, a local business organization offers to help. It sends four volunteers to staff the check-in table, provides the printed programs, and asks that its logo go on the flyer. The Event Chair adds the logo to the flyer, thanks them, and leaves the co-sponsor box unchecked because "they're not really planning it, they're just helping out."

(b) The hotel's banquet manager offers a discounted "beverage package" — the chapter pays a flat $2,400 in advance and guests drink at no charge until the package is exhausted. The Keeper of Exchequer accepts, and the flyer is updated to read "Hosted bar until 10 PM."

(c) The caterer's renewal certificate never arrives. On day 23 the Keeper of Records emails once more, gets no reply, and submits the packet with the original certificate attached — the one expiring April 1 — planning to forward the renewal "as soon as it comes in."

Identify all three mistakes, why each one is a problem, and what should have been done instead.

Mistake (a) — Undeclared co-sponsor. The test is involvement in planning or working the event. Four volunteers staffing the check-in table are working the event, and check-in is an attendance-control function — the chapter has handed a control function to people it does not manage and has not briefed. Providing the programs and appearing on the flyer reinforce it. The logo also creates the fastest kind of kickback: an organization visible on the flyer that appears nowhere in the submission.

What should have happened: check the co-sponsored box; name the organization with its full legal name; identify a responsible contact with email and cell; request its certificate of insurance, which is a required attachment; and put the division of responsibilities in writing. If the certificate cannot be produced before submission, reconsider whether the organization staffs the check-in table at all — it can still provide the programs and receive thanks in the program without working the door.

Mistake (b) — Chapter-funded alcohol. A $2,400 pre-paid beverage package is alcohol purchased with chapter funds, which is prohibited. It also converts the licensed-vendor model from per-drink sales to individuals — which is what makes that model lawful — into a chapter-hosted bar. The flyer change compounds it: "Hosted bar until 10 PM" is now a public advertisement of a prohibited arrangement, and it contradicts the alcohol section of the submitted form. There is a fourth problem hiding in the structure: a package that runs "until exhausted" removes per-drink accountability and rewards rapid consumption.

What should have happened: decline the package. The bar stays a cash bar with all sales cash or credit to individuals. If the chapter wants to give attendees something, it funds the food, the venue, or the program — never the alcohol. The flyer reverts, and if the "hosted bar" version was posted, it comes down and the chapter discloses it rather than hoping nobody saw it.

Mistake (c) — Certificate that does not cover the event date. Submitting a certificate expiring April 1 for an April 18 event is worse than submitting none, because the chapter knows and has represented otherwise by checking the insurance boxes. "Forward it when it comes in" is not a plan — it is a hope, and the vendor has already stopped responding. This is one of the named causes of returned submissions, and it would be caught on the first read.

What should have happened: escalate past the day-23 email — call the caterer's agent directly, since the agent issues the certificate and usually responds faster than the caterer. If the renewal cannot be produced, the chapter needs a different caterer or a hotel-catered menu. A vendor who will not produce a current certificate is a vendor the chapter cannot use, and the honest answer to the insurance field is no.

The pattern behind all three. Each mistake started as a favor — free help, a discount, a vendor the chapter liked. That is how good packets go wrong: not through carelessness, but through accommodation. Notice also that all three were introduced after day 30, and the packet slipped from day 30 to day 22 as a result. Late changes are where clean packets break, which is exactly why the chapter's own target was day 30 rather than day 21 — and why every late change has to be run back through the cross-check pass before submission.

Knowledge Check

Module 13 · Question 1

Why did the chapter set an internal submission target of day 30 rather than day 21?

✓ Correct answer: A. The requirement is 21 days. Submitting at day 30 builds a nine-day buffer, which is the difference between a kickback that is an inconvenience and one that is an emergency. B, C, and D are not accurate — the buffer is a chapter practice, not a rule.
Module 13 · Question 2

Total planned occupancy in the walkthrough was 273 against a capacity of 350, yet the committee set a door stop at 330. Why not 350?

✓ Correct answer: C. Counting a live crowd is imprecise, alumni arrive unannounced, and the person at the door at 11 PM should not be doing arithmetic under pressure. A pre-decided stop below the legal limit gives him a number and the authority to hold it. D is invented — there is no such tolerance, which is precisely why you build your own.
Module 13 · Question 3

Which single early action most reduced the chapter's risk of a late-stage emergency?

✓ Correct answer: B. The additional-insured request travels the longest road and may not be granted at all — and in this case the venue made a certificate a condition of releasing the ballroom. Finding the clause on day 74 turned a potential three-day emergency into a routine sixty-nine-day process. A is actually the opposite of good practice: booking quickly before asking the eight venue questions surrenders the chapter's leverage.
